+.meaning: Adds two quantities; the binary plus sign, also used as a unary sign for positive numbers.
+.usage: Typing + in math mode gives a binary operator, so TeX places a medium space on each side automatically, as in a + b. When the plus starts an expression or follows another operator or a relation, as in -(+3) or x = +1, TeX treats it as unary and drops the space. In a multline or split equation that breaks before a plus, write {}+ at the start of the continuation line to restore binary spacing. For a superscript plus, as in the ion Na^+ or the set \mathbb{R}^+, no braces are needed. Avoid \oplus unless you mean a direct sum or XOR, which is a different symbol.

-.meaning: Subtracts one quantity from another; in math mode the hyphen key becomes a true minus sign, not a hyphen.
-.usage: Inside math mode the hyphen character is converted into a proper minus sign, which is longer than a text hyphen and gets binary operator spacing in a - b. Outside math you only get a short hyphen, so a negative number in running text should still be written as $-5$ rather than typed bare. When the minus is unary, as in -x or e^{-t}, TeX removes the surrounding space automatically. Do not confuse it with \setminus, which denotes set difference A \setminus B, or with the en dash used for ranges. For a superscript minus, as in x^{-1} or Cl^-, braces are needed only when more than one character follows.

\\times.meaning: Produces the cross sign ×, used for multiplication, the vector cross product, and Cartesian products.
\\times.usage: In arithmetic, \times writes 3 \times 4 or scientific notation like 6.02 \times 10^{23}. In linear algebra and physics it is the cross product of vectors, \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}, and it also gives matrix dimensions such as an m \times n matrix. Set theory uses it for the Cartesian product A \times B. Compare \cdot, which is the usual choice for dot products and for multiplication between variables, and the asterisk *, which normally means convolution. The large operator \bigtimes is not in standard LaTeX, so for an indexed Cartesian product many authors write \prod instead.

\\div.meaning: Gives the obelus ÷, the elementary-school division sign with a dot above and below a bar.
\\div.usage: The obelus appears in arithmetic worksheets, calculator-style expressions, and some tables, as in 12 \div 4 = 3. Research mathematics almost never uses it; instead write a fraction with \frac{12}{4}, an inline slash 12/4, or a colon for ratios. In some countries the obelus is avoided entirely, and ISO 80000-2 recommends against it. Because \div is a binary operator, TeX spaces it like + and -. Do not confuse it with \mid or the slash /, which mean divides and quotient respectively in number theory and group theory, for instance G/N.

\\frac{a}{b}.meaning: Typesets a built-up fraction with numerator a over denominator b, separated by a horizontal rule.
\\frac{a}{b}.usage: \frac takes two arguments, the numerator and the denominator, so \frac{a}{b} is just a placeholder for any ratio such as \frac{dy}{dx} or \frac{n(n+1)}{2}. In inline math it shrinks to text size, which can be cramped; \dfrac forces display size and \tfrac forces text size. For simple inline ratios a slash, a/b, often reads better than a stacked fraction. Binomial coefficients use \binom{n}{k}, not \frac with no rule. Continued fractions look cleaner with \cfrac, which keeps every level at full size. When a fraction sits inside parentheses, use \left( and \right) so the brackets grow to match its height.

\\sqrt{x}.meaning: Draws a radical sign over its argument, giving the principal square root of x.
\\sqrt{x}.usage: \sqrt automatically stretches the radical to cover whatever you put in braces, so \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} gets a longer vinculum and a taller sign. It is the standard way to write the Euclidean norm, the quadratic formula, and standard deviation as \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}. Radicals over arguments with different heights can look uneven; adding \vphantom{y} or \mathstrut inside makes neighboring roots match. For an index such as a cube root, use the optional argument \sqrt[3]{x}. In inline text, x^{1/2} is sometimes clearer than a radical over a tall fraction.

\\sqrt[n]{x}.meaning: Writes the n-th root of x, with the index n placed in the crook of the radical sign.
\\sqrt[n]{x}.usage: The index goes in square brackets before the radicand, so \sqrt[3]{8} = 2 is a cube root and \sqrt[n]{x} denotes x^{1/n}. It shows up in the root test for series, \limsup \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}, and in geometric means \sqrt[n]{x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n}. TeX sometimes places the index awkwardly, especially for tall indices; \leftroot{} and \uproot{} nudge it, as in \sqrt[\leftroot{-2}\uproot{2}n]{x}. Keep the index short: for complicated exponents, writing the power x^{1/(k+1)} is easier to read than a radical.

\\sum_{i=1}^{n}.meaning: Sums a sequence of terms as the index i runs from 1 to n, using the capital-sigma large operator.
\\sum_{i=1}^{n}.usage: \sum is a large operator: in display math the limits i=1 and n sit below and above the sigma, while in inline math they move to the side as subscripts and superscripts. Add \limits to force stacked limits inline, or \nolimits for side limits in display, though stacked limits inline can disturb line spacing. For multi-line conditions under the sigma use \substack{0 \le i \le m \\ 0 < j < n}. Do not use the Greek letter \Sigma for summation; it is a smaller ordinary symbol without operator spacing. Typical uses include series, expectations, and \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.

\\prod_{i=1}^{n}.meaning: Multiplies a sequence of factors for i from 1 to n, using the capital-pi large operator.
\\prod_{i=1}^{n}.usage: \prod behaves like \sum: limits stack above and below in display style and sit to the side in inline text. It writes factorials as n! = \prod_{i=1}^{n} i, likelihoods L(\theta) = \prod_{i} p(x_i \mid \theta), and Euler products over primes. Do not substitute the Greek letter \Pi, which is a fixed-size ordinary symbol. The upside-down version \coprod denotes coproducts in category theory. When the product is a likelihood that you will take the log of, it is common to show the conversion to a sum explicitly, since \log turns \prod into \sum.

\\int_{a}^{b}.meaning: Writes a definite integral sign with lower limit a and upper limit b.
\\int_{a}^{b}.usage: Unlike \sum, the limits of \int sit to the side by default even in display math; add \limits, as in \int\limits_a^b, if your style requires them stacked. Put a thin space \, before the differential, as in \int_a^b f(x)\,dx, and some authors use an upright d via \mathrm{d}x. Multiple integrals have dedicated commands \iint and \iiint, which space the signs better than repeating \int. Contour integrals use \oint. For an evaluation bar after integration, write \Big|_a^b or \left. F(x) \right|_a^b.

\\lim_{x \\to \\infty}.meaning: Writes the limit operator with x approaching infinity placed beneath "lim".
\\lim_{x \\to \\infty}.usage: \lim is a predefined operator name, so it prints in upright roman and, in display math, places the subscript x \to \infty directly below. Inline, the subscript moves to the side to keep line spacing tidy. The arrow inside is \to, a short alias for \rightarrow. One-sided limits are written x \to 0^+ or x \downarrow 0. Related operators \limsup and \liminf work the same way. If you need a custom limit-like word with stacked subscripts, define it with \DeclareMathOperator* (the star enables limits) rather than writing \text{lim}.

\\infty.meaning: Draws the lemniscate ∞, representing an unbounded quantity or a limit that grows without bound.
\\infty.usage: You will see \infty in limits like x \to \infty, improper integrals \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx, and series bounds \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}. It also names the sup norm \|f\|_\infty, the space L^\infty, and smooth functions C^\infty. Write -\infty and +\infty with the sign attached; TeX spaces the sign correctly as unary. Remember that \infty is not a real number, so an interval containing it should be open at that end, as in [0, \infty). For the extended reals, \overline{\mathbb{R}} is a common notation.

\\approx.meaning: States that two values are approximately equal, such as a numerical estimate or a rounded constant.
\\approx.usage: Use \approx for numerical approximations like \pi \approx 3.14159 and for first-order expansions such as \sin x \approx x for small x. It is a relation, so TeX gives it thick spacing like =. Several look-alikes carry other meanings: \simeq often means asymptotically equal or isomorphic, \sim means asymptotic or distributed as, \cong denotes congruence or isomorphism, and \approxeq is a rarer variant. In finance and engineering texts, \approx usually marks rounded results; state the precision, for example to three decimal places, so readers know how loose the estimate is.

\\neq.meaning: Says two quantities are not equal; the negation of the equals sign.
\\neq.usage:
eq and its short alias 
e produce the same slashed equals sign, and either can be used. It appears in conditions like x 
eq 0, in distinctness claims i 
eq j, and in programming-oriented papers as the inequality test. Writing 
ot= also works but the slash placement can differ slightly from the dedicated glyph. In computer science writing, avoid typing != in math mode; it prints as an exclamation mark followed by an equals sign. For "not equivalent" or "not congruent", use 
ot\equiv or 
cong rather than 
eq.

\\leq.meaning: Expresses that the left side is less than or equal to the right side.
\\leq.usage: \leq has a shorter alias \le, and both print the same glyph with a single horizontal bar. Typing <= in math mode gives two separate symbols, so always use the command. Inequalities such as the triangle inequality \|x+y\| \leq \|x\|+\|y\| and bounds like 0 \leq p \leq 1 are its daily work. The slanted variant \leqslant is preferred in some European and Russian traditions, and \leqq has a double bar. In order theory and lattices, \leq names a partial order, while \preceq is used for more general preorders.

\\geq.meaning: Expresses that the left side is greater than or equal to the right side.
\\geq.usage: \geq and its alias \ge are interchangeable. Typing >= in math mode prints two separate characters, so use the command. Common contexts are lower bounds such as n \geq 1, the AM-GM inequality, and constraints in optimization like x_i \geq 0. The slanted form \geqslant is favored by some journals, and \geqq has a double bar. In order theory the reversed relation \succeq generalizes \geq. Keep a chain of inequalities pointing one direction where possible, since a \leq b \leq c reads more easily than mixing \leq and \geq.

\\implies.meaning: Writes a long double arrow for logical implication, meaning the left statement implies the right.
\\implies.usage: \implies produces \Longrightarrow surrounded by extra thick spacing, which suits implications between whole statements, as in x > 2 \implies x^2 > 4. For implication between formulas inside a logic expression, many logicians prefer the shorter \Rightarrow or \to without the wide gap. Its converse is \impliedby. In proofs, avoid stacking several \implies in a row across a page; full sentences with "hence" often read better. In propositional logic notation, p \to q is more common than p \implies q.

\\iff.meaning: Writes a long double-headed arrow for logical equivalence, read "if and only if".
\\iff.usage: \iff produces \Longleftrightarrow with extra thick spacing on both sides. It joins two statements that imply each other, as in a theorem like n \text{ is even} \iff n^2 \text{ is even}. Logic texts often prefer \leftrightarrow or \Leftrightarrow for the biconditional inside formulas, keeping \iff for statements in prose. Because of that padding, \iff looks too loose inside compact subscripts or set-builder conditions. Do not confuse it with \equiv, which means identically equal or congruent modulo n.

\\forall.meaning: Gives the universal quantifier ∀, read "for all" or "for every".
\\forall.usage: \forall begins universally quantified statements, as in the epsilon-delta definition \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists \delta > 0. TeX treats it as an ordinary symbol, so there is no automatic space after the bound variable; add \, or \ or a separator like a colon or period depending on your convention. In prose-heavy proofs, many style guides prefer writing "for all" in words rather than \forall. In typed lambda calculus and type theory it also introduces polymorphic types, for example \forall \alpha.\, \alpha \to \alpha.

\\exists.meaning: Gives the existential quantifier ∃, read "there exists" or "for some".
\\exists.usage: \exists asserts that at least one element satisfies a property, as in \exists x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = 2. Uniqueness is written \exists! (there exists exactly one), and \nexists gives the negated symbol for "there does not exist". Like \forall it is an ordinary symbol, so insert a thin space or a colon after the bound variable for readability. Quantifier order matters: \forall x\, \exists y differs from \exists y\, \forall x, so keep them in the intended sequence. In formal logic writing, parentheses around the scope, \exists x\,(P(x)), avoid ambiguity.

\\in.meaning: States membership: the element on the left belongs to the set on the right.
\\in.usage: \in is the basic set-membership relation, as in x \in \mathbb{R} or n \in \mathbb{N}, and it gets relation spacing. Its mirror \ni reads "contains as an element", and \notin negates it. Do not confuse it with \epsilon or \varepsilon, which are Greek letters that look similar but have different spacing and meaning. In sums and set-builder notation it binds the index, as in \sum_{x \in S} f(x) or \{x \in X : f(x) > 0\}. For subset relations between two sets use \subseteq, not \in.

\\notin.meaning: States non-membership: the element on the left does not belong to the given set.
\\notin.usage:
otin is a dedicated slashed version of \in, typeset as a relation, as in \sqrt{2} 
otin \mathbb{Q}. Writing 
ot\in gives a similar result, but 
otin positions the slash better and is the standard choice. Its natural companions are \in and 
i, and for negated subsets you would use 
ot\subset or 
subseteq. Typical sentences include proofs by contradiction and descriptions of complements, such as x \in A^c \iff x 
otin A. In quantifiers,  orall x 
otin S is acceptable shorthand but spelling out the domain is clearer.

\\subset.meaning: Shows that one set is contained in another; often read as proper or strict subset.
\\subset.usage: Conventions differ: some authors use \subset for any subset, others reserve it for proper subsets and use \subseteq when equality is allowed. To be unambiguous, many papers write \subseteq for "subset or equal" and \subsetneq for "proper subset", and state the convention once. The reversed relation is \supset. Typical statements include \mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} and subspace inclusions in linear algebra. The negation \not\subset works, and \nsubseteq gives a cleaner negated subset-or-equal glyph. Whichever reading you adopt, avoid switching between the two within one document.

\\cup.meaning: Forms the union of sets: all elements that belong to at least one of them.
\\cup.usage: \cup is a binary operator, as in A \cup B, and gets medium spacing on both sides. For a union over an indexed family, use the large operator \bigcup, which stacks limits in display mode: \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i. The disjoint union is often written \sqcup or \dot\cup. In probability, A \cup B corresponds to the event "A or B", giving P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B). Do not use the letter U or the logical \lor in place of set union.
\\cup.example: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)

\\cap.meaning: Forms the intersection of sets: the elements common to all of them.
\\cap.usage: \cap is a binary operator written between sets, as in A \cap B, while \bigcap is the large-operator version for families, \bigcap_{n} U_n. In probability it represents joint events, so P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B) defines independence. Its logical counterpart is \land (and), and the lattice-theory meet \wedge looks similar but is a different glyph. De Morgan laws pair it with union: (A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c. If A \cap B = \emptyset, the sets are disjoint.

\\emptyset.meaning: Denotes the empty set, the unique set that contains no elements at all.
\\emptyset.usage: \emptyset prints the default empty-set glyph, a circle with a slash. Many mathematicians prefer the rounder form \varnothing, which is distinct from a zero with a slash and is common in modern texts. Choose one and use it consistently. Typical uses are disjointness A \cap B = \emptyset and set builder results. Do not confuse it with the Scandinavian letter Ø or with \phi and \varphi. Writing \{\} for the empty set is also acceptable, but note that \{\emptyset\} is a set with one element.
\\emptyset.example: A \cap B = \emptyset \implies P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)

\\partial.meaning: Writes the curly ∂ for partial derivatives, and also boundaries of sets in topology.
\\partial.usage: \partial appears in partial derivatives such as \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} and mixed partials \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}. In topology and geometry, \partial A is the boundary of a set or manifold, used in Stokes' theorem \int_{\partial M} \omega = \int_M d\omega. For short subscripted forms, \partial_x f and \partial_t u are common in PDE papers. Do not mix it up with \delta (variation) or d (total derivative). Placing a thin space between \partial factors in the denominator improves spacing.

\\nabla.meaning: Writes the nabla ∇, the vector differential operator for gradient, divergence, and curl.
\\nabla.usage:
abla f is the gradient, 
abla \cdot \mathbf{F} the divergence, 
abla 	imes \mathbf{F} the curl, and 
abla^2 or \Delta the Laplacian. In machine learning, 
abla_	heta L(	heta) denotes the gradient of a loss with respect to parameters, as in gradient descent 	heta \leftarrow 	heta - \eta 
abla_	heta L. Differential geometers use 
abla for a connection or covariant derivative, 
abla_X Y. It is an ordinary symbol, so no extra spacing is inserted. Some authors bold it with  oldsymbol{
abla} to stress that it is a vector operator.

\\pm.meaning: Gives the plus-or-minus sign ±, for two alternatives or a tolerance around a value.
\\pm.usage: \pm appears in the quadratic formula x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} and in measurement uncertainty like 9.81 \pm 0.02. Its counterpart \mp (minus-plus) is used when signs must flip in tandem, as in \cos(a \pm b) = \cos a \cos b \mp \sin a \sin b. It is a binary operator, so TeX spaces it like +. In tables of experimental results, align numbers around the \pm sign for readability. Finance texts use it for ranges such as a return of 5\% \pm 2\%.

\\cdot.meaning: Places a centered dot, used for the dot product and for multiplication between factors.
\\cdot.usage: \cdot is a binary operator sitting at the math axis, as in \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum u_i v_i and in products like 2 \cdot 3. It also marks a placeholder argument, as in \|\cdot\| or f(\cdot). Do not use a period, which sits on the baseline, or \bullet, which is larger. For an ellipsis between multiplied factors use \cdots, which is vertically centered, versus \ldots for lists. Use \times for cross products and scientific notation, keeping \cdot for scalar and inner products.

\\alpha.meaning: Lowercase Greek alpha, a default name for angles, significance levels, learning rates, and coefficients.
\\alpha.usage: In statistics \alpha is the significance level of a test, as in \alpha = 0.05, and the shape parameter of the Beta and Gamma distributions. Physicists use it for the fine-structure constant \alpha \approx 1/137 and for alpha particles. Geometry assigns it to angles, often alongside \beta and \gamma. There is no capital \Alpha command, because capital alpha is identical to the Latin A; write A or \mathrm{A}. Take care that \alpha and the Latin a, or the proportional sign \propto, are not confused in handwriting-style fonts.

\\beta.meaning: Lowercase Greek beta, standard for regression coefficients, angles, and the second parameter of a distribution.
\\beta.usage: Regression models write y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon, and \hat{\beta} marks the estimated coefficients. In hypothesis testing \beta is the Type II error rate, so power is 1 - \beta. Physics uses it for v/c in relativity and for inverse temperature \beta = 1/(k_B T). Finance uses a stock's beta against the market. No \Beta command exists since capital beta looks like Latin B. The German sharp s, ß, is a different character written \ss and should not be substituted for \beta.

\\gamma.meaning: Lowercase Greek gamma, used for the Euler-Mascheroni constant, the Lorentz factor, and discount factors.
\\gamma.usage: \gamma is the Lorentz factor \gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} in special relativity and the Euler-Mascheroni constant \gamma \approx 0.5772 in analysis. Reinforcement learning uses it as the discount factor in \sum_t \gamma^t r_t, and physics uses it for gamma rays and photons. In geometry it often names the third angle of a triangle after \alpha and \beta, and in complex analysis \gamma is a curve or contour. Note the uppercase \Gamma, which is the gamma function, is a separate command; do not write \Gamma for the constant.

\\Gamma.meaning: Uppercase Greek Gamma, best known as the gamma function Γ(z) that extends the factorial.
\\Gamma.usage: \Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for positive integers, and \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt in general. It also writes Christoffel symbols \Gamma^k_{ij} in differential geometry, the Gamma distribution, and a typing context \Gamma \vdash e : \tau in type theory. Capital Greek letters are upright by default in LaTeX; for an italic version use \varGamma. Graph theorists sometimes use \Gamma(v) for the neighborhood of a vertex. Do not confuse it with the Latin letter L rotated or with \gamma, the lowercase constant.

\\delta.meaning: Lowercase Greek delta, used for small quantities, the Dirac delta function, and the Kronecker delta.
\\delta.usage: Analysis pairs it with epsilon in definitions of limits and continuity, as in |x - a| < \delta. The Dirac delta \delta(x) satisfies \int f(x)\delta(x - a)\,dx = f(a), and the Kronecker delta \delta_{ij} equals 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise. Calculus of variations writes \delta S for a variation, and chemistry uses \delta+ and \delta- for partial charges. It differs from \partial, which is the curly partial-derivative sign, and from the uppercase \Delta used for finite changes.

\\Delta.meaning: Uppercase Greek Delta, used for a finite change in a quantity, the Laplacian, and discriminants.
\\Delta.usage: Physics and chemistry write \Delta x for a change in position and \Delta H for enthalpy change, as in \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S. In analysis \Delta is the Laplace operator \Delta u = \nabla^2 u, and in algebra it is the discriminant \Delta = b^2 - 4ac. Geometers use it for a triangle, although \triangle is a separate, unfilled symbol better suited to that. Capital Greek letters are upright; use \varDelta for an italic version. Do not confuse \Delta with \nabla, which is the same triangle inverted.

\\epsilon.meaning: Lowercase lunate epsilon ϵ, used for small positive quantities and error terms.
\\epsilon.usage: \epsilon prints the lunate form ϵ, while \varepsilon gives the open, curly form ε that many readers associate with handwritten epsilon. Analysts use either for an arbitrarily small number in \forall \epsilon > 0, but keep one form consistent throughout a paper. Many authors reserve \epsilon for small quantities and use \varepsilon for error terms or noise. Do not confuse either with the set membership sign \in, which looks similar to ϵ but is a relation with different spacing. Physics also uses \epsilon_0 for the vacuum permittivity.

\\varepsilon.meaning: Lowercase variant epsilon ε, the open curly form often preferred for error terms and small numbers.
\\varepsilon.usage: \varepsilon renders the rounded ε shape, which looks closer to handwritten epsilon than the lunate \epsilon. Statistics writes the noise term of a regression as \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), and many analysis textbooks prefer \varepsilon in epsilon-delta proofs. Physics uses \varepsilon_0 for vacuum permittivity and \varepsilon_{ijk} for the Levi-Civita symbol. Since the two forms are easily mixed by accident, consider redefining one in your preamble so you only type a single command. Avoid using it as a stand-in for set membership \in.

\\zeta.meaning: Lowercase Greek zeta, best known for the Riemann zeta function and the damping ratio.
\\zeta.usage: The Riemann zeta function \zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s} is the signature use, with the Basel result \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6. Engineers use \zeta as the damping ratio of a second-order system, as in \ddot{x} + 2\zeta\omega_n \dot{x} + \omega_n^2 x = 0. Complex analysis uses it for a dummy complex variable, and number theory for roots of unity \zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}. There is no \Zeta command because capital zeta equals Latin Z. Its handwritten form is easily confused with \xi, so check which letter a source intends.

\\eta.meaning: Lowercase Greek eta, used for learning rates, efficiency, viscosity, and the Minkowski metric.
\\eta.usage: In machine learning \eta is the conventional learning rate in updates like w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L(w). Thermodynamics writes efficiency as \eta = W/Q_h, fluid dynamics uses it for dynamic viscosity, and relativity writes the Minkowski metric \eta_{\mu\nu}. Statistics sometimes uses it for the linear predictor \eta = X\beta of a generalized linear model. Capital eta looks like Latin H, so there is no \Eta command. Do not confuse \eta with the Latin n in sans-serif slides, where the descender may be hard to see.

\\theta.meaning: Lowercase Greek theta, the usual name for angles and for model parameters in statistics and ML.
\\theta.usage: Trigonometry and polar coordinates use \theta for angles, as in (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta). Statistics and machine learning use it for parameter vectors, with \hat{\theta} for an estimator and \theta^* for the optimum. Big-Theta complexity bounds use the uppercase \Theta, not \theta. The variant \vartheta is a script-like form occasionally used for a second angle or in physics. When writing an estimator, \hat{\theta} keeps the hat centered better than \widehat{\theta}, which is meant for wider arguments. In Bayesian notation, \theta also names the unknown quantity in the posterior p(\theta \mid x).

\\Theta.meaning: Uppercase Greek Theta, standard for tight asymptotic bounds and parameter spaces.
\\Theta.usage: Algorithm analysis writes \Theta(n \log n) for a bound that holds both above and below, alongside O and \Omega. Statistics uses \Theta for a parameter space, as in \theta \in \Theta. Physics uses it for the Heaviside step function \Theta(x) and for temperature in some texts. Capital Greek letters are upright in LaTeX; \varTheta gives an italic form if a style calls for it. Do not confuse \Theta with the empty set glyph or with the digit 0 crossed by a bar.

\\iota.meaning: Lowercase Greek iota, a dotless narrow letter used for inclusion maps and index notation.
\\iota.usage: \iota commonly names an inclusion or embedding map, as in \iota : A \hookrightarrow X, and the interior product \iota_X \omega in differential geometry. APL and some functional languages use iota for an index generator, which shows up in computer science writing. Because it resembles a dotless i, make sure it is not confused with \imath, the dotless i used under accents. There is no \Iota command; capital iota looks like Latin I. It is rare enough that a one-line definition the first time you use it helps readers.

\\kappa.meaning: Lowercase Greek kappa, used for curvature, condition numbers, and Cohen's kappa.
\\kappa.usage: Differential geometry writes the curvature of a curve as \kappa = |\gamma''(s)|, and numerical analysis uses \kappa(A) = \|A\|\|A^{-1}\| for the condition number of a matrix. Statistics has Cohen's \kappa for inter-rater agreement, and physics uses it for thermal conductivity or the dielectric constant. The variant \varkappa gives a different glyph some authors prefer. There is no \Kappa command because capital kappa is identical to Latin K. Do not swap \kappa with the Latin k, since many formulas use both.

\\lambda.meaning: Lowercase Greek lambda, used for eigenvalues, wavelengths, rates, and regularization strength.
\\lambda.usage: Linear algebra writes Av = \lambda v for an eigenvalue and eigenvector. Physics uses \lambda for wavelength in c = \lambda f, probability uses it for the rate of a Poisson or exponential distribution, and optimization uses it for Lagrange multipliers and the penalty weight in ridge or lasso, \lambda\|w\|^2. Computer science writes anonymous functions with lambda calculus, \lambda x.\, x + 1. Its uppercase \Lambda is a separate command with different uses. Learning-rate schedules and exponential smoothing also borrow \lambda for decay factors.

\\Lambda.meaning: Uppercase Greek Lambda, common for diagonal eigenvalue matrices and the cosmological constant.
\\Lambda.usage: The spectral decomposition A = Q\Lambda Q^{-1} uses \Lambda for the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. Cosmology writes the cosmological constant as \Lambda, and the standard model of cosmology is typeset \Lambda\text{CDM}. Particle physics uses it for the Lambda baryon, and lattice theory or number theory may use \Lambda for a lattice or the von Mangoldt function \Lambda(n). Capital Greek is upright in LaTeX; use \varLambda for an italic form. Do not mistake it for the logical and \wedge, which is a different, operator-spaced glyph.

\\mu.meaning: Lowercase Greek mu, standard for the mean, measures, friction coefficients, and the micro prefix.
\\mu.usage: Probability writes the mean as \mu = E[X], so a normal distribution is \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2). Measure theory uses \mu for a measure, and physics uses it for the coefficient of friction, magnetic permeability \mu_0, and reduced mass. As a unit prefix in \mu m or \mu s it renders in math italic, whereas typographic standards ask for an upright micro sign, and wrapping it in \mathrm does not change a Greek letter's shape. Optimization uses \mu for barrier parameters in interior-point methods.

\\nu.meaning: Lowercase Greek nu, used for frequency, degrees of freedom, and kinematic viscosity.
\\nu.usage:
Physics writes photon energy as E = h
u, where 
u is frequency, and fluid dynamics uses 
u for kinematic viscosity. Statistics uses 
u for degrees of freedom in Student's t distribution, and particle physics writes neutrinos as 
u_e, 
u_\mu. Relativity uses Greek indices \mu
u for tensor components, as in g_{\mu
u}. In many fonts 
u looks very similar to the Latin v, so avoid using both letters in the same formula. There is no \Nu command; capital nu is Latin N.

\\xi.meaning: Lowercase Greek xi, a squiggly letter used for random variables, dummy variables, and damping.
\\xi.usage: Probability texts often use \xi for a random variable or noise term, and analysis uses it for an intermediate point, as in the mean value theorem f(b) - f(a) = f'(\xi)(b - a). Fourier analysis writes frequency variables as \xi in \hat{f}(\xi). Some engineering texts use \xi for the damping ratio instead of \zeta. Because \xi and \zeta are hard to tell apart when handwritten, check which letter a source means. Its uppercase form \Xi is a separate command.

\\Xi.meaning: Uppercase Greek Xi, a three-bar letter used for the Xi baryon and some special functions.
\\Xi.usage: \Xi is comparatively rare in mathematics. Particle physicists use it for the Xi baryons, written \Xi^0 and \Xi^-, and it sometimes names Riemann's xi function \Xi(t) in analytic number theory. Statistical mechanics occasionally writes the grand canonical partition function as \Xi. Like other capital Greek letters in LaTeX, it is upright; \varXi gives the italic form. Do not confuse it with the equivalence sign \equiv, which has three bars of equal length and relation spacing.

\\pi.meaning: Lowercase Greek pi, the circle constant 3.14159…, also used for permutations and policies.
\\pi.usage: \pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, appearing in A = \pi r^2, e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0, and radian angles like \pi/2. Reinforcement learning uses \pi for a policy \pi(a \mid s), combinatorics uses it for a permutation, and number theory writes \pi(x) for the prime-counting function. The variant \varpi is a different glyph. When pi is a constant some style guides prefer an upright form, but standard LaTeX gives an italic \pi. Do not use the large operator \prod in place of \pi, or vice versa.

\\Pi.meaning: Uppercase Greek Pi, an ordinary letter used for projections, profit, and osmotic pressure.
\\Pi.usage: \Pi is a fixed-size letter, not the product operator; for products over an index use \prod, which scales and positions limits. As a letter, \Pi names projection maps, the profit function in economics, osmotic pressure, and the pi-calculus in computer science. Type theory writes dependent function types as \Pi_{x:A} B(x). Complexity theory uses \Pi_k for levels of the polynomial hierarchy. Capital Greek letters are upright by default, and \varPi gives an italic variant if needed.

\\rho.meaning: Lowercase Greek rho, used for density, correlation coefficients, and charge density.
\\rho.usage: Physics uses \rho for mass density, \rho = m/V, and charge density in Maxwell's equations \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = \rho/\varepsilon_0. Statistics writes Pearson correlation as \rho_{XY} and Spearman's rank correlation as \rho. Representation theory uses \rho for a representation, and quantum mechanics uses it for a density matrix. The variant \varrho has a curly tail that some authors use to keep two meanings apart. Do not confuse \rho with the Latin p, which looks similar in many fonts.

\\sigma.meaning: Lowercase Greek sigma, the standard deviation, activation functions, and the sigma-algebra.
\\sigma.usage: Statistics writes the standard deviation as \sigma and variance as \sigma^2. Machine learning uses \sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x}) for the logistic sigmoid and \sigma for a generic activation function. Measure theory talks of \sigma-algebras, physics uses \sigma for cross-sections, conductivity, and Pauli matrices \sigma_x, and linear algebra uses \sigma_i for singular values. The final-sigma variant \varsigma resembles a Latin s and is rarely used in math. Do not use the capital \Sigma for summation; that is \sum.

\\Sigma.meaning: Uppercase Greek Sigma as a letter, used mainly for covariance matrices and alphabets.
\\Sigma.usage: In statistics \Sigma denotes a covariance matrix, as in \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma), and the SVD writes A = U\Sigma V^\top. Formal language theory uses \Sigma for an alphabet and \Sigma^* for all strings over it. For summation, use \sum instead: \Sigma is an ordinary fixed-size letter that does not grow in display mode or carry limits. Complexity theory uses \Sigma_k^p for the polynomial hierarchy. Capital Greek letters are upright; \varSigma is the italic variant.

\\tau.meaning: Lowercase Greek tau, used for time constants, torque, proper time, and Kendall's rank correlation.
\\tau.usage: Physics writes torque as \boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}, a time constant in e^{-t/\tau}, and proper time \tau in relativity. Statistics has Kendall's \tau, and some authors use \tau = 2\pi as a circle constant. Number theory uses \tau(n) for the number of divisors, and modular forms use \tau for a point in the upper half-plane. Type theory often writes types as \tau and \sigma. There is no \Tau command, since capital tau equals Latin T. In some fonts \tau resembles a small t, so pick distinct names for nearby variables.

\\upsilon.meaning: Lowercase Greek upsilon, a rarely used letter that closely resembles the Latin u or v.
\\upsilon.usage: Lowercase \upsilon is uncommon in mathematics, largely because it is easily confused with u and with \nu. It appears in particle physics, for the Upsilon meson usually written in uppercase, and occasionally as a velocity or a generic index variable. If you need a new variable, a less ambiguous letter is often a better choice. When you do use it, define it explicitly. LaTeX's \upsilon is italic like other lowercase Greek letters, while the capital \Upsilon has its own command.

\\Upsilon.meaning: Uppercase Greek Upsilon, best known for the Upsilon meson in particle physics.
\\Upsilon.usage: \Upsilon denotes the bottomonium meson family, \Upsilon(1S), \Upsilon(2S), in particle physics. In mathematics it is rare, occasionally naming a function or a set when other letters are taken. Unlike capital alpha or beta, capital upsilon has a distinct shape in Computer Modern with curled arms, so it is not just a Latin Y and has its own command. Like other capital Greek letters it is upright; \varUpsilon gives the italic form. Watch its readability on slides, where it can look like a Y.

\\phi.meaning: Lowercase Greek phi, used for angles, the golden ratio, Euler's totient function, and feature maps.
\\phi.usage: \phi gives the closed, stroked form, while \varphi gives the open, loopy form; many authors choose \varphi for functions and keep \phi for angles. Number theory writes Euler's totient as \varphi(n) or \phi(n), the golden ratio is \phi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2, and spherical coordinates use \phi for an angle. Machine learning uses \phi(x) for a feature map in kernel methods, and physics uses it for scalar potentials and wavefunctions. Do not confuse \phi with \emptyset or the Scandinavian Ø.

\\Phi.meaning: Uppercase Greek Phi, used for the standard normal CDF, magnetic flux, and potentials.
\\Phi.usage: Statistics writes the standard normal cumulative distribution function as \Phi(z), with lowercase \phi(z) for the density. Physics uses \Phi_B for magnetic flux and \Phi for electric potential, while engineering uses it for flux in general. In linear algebra and optimization \Phi can name a design matrix of basis functions. Capital Greek is upright in LaTeX; \varPhi gives the italic variant. Do not confuse \Phi with \emptyset or with the circled \oslash. Its inverse \Phi^{-1} gives normal quantiles such as z_{0.975} \approx 1.96.

\\chi.meaning: Lowercase Greek chi, used for the chi-squared distribution, characteristic functions, and susceptibility.
\\chi.usage: The chi-squared statistic \chi^2 = \sum (O_i - E_i)^2/E_i is its best-known use, along with \chi^2_k for the distribution with k degrees of freedom. Set theory and probability write the indicator or characteristic function of a set as \chi_A. Topology uses \chi(M) for the Euler characteristic, graph theory uses \chi(G) for the chromatic number, and physics uses \chi for magnetic susceptibility. Note that \chi descends below the baseline, so check subscript placement. Do not confuse it with the Latin x or the \times operator.

\\psi.meaning: Lowercase Greek psi, the conventional letter for a quantum wavefunction and the digamma function.
\\psi.usage: Quantum mechanics writes wavefunctions as \psi(x, t) and states as |\psi\rangle in Dirac notation, with the Schrödinger equation i\hbar\,\partial_t \psi = \hat{H}\psi. Special functions use \psi(x) = \Gamma'(x)/\Gamma(x) for the digamma function. Fluid dynamics uses \psi for the stream function, and wavelet analysis uses \psi for a mother wavelet. For bra-ket notation, \langle \psi | \phi \rangle uses \langle and \rangle, not less-than and greater-than signs. The uppercase \Psi is a separate command. Normalization requires \int |\psi|^2\,dx = 1.

\\Psi.meaning: Uppercase Greek Psi, often a many-body wavefunction or a state in quantum mechanics.
\\Psi.usage: Physics uses \Psi for a total or many-particle wavefunction and keeps \psi for single-particle states, as in the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for \Psi(\mathbf{r}, t). Particle physics writes the J/\psi meson in lowercase, but \Psi is used for some charmonium states. In mathematics it may name a function or functor when other letters are taken. Capital Greek letters are upright; \varPsi gives an italic version. Psychology also uses the symbol as an emblem, but that use rarely appears in formulas.

\\omega.meaning: Lowercase Greek omega, used for angular frequency, sample outcomes, and the first infinite ordinal.
\\omega.usage: Physics writes angular frequency as \omega = 2\pi f, so a harmonic oscillator is x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \varphi). Probability uses \omega \in \Omega for an outcome in the sample space, and set theory uses \omega for the first infinite ordinal. Complexity theory writes little-omega \omega(n) for strict lower bounds, and differential geometry uses \omega for differential forms. Number theory has \omega(n), the number of distinct prime factors. Be careful not to confuse \omega with the Latin w in handwritten notes.

\\Omega.meaning: Uppercase Greek Omega, used for the ohm unit, sample spaces, and asymptotic lower bounds.
\\Omega.usage: As a unit, \Omega is the ohm, so a resistor is 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega; keep the number and unit separated by a thin space. Probability writes the sample space as \Omega in the triple (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P). Algorithm analysis uses \Omega(n \log n) for a lower bound, alongside O and \Theta. Analysis often writes an open domain as \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n. Capital Greek letters are upright, and \varOmega gives an italic variant. Do not confuse \Omega with the mho, an inverted omega once used for siemens.

\\ddot{o}.meaning: Puts two dots over o, giving ö as a math accent; in running text the same letter is written \"o.
\\ddot{o}.usage: \ddot is a math-mode accent, so \ddot{o} yields an italic o with two dots, suitable inside formulas but not for words. For German, Swedish, Finnish, Turkish, or Hungarian words such as Köln or Gödel, use the text accent \"{o} or type ö directly in a UTF-8 source. In mathematics and physics \ddot{x} is Newton's notation for the second time derivative, and \dddot{x} gives a third. The single-dot version \dot{x} marks a first derivative. Writing \ddot in running text causes a missing-dollar error, a common beginner mistake when copying accented names.

\\grave{o}.meaning: Places a grave accent over o, producing ò as a math accent; for words, the text command \`o is used.
\\grave{o}.usage: The grave accent marks stress or vowel quality in Italian (però, città), Catalan, and Vietnamese, and appears in French words such as où. In a document, write such words with \`{o} or by typing the accented letter, because \grave only works in math mode and sets the letter in math italic. Mathematical use of \grave is rare; occasionally an author uses it to decorate a variable when \hat, \tilde, and \bar are taken. Do not confuse the grave with the acute accent \acute, which slants the other way.

\\acute{o}.meaning: Places an acute accent over o, giving ó as a math accent; in words the text form \'o is used.
\\acute{o}.usage: The acute accent appears in Spanish (canción, José), Portuguese, Polish (ó in Kraków), Icelandic, and Hungarian. For any of those words, write \'{o} or type ó directly, since \acute{o} works only in math mode and yields an italic letter. In mathematics \acute is a rarely used decoration, sometimes used to distinguish a transformed variable. Keep in mind that a prime x' is different from an acute accent. Hungarian long ő uses the double acute \H{o}, not two acute accents.

\\hat{o}.meaning: Places a circumflex hat over o, giving ô; in math the same \hat command marks estimators and unit vectors.
\\hat{o}.usage: For French, Portuguese, or Vietnamese words such as hôtel or côte, use the text accent \^{o} or type ô directly; \hat works only in math mode. In mathematics \hat is everywhere: \hat{\theta} for an estimator, \hat{y} for a prediction, \hat{\mathbf{x}} for a unit vector, \hat{H} for a quantum operator, and \hat{f} for a Fourier transform. For accents over several characters use \widehat{AB}, which stretches. When placing a hat over i or j, use \hat{\imath} so the dot is removed.

\\tilde{o}.meaning: Puts a tilde over o, giving õ; as a math accent \tilde also decorates variables like \tilde{x}.
\\tilde{o}.usage: In Portuguese (põe, Camões) and Estonian (õ is its own letter), the text command \~{o} or a typed õ is the right choice in prose. In math mode \tilde marks a transformed, approximate, or alternative quantity, such as a normalized variable \tilde{x} or soft-O notation \tilde{O}(n). For wide arguments, \widetilde{AB} stretches across the whole expression. Do not confuse the accent with \sim, the standalone tilde relation meaning "is distributed as" or "asymptotic to". Tilde accents on capitals can sit high, so check the line spacing.

\\bar{o}.meaning: Puts a macron bar over o, giving ō; the same \bar accent denotes means and complex conjugates in math.
\\bar{o}.usage: Macrons mark long vowels in Latin dictionaries, Japanese romanization (Tōkyō, Ōsaka), Māori, and Hawaiian; in text use \={o} or type ō. In mathematics \bar{x} is a sample mean, \bar{z} a complex conjugate, and \bar{A} sometimes a closure or complement. The bar from \bar has a fixed short width, so for longer expressions use \overline{A \cup B}, which spans the whole argument. Some authors prefer \overline even for single letters so that conjugates and closures look uniform.

\\dot{o}.meaning: Places a single dot over o, giving ȯ; in math the \dot accent is Newton's notation for a time derivative.
\\dot{o}.usage: As a letter, ȯ is uncommon; it appears in some transliterations and in Livonian. For text use the accent \.{o} or a typed character, since \dot works only in math mode. In physics and engineering, \dot{x} denotes dx/dt, so velocity is \dot{\mathbf{r}} and a state-space model reads \dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} + B\mathbf{u}. Two dots, \ddot{x}, give the second derivative. Do not confuse the accent with \cdot, which is a centered multiplication dot on the math axis, not above a letter.

\\breve{o}.meaning: Places a breve, a small cup, over o, giving ŏ; for words the text accent \u{o} is used instead.
\\breve{o}.usage: The breve marks short vowels in Latin prosody and appears in the McCune-Reischauer romanization of Korean, as in Chŏng. Romanian ă and Turkish ğ use the same mark on other letters. In prose, write \u{o} or type ŏ; \breve works only in math mode and sets the letter in italic. Mathematical use is rare, usually as one more decoration for a modified variable after hats and tildes. Do not confuse the breve with the háček \check, which is pointed rather than rounded.

\\check{o}.meaning: Places a caron or háček over o, giving ǒ; in prose the same mark is written with \v{o}.
\\check{o}.usage: In Hanyu Pinyin, ǒ marks the third tone, as in wǒ, and the háček is central to Czech, Slovak, and other Slavic orthographies on letters like č and š. Use \v{o} or a typed ǒ in text; \check is the math-mode accent. Mathematicians use \check for Čech cohomology \check{H}, inverse Fourier transforms \check{f}, and dual objects. It is pointed, unlike the rounded breve \breve, and it points down, unlike the circumflex \hat. For wide arguments, \widecheck is not standard, so keep \check to single letters.

\\H{o}.meaning: Writes the Hungarian long ő with a double acute accent, a text-mode command for names like Erdős.
\\H{o}.usage: \H is a text accent, not a math accent, so use it in prose or inside \text{...}; in bare math mode it raises an error. Hungarian distinguishes ö from ő and ü from ű, so the mathematician's name is Erdős, not Erdös, and getting it right in a bibliography is a courtesy worth the extra command. In BibTeX, wrap the accent in braces, {\H{o}}, so sorting and case changes do not mangle it. Do not try to fake it with two acute accents.

\\text{o̧}.meaning: Writes o with a cedilla hook below, a rare letter that LaTeX normally produces with the text accent \c{o}.
\\text{o̧}.usage: The cedilla is familiar from ç in French and Portuguese, but on o it is unusual; it appears in Marshallese orthography and in a few transcription systems. Typing the precomposed character inside \text works in many web renderers, but a classic LaTeX build may not know the combining cedilla, so \c{o} in text is the dependable source form. Do not confuse the cedilla with the ogonek, the hook on Polish ą and ę, which turns the other way and is written \k. Neither works in math mode without \text.

\\text{ọ}.meaning: Writes o with a dot beneath it, ọ, used in Yoruba and Vietnamese and written \d{o} in LaTeX text.
\\text{ọ}.usage: Yoruba uses ọ as a separate vowel (as in Yorùbá words like ọjọ́), and Vietnamese uses the dot below as the heavy tone mark. In a LaTeX source, the text accent \d{o} gives this letter, while typing ọ directly also works with a font that has the glyph. Like other text accents, \d is invalid in bare math mode; wrap words in \text. Do not use \dot, which puts the dot above and is a math accent for derivatives. Combining tones with a dot below may need a font with precomposed glyphs.

\\underline{o}.meaning: Underlines o; in math \underline marks vectors, lower bounds, or emphasized symbols.
\\underline{o}.usage: \underline works in both text and math mode and draws a rule under its whole argument, so \underline{o} gives an underlined o. Some engineering and mechanics texts use \underline{u} for vectors instead of bold, and optimization papers write \underline{x} for a lower bound paired with \overline{x} for an upper bound. In transliterations a macron below is a separate text accent, \b{o}, which is shorter and centered under the letter. For emphasis in prose, prefer \emph over underlining, because underlines do not break across lines.

o\\!\\!-\\!\\!o.meaning: Joins two o's with a minus sign pulled tight by negative spaces, imitating a linked o-o glyph.
o\\!\\!-\\!\\!o.usage: This construct is not a standard command: each \! inserts a negative thin space, so o\!\!-\!\!o drags a math minus sign against both letters and the result looks like two linked rings. Because it is assembled in math mode, the o's are italic and the spacing depends on the font. If you need the medieval oo ligature or a similar historic letter, a font that includes that character is cleaner than this hack. For a dumbbell-like bond or link drawing, a proper diagram tool gives better control. Use it only for a quick visual effect.

\\text{œ}.meaning: Writes the lowercase œ ligature used in French words such as cœur and œuvre; in LaTeX it is \oe.
\\text{œ}.usage: French spelling requires the ligature in words like sœur, cœur, and œil, so writing oe is a spelling error, not just a typographic choice. In LaTeX source use \oe or type œ directly; \oe is a text command, so use \text inside math. English uses it in older or British spellings such as fœtus. Unlike the ff or fi ligatures, which TeX forms automatically, œ is a separate letter and is never created from typing oe. Remember a following space after \oe, as in c\oe ur, or use braces like c{\oe}ur.

\\text{Œ}.meaning: Writes the capital Œ ligature used in French, as in Œuvres complètes; in LaTeX it is \OE.
\\text{Œ}.usage: Capital Œ appears at the start of French words and in all-caps titles, so ŒUVRES rather than OEUVRES. Type the character directly or use \OE in text mode; inside math it must sit in \text. In small caps or uppercase headings, check that \MakeUppercase turns \oe into \OE, which LaTeX does correctly. Avoid confusing it with Æ, the ash, which uses an a instead of an o. Older English spellings such as Œdipus also use it.

\\text{æ}.meaning: Writes the lowercase æ, called ash, a letter of Danish, Norwegian, Icelandic, and Old English; in LaTeX it is \ae.
\\text{æ}.usage: In Danish and Norwegian, æ is a full letter of the alphabet sorted after z, so it should never be replaced with ae in names. English uses it in stylized spellings like encyclopædia and Cæsar, and the IPA symbol æ marks the vowel in cat. In LaTeX use \ae or type æ directly; it is a text command, so wrap it in \text inside math. Separate a following letter with braces or a space, as in \ae{}ble. It is distinct from œ, which pairs o and e.

\\text{Æ}.meaning: Writes the capital Æ, the uppercase ash used in Danish, Norwegian, Icelandic, and Old English.
\\text{Æ}.usage: Capital Æ starts Danish and Norwegian words and appears in Old English names like Ælfred. LaTeX provides \AE in text mode, or you can type Æ directly. In all-caps headings, LaTeX's uppercasing converts \ae to \AE automatically. Bibliographies with Scandinavian names should keep the letter as is, because sorting rules place it near the end of the alphabet. Do not confuse it with Œ, which joins O and E and belongs to French spelling. Typing it directly in a UTF-8 file is the simplest option today.

\\text{å}.meaning: Writes å, a with a ring, a letter of Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, and Finnish; in LaTeX text it is \aa.
\\text{å}.usage: In Scandinavian languages å is a separate vowel sorted at the end of the alphabet, as in på or Århus. LaTeX writes it with \aa or the general ring accent \r{a}, or you can type å directly. These are text commands, so wrap them in \text in math. Do not use the math accent \mathring{a}, which places a ring on an italic math letter and is meant for things like the interior of a set. Bibliography software should treat {\aa} as a single letter for sorting.

\\text{Å}.meaning: Writes capital Å, used in Scandinavian words and as the symbol of the ångström unit (10^{-10} m).
\\text{Å}.usage: Physicists and chemists write bond lengths and wavelengths in ångströms, as in 1.54 Å, and LaTeX's \AA command gives the right glyph in text mode. In math, write \text{\AA} or a dedicated units macro, since \AA alone is a text command. As a letter it begins Swedish and Danish place names like Åland. The separate Unicode ångström sign normalizes to this same letter, so using Å is correct. Put a thin space between number and unit, as in 1.54\,\text{Å}.

\\text{ø}.meaning: Writes ø, the slashed o of Danish, Norwegian, and Faroese; in LaTeX it is the text command \o.
\\text{ø}.usage: ø is a full vowel in Danish and Norwegian, as in København or Søren Kierkegaard, and should not be replaced by o or oe in names. Use \o or type ø directly; it is a text command, so use \text in math. It looks similar to the empty set symbols \emptyset and \varnothing, and to the diameter sign, but those are different characters with different meanings, so do not borrow ø for the empty set. Phonetic transcription also uses ø for a front rounded vowel.

\\text{Ø}.meaning: Writes capital Ø, as in Øresund, the uppercase slashed O written \O in LaTeX text.
\\text{Ø}.usage: Capital Ø begins Danish and Norwegian words such as Øresund and Østergaard. In LaTeX, use \O in text mode or type Ø directly; \O is undefined in math without \text. Because it resembles the empty set \emptyset and the diameter symbol, it is tempting to reuse it, but those are separate characters and screen readers and search engines treat them differently. Sorting in Scandinavian alphabets puts Ø after Æ and before Å in Norwegian and Danish.

\\text{ł}.meaning: Writes ł, the Polish barred l pronounced like English w; in LaTeX text it is \l.
\\text{ł}.usage: Polish uses ł in many common words and names, such as złoty, Wrocław, and Łukasiewicz, the logician behind Polish notation. In a LaTeX source write \l or type ł directly; it is a text command, so use \text in math. When a letter follows it directly, separate it with braces, as in z\l{}oty. Some fonts lack ł, which can produce a missing glyph rather than a warning, so check the PDF. It is distinct from the crossed lowercase lambda ƛ.

\\text{Ł}.meaning: Writes capital Ł, as in Łódź, the uppercase Polish barred L written \L in LaTeX.
\\text{Ł}.usage: Capital Ł starts names such as Łódź and Łukasiewicz, so bibliographies citing Polish authors need it to spell names correctly. Use \L in text mode, or type Ł directly; wrap it in \text inside math. In BibTeX keep it in braces, {\L}ukasiewicz, so case changes and sorting work. Do not confuse \L with \pounds, the pound sterling sign, which is a different symbol even though both have a crossbar on an L-like shape. Typing Ł directly in a UTF-8 source is the simplest option in modern setups.

\\imath.meaning: Gives a dotless math italic i, so accents like \hat or \vec sit on it without a clashing dot.
\\imath.usage: The main reason to use \imath is accent placement: \hat{\imath} gives the unit vector i-hat in physics without a dot under the hat, while \hat{i} keeps the dot. It also appears as \vec{\imath} in vector calculus and sometimes as a typeset complex unit. In text, the dotless i is \i, which you would use for Turkish words such as ılık or for accented i in older encodings. Do not confuse \imath with \iota, which is the Greek letter and has a different shape.

\\jmath.meaning: Gives a dotless math italic j, used under accents such as the unit vector j-hat.
\\jmath.usage: Physics and engineering write the Cartesian unit vectors as \hat{\imath}, \hat{\jmath}, \hat{k}, and \jmath removes the dot so the hat sits cleanly. Electrical engineers who use j for the imaginary unit sometimes put accents on it as well. In text mode the corresponding command is \j. There is no standard accent-free reason to use \jmath elsewhere, so keep it for accented forms. Note that \vec{\jmath} and \hat{\jmath} position the accent slightly differently, so check the spacing.

\\text{¿}.meaning: Writes ¿, the inverted question mark that opens a question in Spanish; LaTeX also accepts ?` for it.
\\text{¿}.usage: Spanish places ¿ at the start of a question and ? at the end, as in ¿Dónde está? In LaTeX, the ligature ?` (question mark followed by a backtick) produces the inverted mark in standard fonts, and \textquestiondown is the named command. Typing ¿ directly also works with UTF-8 input. It is a text character, so put it inside \text in math. Galician and Asturian use it too, while Catalan generally does not. Because ?` is a ligature, a stray backtick after a question mark can accidentally create the inverted glyph, so check sentences ending in a question that is followed by a quote.

\\text{¡}.meaning: Writes ¡, the inverted exclamation mark that opens a Spanish exclamation; LaTeX also accepts !` for it.
\\text{¡}.usage: Spanish brackets exclamations with ¡ and !, as in ¡Hola!, and the same pairing applies even mid-sentence. LaTeX produces it from the ligature !` (exclamation mark followed by a backtick) or the named command \textexclamdown, and typing ¡ in a UTF-8 file works too. In math it must go inside \text. Do not confuse it with the lowercase i or with the vertical bar |, which can look similar in some sans-serif fonts. Like the question-mark ligature, a literal !` sequence in your source will turn into ¡, which occasionally surprises authors quoting code.

\\leftarrow.meaning: Draws a short single arrow pointing left, used for assignment in algorithms and reversed maps.
\\leftarrow.usage: Pseudocode writes assignment as x \leftarrow x + 1, and \gets is a built-in alias for exactly this arrow, which reads more naturally in algorithm listings. In mathematics it sometimes shows a map written right to left, B \leftarrow A, or a limit approached from the right in older texts. Machine learning papers use it for parameter updates, \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta g. It is a relation, so TeX adds thick spacing around it. For a longer arrow use \longleftarrow, and for a labeled one the extensible \xleftarrow{text}.

\\rightarrow.meaning: Draws a short single arrow pointing right, for function signatures, limits, and reaction arrows.
\\rightarrow.usage: \rightarrow has the shorter alias \to, which is the usual choice in f : A \to B and in limits x \to 0. Use \mapsto instead when describing what happens to an element, as in x \mapsto x^2. In logic, p \rightarrow q is material implication, distinct from the double arrow \Rightarrow used between statements. Chemists write simple reactions with it, and graph theorists use it for directed edges u \rightarrow v. When you need a label above the arrow, the extensible \xrightarrow{\text{label}} grows to fit.

\\uparrow.meaning: Draws an upward arrow, used for increasing limits, spin up, gas evolution, and Knuth's notation.
\\uparrow.usage: Analysis writes x_n \uparrow x for a sequence increasing to its limit, as in the monotone convergence theorem. Physics uses it for spin up, |\uparrow\rangle, and chemistry marks a gas leaving a reaction with an up arrow after the product. Knuth's up-arrow notation for huge numbers writes 3 \uparrow\uparrow 3 for iterated exponentiation. \uparrow also works as a delimiter, so \big\uparrow or \left\uparrow ... \right. produce taller versions. The double-shafted \Uparrow is a separate symbol.

\\longleftarrow.meaning: Draws a long single left arrow, a stretched version of \leftarrow for wide or emphasized maps.
\\longleftarrow.usage: \longleftarrow is a fixed-length long arrow, about twice the length of \leftarrow, built from a minus sign and an arrowhead. It is useful when arrows point between long expressions or in inline diagrams of exact sequences written right to left. For text above the arrow, the extensible \xleftarrow{f} is better because it grows with the label. Assignment in algorithms usually uses the short \gets instead. Its double-shafted counterpart is \Longleftarrow, which underlies the implied-by symbol \impliedby.

\\longrightarrow.meaning: Draws a long single right arrow, often for convergence statements and arrows between long expressions.
\\longrightarrow.usage: Writers use \longrightarrow when a short \to looks cramped, for instance in a_n \longrightarrow L or between two long terms in a reduction. A condition under the arrow can be added with \xrightarrow[n \to \infty]{}, which stretches to the label, or with \underset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}. Chemistry uses long arrows for reactions with conditions written above. It is a fixed-length symbol, unlike the extensible arrows. The double version is \Longrightarrow, which is what \implies prints with extra spacing.

\\downarrow.meaning: Draws a downward arrow, used for decreasing limits, spin down, precipitates, and big-step reductions.
\\downarrow.usage: A sequence decreasing to its limit is written x_n \downarrow x, and one-sided limits appear as t \downarrow 0. Physicists write spin down as |\downarrow\rangle, and chemists put an arrow after a solid precipitate. In domain theory and programming language semantics, e\downarrow means a computation converges. Like \uparrow, it is a delimiter, so \Big\downarrow gives a taller arrow, handy in vertical diagram sketches. The double-shafted version is \Downarrow. Some topology and order-theory texts also write {\downarrow}x for the down-set of an element.

\\Leftarrow.meaning: Draws a short double-shafted left arrow, read "is implied by" or marking the converse half of a proof.
\\Leftarrow.usage: In proofs of an equivalence, authors label the two directions (\Rightarrow) and (\Leftarrow), the latter proving the converse. Between formulas, A \Leftarrow B means B implies A. For a long, spaced version between full statements, \impliedby gives \Longleftarrow with extra space, mirroring \implies. Be careful not to confuse \Leftarrow with \leq in quick reading, since some readers misread the shape. Logic texts more often rearrange to use a right arrow, so reserve \Leftarrow for converse directions.
\\Leftarrow.example: (\Leftarrow)\ \text{Suppose } n^2 \text{ is even. Then } n \text{ is even.}

\\Rightarrow.meaning: Draws a short double-shafted right arrow, the standard implication sign between formulas.
\\Rightarrow.usage: \Rightarrow states that one formula implies another, as in p \Rightarrow q, and labels the forward direction (\Rightarrow) in proofs of equivalence. \implies prints the longer \Longrightarrow with extra thick spacing and suits implications between complete statements. Probability writes weak convergence of distributions as X_n \Rightarrow X, and term rewriting uses it for a reduction step. Boolean algebra uses it for the conditional. Prefer it over the single arrow \to when the objects are statements rather than sets or functions.

\\Uparrow.meaning: Draws an upward double-shafted arrow, a rare symbol also usable as an extensible delimiter.
\\Uparrow.usage: \Uparrow has no single standard meaning in mathematics. It turns up occasionally in diagrams, in some logic and proof-theory texts, and in physics for a strongly polarized state. Because it is a delimiter, \Big\Uparrow and \left\Uparrow ... \right. scale it vertically. If you only need an upward direction, \uparrow is the usual choice. If you use \Uparrow for a custom relation, define it in the text the first time it appears so readers do not guess.

\\Longleftarrow.meaning: Draws a long double-shafted left arrow; with added spacing it is the "implied by" sign.
\\Longleftarrow.usage: \Longleftarrow is the glyph behind \impliedby, which adds thick spaces on each side for use between whole statements. Use \Longleftarrow directly when you want the long arrow without that padding, for example inside a tight chain in a table. In proofs it can introduce the converse direction, (\Longleftarrow). Its right-pointing twin \Longrightarrow underlies \implies, and the two-headed \Longleftrightarrow underlies \iff. Avoid mixing short and long forms in the same proof. Converse arrows read best when the stronger hypothesis is on the right.

\\Longrightarrow.meaning: Draws a long double-shafted right arrow; padded with spaces it becomes the \implies sign.
\\Longrightarrow.usage: \Longrightarrow is the raw glyph that \implies uses, without the extra thick spacing. Choose \Longrightarrow when you need implication inside a cramped space, such as a subscript, a matrix cell, or a tight table, and \implies between full clauses in display math. It is also used for multi-step reductions in rewriting systems and for convergence in some probability texts. The short version \Rightarrow is better between short formulas. Write the converse with \Longleftarrow. In a sequence of displayed steps, align the arrows with the align environment so each step starts in the same column.
\\Longrightarrow.example: a \mid b \text{ and } b \mid c \Longrightarrow a \mid c

\\Downarrow.meaning: Draws a downward double-shafted arrow, used for big-step evaluation in programming language semantics.
\\Downarrow.usage: Operational semantics writes e \Downarrow v to mean expression e evaluates to value v in big-step style, the main technical use of this symbol. In diagrams and logic proofs it can mark a vertical inference step. Like the other vertical arrows, \Downarrow is a delimiter, so \Big\Downarrow makes a taller version. Do not confuse it with \downarrow, which in the same semantics may mean termination. Define your convention when introducing the judgment. Small-step semantics, by contrast, uses \to or \longrightarrow for single reduction steps, and \to^* for their reflexive transitive closure.

\\leftrightarrow.meaning: Draws a short two-headed arrow, for correspondences, the biconditional, and resonance structures.
\\leftrightarrow.usage: Logic uses p \leftrightarrow q for the biconditional connective inside formulas, while \Leftrightarrow and \iff are more common between whole statements. In combinatorics it describes a bijective correspondence between objects, and chemistry uses it between resonance structures, not for equilibrium, which uses \rightleftharpoons. Graph theory may use it for undirected or bidirectional edges. It is a relation and gets thick spacing. For a longer version use \longleftrightarrow. In truth-table discussions it is equivalent to XNOR, true exactly when both sides agree.

\\longleftrightarrow.meaning: Draws a long two-headed single arrow, a stretched \leftrightarrow for correspondences between long expressions.
\\longleftrightarrow.usage: \longleftrightarrow suits a correspondence between two lengthy objects, for example a bijection between subsets and binary strings, where the short arrow looks lost. It is a fixed-length symbol, so labels need \overset or a stacked construction. Note that \iff is built from the double-shafted \Longleftrightarrow, not from this single-shaft version, so do not use \longleftrightarrow for logical equivalence in proofs. Physics uses it for a duality between two theories. The extra length also helps when the arrow carries text stacked above it.

\\updownarrow.meaning: Draws a vertical two-headed arrow, mostly used as a scalable delimiter or in diagrams.
\\updownarrow.usage: \updownarrow points both up and down, making it handy in vertical diagrams to show a two-way relation between rows. Being a delimiter, it can be enlarged with \big, \Big, or \left and \right. In physics it occasionally indicates a superposition of spin states or a vertical oscillation. Its double-shafted variant is \Updownarrow. If you are drawing a full commutative diagram, a dedicated diagram environment will align vertical arrows better than placing \updownarrow by hand. It is rarely needed in modern papers but useful in lecture notes.

\\Leftrightarrow.meaning: Draws a short double-shafted two-headed arrow for logical equivalence between formulas.
\\Leftrightarrow.usage: \Leftrightarrow states that two formulas imply each other, as in A \Leftrightarrow B. For equivalence between full statements in display math, \iff gives the longer \Longleftrightarrow with extra spacing. Boolean algebra uses it for XNOR or the biconditional. In chains of equivalent equations, aligning a column of \Leftrightarrow with align is a common pattern in solution manuals. Do not confuse it with \equiv, which expresses identity or congruence rather than logical equivalence. Only write it when every step really is reversible; squaring both sides, for example, breaks equivalence.

\\Longleftrightarrow.meaning: Draws a long double-shafted two-headed arrow, the same glyph that \iff uses.
\\Longleftrightarrow.usage: \Longleftrightarrow prints the same arrow as \iff but without the extra thick spaces that \iff adds. That makes it the better choice inside subscripts, tables, or tight inline text, while \iff reads better in displayed theorems. It also appears in proofs where both directions are argued together. The short \Leftrightarrow is preferred between brief formulas. Keep a consistent choice throughout a document, especially in theorem statements. It also serves in chains of reversible algebraic steps aligned in an align environment, where the extra length separates long equations visually. Like the other arrows, it is a relation, so TeX gives it thick spacing on both sides.

\\Updownarrow.meaning: Draws a vertical double-shafted two-headed arrow, a delimiter-capable symbol for vertical equivalence.
\\Updownarrow.usage: \Updownarrow is mainly used in vertical layouts, such as two stacked statements in an array that are equivalent, where it plays the role of \Leftrightarrow turned on its side. It is a delimiter, so \Big\Updownarrow and \left ... \right versions grow vertically. Outside such diagrams it has no widely established meaning. If you need a single-shafted version, use \updownarrow. A plain array with a centered column keeps the statements and the arrow aligned. In lecture slides it can also show that two vertically stacked definitions are interchangeable. Pair it with \Leftrightarrow when the same equivalence also appears horizontally elsewhere.

\\mapsto.meaning: Draws a barred arrow showing where a function sends an individual element, as in x ↦ x².
\\mapsto.usage: Use \mapsto for elements and \to for sets: f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},\ x \mapsto x^2 states the domain, codomain, and rule together. Lambda calculus and functional programming papers use it for anonymous functions, and semantics write substitutions or environment updates as [x \mapsto v]. It differs from \to only by the small bar at its tail, so make sure it renders clearly at small sizes. For long expressions use \longmapsto. In commutative diagrams, element-level arrows are also drawn with a mapsto tail.

\\longmapsto.meaning: Draws a long barred arrow mapping an element to its image, for wider expressions than \mapsto.
\\longmapsto.usage: \longmapsto gives more room when the input or output is long, as in (x, y) \longmapsto x^2 + y^2, or when you want the element rule to line up with a \longrightarrow above it. It reads the same as \mapsto and should be paired with \to or \longrightarrow on the line that states the domain and codomain. The fixed length means a label above still needs \overset. Using it consistently in displayed function definitions gives a clean two-line look.

\\nearrow.meaning: Draws a diagonal arrow pointing up and to the right, for increasing trends and diagram edges.
\\nearrow.usage:
earrow is often used informally for "increases to", as in a_n 
earrow a, the diagonal counterpart of \uparrow. It also connects entries in hand-built diagrams, matrix illustrations, and Hasse-style sketches. With \searrow, \swarrow, and 
warrow it forms a full set of diagonal arrows. These do not stretch, so for long diagonal arrows a diagram tool is a better fit. In economics and data-analysis notes it can summarize a rising trend in a table cell. Define the meaning once, since it is notation rather than a formal symbol.

\\hookleftarrow.meaning: Draws a left arrow with a hook on its tail, the reversed form of the inclusion arrow.
\\hookleftarrow.usage: \hookleftarrow mirrors \hookrightarrow and is used when an inclusion or injection is drawn from right to left, for example in an exact sequence written in reverse or in a diagram where the target sits on the left. It is otherwise rare. In keyboard documentation a similar glyph represents the Enter key, but that is a separate meaning. If your arrows mostly point right, rewriting the statement with \hookrightarrow is often clearer. It has relation spacing like the other arrows. Its length matches \hookrightarrow, so mirrored diagrams stay balanced. When you need many such arrows, a dedicated diagram environment handles hooks automatically.

\\hookrightarrow.meaning: Draws a right arrow with a hooked tail, the standard symbol for an injective map, inclusion, or embedding.
\\hookrightarrow.usage: Writing \iota : A \hookrightarrow X tells the reader that the map is an inclusion or injection, without saying so in words. Analysis uses it for continuous embeddings of function spaces, as in H^1(\Omega) \hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega), and compact embeddings are sometimes marked with a further decoration. Category theory uses it for monomorphisms. The surjective counterpart is \twoheadrightarrow. The hook makes the arrow longer than \to, so check alignment in diagrams. It is a relation, so TeX surrounds it with thick spacing.

\\searrow.meaning: Draws a diagonal arrow pointing down and to the right, for decreasing trends and diagram edges.
\\searrow.usage:
\searrow often abbreviates "decreases to", as in \varepsilon_n \searrow 0 for a monotone decreasing sequence. It complements 
earrow, \swarrow, and 
warrow in informal diagrams, such as a 2 by 2 grid of objects. Physicists use it in sketches of energy levels or decay chains. The arrows are fixed size, so they suit quick inline use rather than polished diagrams. The name stands for southeast, not search. Readers new to it may expect a search icon, so a brief definition helps. In tables summarizing monotonicity, 
earrow and \searrow give a compact visual.

\\leftharpoonup.meaning: Draws a left-pointing harpoon with its barb on top, half of an arrowhead pointing left.
\\leftharpoonup.usage: \leftharpoonup is mainly used as a building block or in specialized notation. Some physics texts put a harpoon over vectors, and stacking \rightharpoonup over \leftharpoondown recreates equilibrium arrows, though \rightleftharpoons already exists. It can also appear in reaction diagrams. Because harpoons look alike at small sizes, choose barb direction deliberately and keep it consistent. In most documents it appears inside other constructions rather than alone. Its relatives are \rightharpoonup, \leftharpoondown, and \rightharpoondown, which differ only in direction and barb side. Like other arrows it receives relation spacing.

\\rightharpoonup.meaning: Draws a right-pointing harpoon with the barb on top, the usual sign for weak convergence.
\\rightharpoonup.usage: Functional analysis writes u_n \rightharpoonup u for weak convergence, distinguishing it from strong convergence u_n \to u. Weak-star convergence is often written \overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}. Physics occasionally uses a right harpoon as a vector accent. It also forms the top half of the equilibrium symbol \rightleftharpoons in chemistry. Keep \rightharpoonup separate from \rightharpoondown, whose barb sits underneath, since readers may treat them as different notations. In KaTeX and LaTeX the glyph has relation spacing, so u_n \rightharpoonup u spaces like an equals sign. When writing, mention the space in which convergence is weak, as in the example.

\\swarrow.meaning: Draws a diagonal arrow pointing down and to the left, mainly for diagrams and flow sketches.
\\swarrow.usage: \swarrow shows a step down and to the left, as in a hand-drawn grid of objects or in illustrating how terms combine in a matrix determinant. Together with \nearrow, \searrow, and \nwarrow it covers the four diagonals. It does not stretch, so long diagonal arrows need a diagram tool. Occasionally it marks a trend in a table, but \searrow is more common for decreasing values. Combine it with \quad spacing in arrays to position it correctly.

\\leftharpoondown.meaning: Draws a left-pointing harpoon with its barb below, the lower half of a split arrowhead.
\\leftharpoondown.usage: \leftharpoondown is the bottom half of the equilibrium symbol \rightleftharpoons, where it sits under \rightharpoonup. On its own it appears rarely, in some reaction diagrams or as a reversed weak-convergence marker. If you want an equilibrium arrow, use \rightleftharpoons directly instead of stacking harpoons by hand. Note that harpoons are distinct from \leftarrow and should not be swapped casually. It has relation spacing like ordinary arrows. Its siblings are \leftharpoonup, \rightharpoonup, and \rightharpoondown. In most papers you will not need it at all, since a plain arrow says the same thing more clearly.

\\rightharpoondown.meaning: Draws a right-pointing harpoon with the barb on the bottom, a lower-barbed variant of the half arrow.
\\rightharpoondown.usage: \rightharpoondown is the mirror of \rightharpoonup in barb position, and appears in some equilibrium notations and in vector accents. Because \rightharpoonup is the established weak-convergence symbol, using \rightharpoondown for that would confuse readers. It sometimes pairs with \leftharpoonup in \leftrightharpoons, which is the reverse-equilibrium arrangement. As with all harpoons, check that the barb is visible in the final PDF at your chosen font size. Its siblings \leftharpoonup and \leftharpoondown complete the set of four harpoons. Like other arrows, it gets relation spacing.

\\nwarrow.meaning: Draws a diagonal arrow pointing up and to the left, used mostly in diagrams and illustrations.
\\nwarrow.usage: \nwarrow is the least common of the four diagonal arrows. It appears in hand-built arrays that show how entries relate, such as the dependencies in a dynamic-programming table where a cell depends on its upper-left neighbor.
