Combined with \nearrow, \searrow, and \swarrow it can sketch small diagrams without a drawing package. For polished commutative diagrams, a dedicated diagram environment gives proper arrow lengths and labels. Its fixed size and relation spacing make it convenient inside arrays and tables. Reading the four diagonal arrows as compass directions (northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest) helps remember the names.

\\hat{x}.meaning: Places a small circumflex over one character, marking estimators, unit vectors or Fourier transforms.
\\hat{x}.usage: Statisticians write \hat{\theta} for an estimator of \theta and \hat{y} for fitted values in regression, physicists use \hat{x} or \hat{\mathbf{n}} for unit vectors and quantum operators, and analysts write \hat{f} for the Fourier transform. The accent has a fixed width, so it only looks right over a single symbol; for several letters switch to \widehat{xy}. Over an i or j, use the dotless forms \imath and \jmath so the hat does not sit on top of a dot. In running text outside math mode the equivalent circumflex accent is \^{o}, not \hat.

\\widehat{xyz}.meaning: Stretches a circumflex across a multi-letter expression, such as the Fourier transform of a product.
\\widehat{xyz}.usage: Use \widehat when the accent must cover more than one glyph, for instance \widehat{f * g} = \hat{f}\,\hat{g} for convolution, \widehat{ABC} for an angle in some geometry traditions, or \widehat{G} for the dual group or completion of a group. The hat grows only up to a limited width in the standard Computer Modern fonts, so over long expressions it stops stretching and looks undersized; in that case a superscript such as (f g)^\wedge or a \mathcal{F}\{\cdot\} operator reads better. For a single letter prefer \hat{x}, which is positioned more precisely over italic characters.

\\tilde{x}.meaning: Puts a small wavy tilde over a single symbol, often marking an approximation, transform or modified variable.
\\tilde{x}.usage: A tilde over a letter usually signals a related but altered object: \tilde{x} for a perturbed or approximate solution, \tilde{f} for a Laplace or other transform, \tilde{O}(n) for soft-O complexity that hides log factors, or \tilde{X} for a universal cover in topology. Like \hat, it has a fixed width, so over two or more letters use \widetilde. Do not confuse it with \sim, which is a relation symbol placed between terms (X \sim N(0,1)), nor with the text-mode accent \~{n} used for words like señor. For dotless letters write \tilde{\imath}.

\\widetilde{xyz}.meaning: Draws a stretchable tilde over a group of symbols, used for covers, closures and modified expressions.
\\widetilde{xyz}.usage: Choose \widetilde when the tilde must span several characters, as in \widetilde{GL}_n for a covering group, \widetilde{AB} for an arc in some geometry texts, or \widetilde{f(x)} for a smoothed function. Its width grows with the content but only up to a font-dependent maximum, after which it stays centered and looks short; for long arguments a postfix notation or a named operator is clearer. Over a single letter, \tilde{x} gives better placement and a smaller accent. When writing the tilde as a standalone character in text, \textasciitilde is the command to reach for instead.

\\dot{x}.meaning: Adds a single dot above a variable, Newton's notation for the first time derivative.
\\dot{x}.usage: In mechanics and dynamical systems \dot{x} means dx/dt, so equations like \dot{x} = Ax or the Lagrangian L(q, \dot{q}, t) are written compactly. Physicists also use it for rates such as \dot{m} for mass flow. The dot is a math accent and works over Greek letters too: \dot{\theta}. Do not confuse it with \cdot (a centered multiplication dot) or with the text-mode accent \.{z} used in Polish words. For the second derivative use \ddot{x} rather than stacking two \dot commands, which misaligns the dots.

\\ddot{x}.meaning: Places two dots above a variable to denote its second time derivative, as in acceleration.
\\ddot{x}.usage: Newton's second law is commonly written m\ddot{x} = F, and the harmonic oscillator as \ddot{x} + \omega^2 x = 0. In Lagrangian mechanics the Euler-Lagrange equations produce \ddot{q} terms. Although it resembles an umlaut, \ddot is a math accent; for German or Turkish words in text use \"{o} instead. The dots are centered over the symbol's slanted axis, so over italic letters they shift slightly right, which is intentional. For a third derivative \dddot{x} exists, though beyond that Leibniz notation or x^{(n)} is clearer.

\\dddot{x}.meaning: Puts three dots over a variable, Newton-style notation for the third time derivative (jerk).
\\dddot{x}.usage: Third derivatives appear in motion planning and control, where \dddot{x} is the jerk, and in the Abraham-Lorentz radiation reaction force proportional to \dddot{\mathbf{x}}. It comes paired with \ddddot for four dots, and neither is part of the minimal LaTeX kernel. Its dots are spaced more tightly than three manual \dot calls could be, and it sits at the same height as \ddot. Because three dots become hard to read in small type or subscripts, many authors switch to x^{(3)} or d^3x/dt^3 for higher orders.

\\bar{x}.meaning: Sets a short horizontal bar over one symbol, typically for a sample mean or a complex conjugate.
\\bar{x}.usage: Statistics uses \bar{x} for the sample mean, (1/n)\sum x_i; complex analysis writes \bar{z} for the conjugate; and \bar{A} may denote the closure of a set. The bar has a fixed width roughly that of one letter, so \bar{xy} looks wrong: use \overline{xy} to span several symbols, which is also the usual choice for conjugating an expression such as \overline{z + w}. In text, the macron accent is \={a}, not \bar. Bold vectors take it fine: \bar{\mathbf{v}}.

\\overline{xyz}.meaning: Draws a line over an entire expression, for conjugates, closures, repeating decimals or segment names.
\\overline{xyz}.usage: Unlike \bar, the \overline rule stretches to the full width of its argument, so it suits \overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar{z}_1 \bar{z}_2, the closure \overline{A \cup B}, Boolean negation \overline{A + B}, the line segment \overline{AB}, and repeating decimals like 0.\overline{3}. Nested overlines stack at increasing heights, which can look uneven next to each other; adding a \vphantom of the tallest content to each helps align them. In text mode an over-rule is not available directly; wrap it in math. Its counterpart for underlining is \underline.

\\underline{xyz}.meaning: Draws a rule beneath an expression, used for emphasis, lower bounds or lower integrals.
\\underline{xyz}.usage: In mathematics \underline is used for lower Darboux integrals, the lower limit \underline{\lim}, lower bounds, and to mark distinguished elements; some fields underline vectors instead of using bold. It works in both text and math mode, but in text it disables hyphenation and line breaking, so it is a poor choice for emphasizing words, where \emph is preferred. The rule depth depends on descenders, so \underline{a} and \underline{y} sit at different heights; adding a \vphantom{y} to each aligns them. Its upper twin is \overline.

\\vec{x}.meaning: Places a small right-pointing arrow over a single letter to mark it as a vector.
\\vec{x}.usage: School physics and many engineering texts write vectors as \vec{F}, \vec{v} or \vec{r}, while pure mathematics more often uses bold \mathbf{v} or plain letters. The arrow has a fixed size meant for one character; over two points such as AB it looks cramped, so use \overrightarrow{AB} instead. The arrow sits slightly right of center over italic letters to follow their slant. Combining it with a hat for unit vectors (\hat{\vec{x}}) works but stacks tall, so many writers use \hat{\mathbf{x}}.

\\overrightarrow{AB}.meaning: Stretches a right-pointing arrow over its argument, the standard notation for a vector from A to B.
\\overrightarrow{AB}.usage: Geometry and vector algebra use \overrightarrow{AB} for the vector from point A to point B, giving identities such as \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}. The arrow widens to match the content, unlike \vec, which only fits one letter. In category theory and functional analysis it sometimes marks a direction of a limit or a directed set. The arrow is drawn at full arrow height, so it adds noticeable vertical space; in inline text with tight leading consider \vec{v} or bold letters. Use \overleftarrow for the reverse direction.

\\overleftarrow{AB}.meaning: Draws a left-pointing arrow spanning the argument, marking reversed direction or a backward-read sequence.
\\overleftarrow{AB}.usage: Less common than its right-pointing counterpart, \overleftarrow{AB} appears when a vector or path is read from B back to A, for the reversed word or string in formal language theory, and for backward-time or adjoint quantities in physics. Its arrow stretches across the full argument just like \overrightarrow. If you need arrows under the expression instead, amsmath supplies \underleftarrow and \underrightarrow. For a single-letter backward vector there is no built-in short form like \vec, so this wide command is the usual choice.

\\overleftrightarrow{AB}.meaning: Draws a double-headed arrow over its argument, the usual notation for the line through points A and B.
\\overleftrightarrow{AB}.usage: School geometry distinguishes three objects built from two points: \overline{AB} for the segment, \overrightarrow{AB} for the ray, and \overleftrightarrow{AB} for the infinite line. The arrow stretches with the content and has heads on both ends. It is also used occasionally for bidirectional relations or two-sided limits. Because it is quite tall, it can collide with the line above in dense paragraphs; display math avoids that. The matching under-arrow version is \underleftrightarrow. Keep the distinction from \overline{AB} in mind, since that one denotes only the finite segment.

\\acute{x}.meaning: Places an acute accent (a rising stroke) over a math symbol, occasionally used as a prime-like marker.
\\acute{x}.usage: Math-mode accents such as \acute exist mainly for completeness; in practice they appear as variable decorations, for example \acute{x} for a transformed coordinate in some physics texts. For accented letters in words, use the text accent \'{e}, as in café; \acute will not work outside math mode. The math version uses the italic math font, so \acute{e} inside an equation does not match an accented roman letter in the surrounding paragraph. If you simply need a derivative-style mark, x' (prime) is far more standard.

\\grave{x}.meaning: Puts a grave accent (a falling stroke) over a math-mode symbol as a variable decoration.
\\grave{x}.usage: \grave is the math-mode counterpart of the text accent \`{a} seen in French words like voilà. In equations it is rarely used and serves as just another way to tell related variables apart, alongside primes, hats and tildes. Because it is a math accent, it typesets its argument in math italic; for an accented word in an equation write \text{\`{a}} instead. If you are choosing a decoration for a new variable, the reader will usually find \tilde, \hat or a prime more familiar.

\\breve{x}.meaning: Adds a breve (a small cup-shaped curve) over a symbol, a less common variable decoration.
\\breve{x}.usage: In mathematics \breve{x} appears as an alternative marker when hat, bar and tilde are already taken, for example in some signal-processing and statistics papers for a modified estimator, and in Lie theory notation. The breve is round at the bottom, unlike \check, which is pointed. For text in Romanian or Turkish (ă, ğ), use the text accent \u{a} instead of the math command. The accent has a fixed width, so it fits single letters only.

\\check{x}.meaning: Sets a caron (hacek), a small v-shaped accent, over a symbol; used notably for Cech cohomology.
\\check{x}.usage: Algebraic topology writes \check{H}^n(X) for Cech cohomology, and some texts use \check{x} for a dual or inverse-transformed object, the opposite of a hat. The v shape distinguishes it from the round \breve and from \hat, which is an inverted v. In text, a Czech hacek like č is produced with \v{c}, not \check. The accent has fixed width; there is no standard \widecheck in core LaTeX, so over long expressions authors use a superscript instead.

\\mathring{x}.meaning: Places a small ring above a symbol, used for interiors of sets and some unit symbols.
\\mathring{x}.usage: Topology sometimes writes \mathring{A} for the interior of A (an alternative to A^\circ or \operatorname{int} A), and differential geometry uses it for traceless or reference quantities. For the angstrom symbol in text use \AA, and for the Scandinavian letter å use \aa; \mathring is only for math mode. It differs from a superscript \circ, which sits to the upper right rather than centered above. The ring is sized for a single letter. Over the letters i and j, use \imath or \jmath so the ring replaces the dot.

\\overbrace{x+y}^{\\text{sum}}.meaning: Draws a horizontal curly brace above an expression, with an optional label set via a superscript.
\\overbrace{x+y}^{\\text{sum}}.usage: Overbraces annotate parts of a formula, for instance labeling n copies in \overbrace{1 + 1 + \cdots + 1}^{n}, or naming a term in a derivation. The superscript after the command is placed above the brace's tip, and wrapping the label in \text keeps it upright and at a readable size. The brace adds a lot of height, so it belongs in display math; inline it will push lines apart. Combine with \underbrace on the same expression to annotate above and below. For a brace with a label on the side, use \left\{ ... \right. instead.

\\underbrace{x+y}_{\\text{sum}}.meaning: Puts a curly brace under an expression, with a label set through a subscript beneath it.
\\underbrace{x+y}_{\\text{sum}}.usage: Textbooks use \underbrace to explain pieces of an equation, such as marking \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}mv^2}_{\text{kinetic}} in an energy balance or counting terms in a product. The label goes in a subscript right after the command; use \text for words and \scriptstyle content for short math. The brace stretches to the exact width of its argument. Nested or overlapping braces need care: you can underbrace part of an expression that is already overbraced, but braces cannot cross each other. Like \overbrace, it is best in display math.

\\cancel{x}.meaning: Strikes through an expression with a diagonal line to show terms cancelling in a derivation.
\\cancel{x}.usage: Teachers and lecture notes use \cancel to show simplification, for example a factor cancelling in a fraction or opposite terms vanishing in a sum. The same package offers \bcancel (back-slash direction), \xcancel (an X through the term) and \cancelto{0}{x}, which draws an arrow to the value the term goes to. The stroke color can be changed separately from the text color, which helps in slides. \cancel works in text mode too, but it is mostly used in math. Formal papers rarely show cancellation this way; it is a teaching device.

\\boxed{x}.meaning: Draws a rectangular frame around a math expression, often to highlight a final result.
\\boxed{x}.usage: Students box final answers and authors highlight key identities with \boxed{E = mc^2}. The command works inside math mode, keeping the content in display or text style as appropriate, unlike \fbox, which switches to text mode and needs $...$ inside it. In align environments, put \boxed around one side or a whole line's content but not across the & alignment point. The padding and rule thickness follow \fboxsep and \fboxrule, so you can adjust them locally. For colored frames, \fcolorbox wrapped around inline math is the usual next step.

\\langle.meaning: Opening angle bracket, used for inner products, expectation values and generated subgroups.
\\langle.usage: The left angle bracket starts notations such as the inner product \langle u, v \rangle, a bra-ket \langle \psi | \phi \rangle, the subgroup \langle g \rangle, or a time average \langle x \rangle. Never use the less-than sign < for this: it is a relation with wide spacing and the wrong shape. It works with \left and \right for automatic sizing, and with \big, \Big and friends for manual sizes. Always pair it with \rangle; if you need only one side visible, use \left. or \right. as the invisible partner.

\\rangle.meaning: Closing angle bracket that ends inner products, kets, averages and other angle-bracket notations.
\\rangle.usage: \rangle closes what \langle opens: \langle f, g \rangle in Hilbert spaces, the Dirac ket |\psi\rangle, and presentations like \langle a, b \mid a^2 = b^3 \rangle. The greater-than sign > is not a substitute, since it is a relation with extra space around it and a flatter angle. When the contents are tall, as with fractions or sums, use \left\langle ... \right\rangle so both sides grow together. A ket used alone is written |\psi\rangle, which needs no matching \langle.

\\langle x \\rangle.meaning: Encloses an expression in angle brackets, for averages, inner products or the span of generators.
\\langle x \\rangle.usage: This pairing is used for expectation values in physics, \langle E \rangle, for inner products \langle x, y \rangle, and for the subgroup or ideal generated by elements, \langle a \rangle. For tall arguments switch to \left\langle \frac{a}{b} \right\rangle. If you write inner products often, define a macro, for instance with a paired-delimiter tool, so sizing is consistent. In Dirac notation, many prefer a dedicated bra-ket macro set because spacing around the vertical bar inside \langle \phi | \psi \rangle can be uneven; \mid adds relation spacing, while | adds none.

\\lceil.meaning: Left ceiling bracket, the opening half of the ceiling function that rounds up to an integer.
\\lceil.usage: \lceil opens the ceiling notation \lceil x \rceil, the least integer at least x. It is a delimiter, so it works with \left\lceil ... \right\rceil for tall content like \frac{n}{2}, and with \big-style sizing. The ceiling bracket has its horizontal stroke on top, while the floor bracket \lfloor has it on the bottom, an easy pair to mix up when proofreading. Some authors also use \lceil and \rceil as corner quotes for Godel numbering, where \ulcorner is an alternative.

\\rceil.meaning: Right ceiling bracket, closing the ceiling function notation for rounding up.
\\rceil.usage: Pair \rceil with \lceil to write \lceil \log_2 n \rceil, the number of bits needed in many algorithms, or \lceil n/k \rceil for the number of size-k blocks needed to cover n items. Unlike parentheses, the ceiling has no ASCII equivalent, so the command is the only way to get the symbol. Use \right\rceil when the matching left bracket was set with \left. If you write ceilings often, a paired-delimiter macro like \ceil{x} keeps the sizes consistent across a document.

\\lceil x \\rceil.meaning: Rounds x up to the smallest integer greater than or equal to it: the ceiling function.
\\lceil x \\rceil.usage: Ceilings show up in algorithm analysis (\lceil \log_2 n \rceil comparisons, \lceil n/2 \rceil in merge sort), in number theory, and in counting problems like the pigeonhole principle, where some box holds at least \lceil n/k \rceil items. For negative inputs remember that \lceil -2.5 \rceil = -2. When the argument is a fraction or a tall expression, use \left\lceil ... \right\rceil so the brackets grow. Do not substitute square brackets [x]: older texts used [x] for the floor, which makes it ambiguous.

\\lfloor.meaning: Left floor bracket, the opening half of the floor function that rounds down to an integer.
\\lfloor.usage: \lfloor begins notations like \lfloor x \rfloor and \lfloor n/2 \rfloor. The floor bracket has its bar at the bottom, in contrast to \lceil, whose bar is at the top. As a delimiter it can be sized with \left\lfloor or \bigl\lfloor. In number theory the same bracket appears in formulas such as Legendre's formula for the power of a prime dividing n!. If your font or renderer shows a plain square bracket, check that you typed \lfloor and not [, which is a different glyph.

\\rfloor.meaning: Right floor bracket, closing the floor function notation for rounding down.
\\rfloor.usage: Close any \lfloor with \rfloor, for example in \lfloor x \rfloor or the integer division \lfloor a/b \rfloor that many programming languages implement for positive operands. When the left bracket was set with \left\lfloor, the right one must be \right\rfloor in the same math group, or LaTeX reports a missing \right. The pair is also used for rounding to the nearest integer via \lfloor x + 1/2 \rfloor. A paired-delimiter macro such as \floor{x} keeps notation consistent in long documents.

\\lfloor x \\rfloor.meaning: Rounds x down to the greatest integer less than or equal to it: the floor function.
\\lfloor x \\rfloor.usage: The floor appears in integer division, in the fractional part \{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor, in the binary search midpoint \lfloor (lo + hi)/2 \rfloor, and in number theory sums like Legendre's formula. For negative numbers it rounds away from zero: \lfloor -2.5 \rfloor = -3, which differs from truncation. Older literature wrote [x] for the floor (the Gauss bracket), but the bracket notation is now preferred because it is unambiguous. Use \left\lfloor ... \right\rfloor around fractions so the brackets match the content height.

\\|.meaning: Double vertical bar, the delimiter for norms and the symbol for parallel in some contexts.
\\|.usage: \| prints two vertical lines and is mostly used in pairs for norms, \|x\|. As a plain symbol it has ordinary spacing, so when you mean the relation is parallel to, use \parallel, which adds relation spacing. For norms, \lVert and \rVert are recommended, because they tell LaTeX which side opens and closes, giving correct spacing next to operators and minus signs. It can be sized with \left\| ... \right\| or \big\|. In text mode \| does not give the bars; use \textbardbl or switch to math.

\\| x \\|.meaning: Encloses a vector or function in double bars to denote its norm, its length or size.
\\| x \\|.usage: Norms are everywhere in analysis and linear algebra: the Euclidean norm \|x\|_2, the sup norm \|f\|_\infty, the Frobenius norm \|A\|_F, and the triangle inequality \|x + y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|. A subscript after the closing bar indicates which norm. Writing \lVert x \rVert instead of \| x \| gives better spacing in expressions like \|{-x}\|, since LaTeX then knows each bar's role. For tall content, such as fractions inside the norm, use \left\| ... \right\|. Single bars |x| are reserved for absolute values.

\\llbracket.meaning: Left double (white) square bracket, used for semantic brackets, integer intervals and Iverson notation.
\\llbracket.usage: In programming-language semantics \llbracket e \rrbracket denotes the meaning of an expression, as in denotational semantics. French-tradition texts and combinatorics write \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket for the integer interval \{1, \dots, n\}, and some authors use it for the Iverson bracket. The command is not in core LaTeX or the AMS symbol fonts, so it needs a symbol package that provides it; KaTeX supports it directly. It grows only with packages that provide extensible versions, so for tall content check your setup. Pair it with \rrbracket.

\\rrbracket.meaning: Right double square bracket, closing semantic-bracket or integer-interval notation.
\\rrbracket.usage: Close \llbracket with \rrbracket to write \llbracket P \rrbracket_\sigma, the meaning of program P in state \sigma, or the integer range \llbracket a, b \rrbracket. Do not fake it with ]] or with ]\!], which give a different shape and spacing than the hollow bracket glyph. Authors with many semantic brackets often define a macro like \sem{e} so the bracket style can be changed in one place, for instance swapping to [\![ e ]\!] if the double-bracket font is unavailable.

\\llbracket x \\rrbracket.meaning: Wraps an expression in double square brackets, for denotational semantics or integer intervals.
\\llbracket x \\rrbracket.usage: This bracket pair gives the semantic function in formal semantics, \llbracket x \rrbracket_\rho for the value of x in environment \rho, and the discrete interval \llbracket m, n \rrbracket in combinatorics. It also appears in the Iverson bracket and in jump notation for discontinuities in numerical PDEs, \llbracket u \rrbracket = u^+ - u^-. Because the glyph is not in the default fonts, the source needs a symbol package; check the package note on this page. The hollow strokes make it visually distinct from nested ordinary brackets.

\\left( x \\right).meaning: Parentheses that automatically grow to the height of whatever they enclose.
\\left( x \\right).usage: \left( and \right) measure their content and pick a matching size, so \left( \frac{a}{b} \right)^2 gets tall parentheses while a plain (x) stays small. Every \left needs a \right in the same group, and a line break inside align cannot separate them. Overusing them makes simple expressions look heavy, and \left...\right adds a little extra space as an inner atom, which can make f\left(x\right) look loose; for function arguments \bigl( ... \bigr) or plain parentheses are often better. They size to the tallest item, including limits on sums.

\\left[ x \\right].meaning: Square brackets that scale to fit their contents, for grouping, commutators or closed intervals.
\\left[ x \\right].usage: Square brackets serve as the next level of grouping outside parentheses, the closed interval [a, b], the commutator [A, B] = AB - BA, the expectation \mathbb{E}[X], and matrices. With \left[ ... \right] the brackets stretch around fractions, integrals or matrices, as in \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_0^1 for evaluated antiderivatives. Inside a bmatrix environment the brackets are already provided, so you do not need \left[ yourself. For nested brackets in a long expression, manual sizes like \Bigl[ ... \Bigr] give finer control.

\\left\\{ x \\right\\}.meaning: Curly braces that stretch to the content height, for set-builder notation and grouped definitions.
\\left\\{ x \\right\\}.usage: Braces must be escaped as \{ and \} because bare braces are LaTeX grouping characters and print nothing. With \left\{ ... \right\} they grow around tall content such as \left\{ \frac{p}{q} : q \neq 0 \right\}. For a set-builder bar that also grows, use \middle| between them. For piecewise definitions, the cases environment already draws the left brace, so you do not need \left\{ ... \right. by hand. In text mode, use \textbraceleft or simply \{ inside math.

\\left| x \\right|.meaning: Vertical bars that resize to their content, for absolute values and determinants.
\\left| x \\right|.usage: Use \left| ... \right| when an absolute value contains a fraction or sum, as in \left| \frac{a}{b} \right|, and for determinants of tall matrices (though vmatrix is simpler). Plain | is ambiguous to LaTeX: it cannot tell an opening bar from a closing one, which can spoil spacing around a leading minus sign. For consistent results define a macro with \lvert and \rvert, or use \left\lvert ... \right\rvert. For set-builder separators and conditional probabilities, use \mid or \middle| instead.

\\Big( x \\Big).meaning: Parentheses fixed at the second size step, larger than \big but smaller than \bigg.
\\Big( x \\Big).usage: TeX offers four manual sizes: \big, \Big, \bigg and \Bigg. \Big( fits around single fractions or sums with small limits, and unlike \left it does not scan the content, so it can span line breaks in multiline environments and gives predictable results. For correct spacing, use \Bigl( to open and \Bigr) to close, since a bare \Big makes an ordinary atom. Manual sizes are often preferable to \left...\right inside function arguments, where \left adds extra space. Sizes are fixed, so they do not shrink in subscripts.

\\Bigg( x \\Bigg).meaning: The largest of TeX's four manual delimiter sizes, for very tall content like nested fractions.
\\Bigg( x \\Bigg).usage: \Bigg( produces parentheses roughly two and a half times the normal size, suitable around stacked fractions, large integrals with limits, or sums of fractions. Because the size is fixed, it is predictable across lines of an align, where \left and \right cannot be split. Use \Biggl and \Biggr for proper opening and closing spacing. If content is taller still, \left( ... \right) can grow beyond \Bigg using extensible pieces. The sequence from small to large is \big, \Big, \bigg, \Bigg.

\\left( x \\right..meaning: Shows a resizable left parenthesis only; \right. is an invisible closing delimiter that satisfies the pairing.
\\left( x \\right..usage: Every \left must be matched by a \right, and the period form \right. lets you close the group without printing anything. This is useful when a bracketed expression continues onto another line of an align (open with \left( on one line, close with \right. and restart with \left. ... \right) on the next), or for one-sided braces. Sizes of the two halves are computed independently, so add a \vphantom of the tall content to keep them equal. For piecewise functions, the cases environment is the cleaner choice than \left\{ ... \right.

\\left. x \\right).meaning: Prints only a resizable closing parenthesis; \left. acts as an invisible opening partner.
\\left. x \\right).usage: \left. is the invisible opener that lets \right) size itself to the content. A common use is the evaluation bar \left. \frac{df}{dx} \right|_{x=0}, where only the right-hand vertical line should appear and stretch. It also finishes a bracket that was opened on a previous line of a multiline equation. Since each half is sized separately, insert \vphantom{...} with the tallest piece from the other line to match heights. The period itself is not printed, but it does add the small null-delimiter space.

\\left[ x \\right).meaning: Pairs a left square bracket with a right parenthesis, the notation for a half-open interval.
\\left[ x \\right).usage: \left and \right do not have to match in shape, so \left[ ... \right) writes the half-open interval [a, b), closed at a and open at b, common in probability (cumulative distribution functions are right-continuous on [x, \infty)) and in measure theory. Mismatched pairs also handle (a, b], written \left( ... \right]. For simple intervals plain [0, 1) without \left/\right is sufficient and cleaner. Some European texts use reversed brackets instead, as in [a, b[, which you can type directly.

<.meaning: The less-than relation, asserting that the left quantity is strictly smaller than the right.
<.usage: Typed directly in math mode, < becomes a relation with proper surrounding space, as in 0 < x < 1 or a strict inequality in an epsilon-delta proof. Do not use it as an angle bracket for inner products; that is \langle. In text mode with the old default font encoding, < may print an inverted exclamation mark, so write \textless or use math mode. Its non-strict form is \leq (or \le), and the negation is \not< or \nless. Web renderers like MathJax also accept \lt, which helps in HTML.

>.meaning: The greater-than relation, stating that the left quantity is strictly larger than the right.
>.usage: In math mode > is a relation symbol and gets relation spacing automatically, so x > 0 needs no manual spaces. It closes strict inequalities such as \lambda_{\max} > 0 or the condition n > N in limit definitions. It should not be used as a closing angle bracket; that is \rangle. In text mode with the older font encoding the character can print as an inverted question mark, so use \textgreater or math mode. Related commands are \geq (or \ge), \gg for much greater, and \ngtr for its negation.

\\equiv.meaning: Triple-bar relation meaning identically equal, congruent modulo n, or logically equivalent.
\\equiv.usage: Number theory writes a \equiv b \pmod{n} for congruence, analysis writes f \equiv 0 to say a function vanishes everywhere, and logic uses it for logical equivalence of formulas. Pair it with \pmod{n} for the parenthesized modulus or \bmod for the binary form a \bmod n. It is distinct from \cong (isomorphism or geometric congruence) and from \triangleq or := (definitions), although some authors also use it for definitions. Negate it with \not\equiv. In physics, \equiv often introduces a shorthand: \omega \equiv 2\pi f.

\\propto.meaning: Says one quantity is proportional to another, equal up to a constant factor.
\\propto.usage: Physics writes F \propto 1/r^2 for inverse-square laws, and Bayesian statistics relies on it constantly: p(\theta \mid x) \propto p(x \mid \theta)\, p(\theta), dropping the normalizing constant. It is a relation, so spacing is automatic. Do not confuse it with the Greek letter \alpha, which looks similar in some fonts but has no relation spacing. A variant \varpropto has a slightly different shape. For scaling in algorithm analysis, \sim or \Theta are usually clearer. Chain it with a constant only when the constant matters; otherwise the point of \propto is to hide it.

\\sim.meaning: Tilde relation for distributed as, asymptotically equal, similar, or equivalent under a relation.
\\sim.usage: In probability X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) reads X is distributed as a standard normal. In asymptotics f \sim g means f/g \to 1, as in Stirling's formula. Algebra uses x \sim y for an equivalence relation, and geometry uses it for similar triangles. As a relation it has spacing on both sides; for a tilde accent on a letter use \tilde{x}. Close cousins are \simeq (asymptotically equal or homotopy equivalent), \approx (approximately), and \thicksim, a bolder version. As a prefix meaning approximately, as in \sim 10^3, the spacing can look odd; write {\sim}10^3.

\\cong.meaning: Tilde over an equals sign denoting isomorphism of structures or congruence of geometric figures.
\\cong.usage: Algebraists write G \cong H for isomorphic groups and V \cong V^{**} for finite-dimensional spaces, while geometry uses \triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF for congruent triangles. Some physics and engineering texts use it to mean approximately equal, but \approx is clearer for that. It differs from \simeq (a single bar, used for homotopy equivalence or asymptotic equality) and from \equiv (three bars). To label the map, place it over the symbol with \overset{\phi}{\cong} or use an arrow like \xrightarrow{\sim}.

\\subseteq.meaning: States that every element of the left set also belongs to the right set; the sets may be equal.
\\subseteq.usage: Use \subseteq for the inclusion that allows equality, as in A \subseteq A, and in definitions like a topology being closed under unions of subfamilies \mathcal{U} \subseteq \tau. Many authors use plain \subset with the same meaning, while others reserve \subset for proper inclusion, so it is worth stating your convention. For proper inclusion unambiguously, use \subsetneq. The negation is \nsubseteq or \not\subseteq. To show two sets are equal, a standard proof shows A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A.
\\subseteq.example: A \subseteq B \land B \subseteq A \iff A = B

\\subsetneq.meaning: A subset symbol with a slashed bar: the left set is contained in the right but not equal to it.
\\subsetneq.usage: \subsetneq states proper inclusion explicitly, removing the ambiguity of \subset, which some texts treat as non-strict. It appears in chains like \mathbb{N} \subsetneq \mathbb{Z} \subsetneq \mathbb{Q} and in maximality arguments for ideals. Variants include \subsetneqq (double bar with slash) and \varsubsetneq, whose stroke crosses only the bar. Do not confuse it with \nsubseteq, which means not a subset at all. Its superset counterpart is \supsetneq. It is a relation, so spacing around it is handled automatically. When writing a proof that inclusion is strict, show A \subseteq B and exhibit one element of B outside A.

\\supset.meaning: Superset relation: the left set contains the right set (often meaning strictly, depending on convention).
\\supset.usage: \supset is the mirror image of \subset, so A \supset B says B is inside A. As with \subset, authors disagree on whether it allows equality; state your convention or use \supseteq and \supsetneq to remove doubt. Logic texts in older traditions, including Principia Mathematica, used \supset for material implication, so you may see p \supset q in philosophy papers. For new writing, \to or \implies is clearer for implication. The negation is \not\supset, and \nsupseteq covers the non-strict version.

\\supseteq.meaning: Superset-or-equal relation: the left set includes every element of the right set.
\\supseteq.usage: Read A \supseteq B as A contains B, possibly with equality. It is natural when the larger set is the subject, as in \overline{A} \supseteq A for closures or \ker f \supseteq \operatorname{im} g in exact sequence arguments. It is simply \subseteq read in the other direction, so choose whichever puts the important set first. The strict version is \supsetneq, and the negation is \nsupseteq. In lattice and order theory it also expresses reverse inclusion order on families of sets.

\\perp.meaning: Perpendicular relation, marking orthogonal lines, vectors or subspaces, and independence of variables.
\\perp.usage: Geometry writes AB \perp CD, linear algebra writes u \perp v when \langle u, v \rangle = 0 and W^\perp for an orthogonal complement, and number theory sometimes uses a \perp b for coprime integers. Probabilists write X \perp Y for independence, often doubled as X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y to imitate the dedicated independence symbol. \perp is a relation with spacing on both sides, whereas \bot has the same shape but ordinary spacing, which suits the logical falsum or a bottom element. In a superscript like W^\perp either works, since spacing is suppressed there.
\\perp.example: W^{\perp} = \{ v \in V : v \perp w \ \forall w \in W \}

\\parallel.meaning: Relation meaning is parallel to, for lines, planes or vectors; also a parallel-composition operator.
\\parallel.usage: Geometry writes \ell_1 \parallel \ell_2, physics writes components like F_\parallel (often via \|), and electrical engineering uses R_1 \parallel R_2 for resistors in parallel. Process calculi use it for parallel composition, P \parallel Q. The glyph is the same as \|, but \parallel gets relation spacing, so use it between objects and \| (or \lVert, \rVert) for norm delimiters. Its negation is \nparallel. For the KL divergence D(P \parallel Q) the relation spacing is standard, though some prefer \|.

\\nparallel.meaning: Negated parallel relation, stating that two lines or vectors are not parallel.
\\nparallel.usage:
parallel draws a slash through the double bar and is used in geometry problems such as \ell_1 
parallel \ell_2, implying the lines meet (in the plane) or are skew (in space). It is a relation with the same spacing as \parallel. Writing 
ot\parallel can work, but the overlaid slash is often poorly centered, so the dedicated glyph looks better. There is also 
shortparallel, a shorter variant. In physics, a not-parallel component is more often written with \perp.

\\ll.meaning: Much-less-than relation, saying the left quantity is smaller than the right by orders of magnitude.
\\ll.usage: Physics and engineering use \ll for approximation regimes: v \ll c for non-relativistic motion, or x \ll 1 to justify \sin x \approx x. Analytic number theory uses Vinogradov notation f \ll g, meaning f = O(g), and measure theory writes \mu \ll \nu for absolute continuity. It is a single glyph, so do not type << or < <, which give two separated relation symbols with wrong spacing. The triple version \lll exists for even stronger inequality.

\\gg.meaning: Much-greater-than relation, indicating one quantity vastly exceeds another.
\\gg.usage: Use \gg in asymptotic or physical reasoning, such as n \gg 1 for large-sample approximations, kT \gg \hbar\omega for the classical limit, or Vinogradov notation f \gg g meaning g = O(f). It is one symbol with relation spacing; typing >> produces two separate relations. The stronger \ggg also exists. Since \gg is not quantitative, papers often follow it with a precise statement, for instance n \gg \log(1/\delta) together with the constant involved. Asymptotic arguments in physics often state the regime once, for example L \gg \lambda, and then drop small terms.

\\prec.meaning: Precedes relation for strict orderings that are not ordinary numeric less-than.
\\prec.usage: \prec writes abstract strict orders: preferences in economics (x \prec y means y is strictly preferred), majorization in matrix analysis, dominance orders on partitions, and the happened-before relation in distributed systems. Its curved shape signals that the order is not numerical <. The non-strict version is \preceq, and \preccurlyeq gives a curly-bar variant favored in some texts. Linear algebra writes A \prec B for the Loewner order, meaning B - A is positive definite. Negations include \nprec.

\\succ.meaning: Succeeds relation, the reverse of \prec, for strict abstract orderings.
\\succ.usage: \succ reads succeeds or is preferred to: in microeconomics x \succ y means x is strictly preferred to y, and in matrix analysis A \succ 0 states that A is positive definite (Loewner order). Optimization papers use it in semidefinite constraints. It is a relation symbol, so spacing is automatic. The non-strict form is \succeq, the curly-bar form \succcurlyeq, and the negation \nsucc. Avoid > for these orders, since readers would take it as numeric comparison.

\\preceq.meaning: Precedes-or-equal relation, the non-strict version of \prec for partial and preference orders.
\\preceq.usage: Order theory writes x \preceq y for a general partial order, keeping \le for numbers. Economists use it for weak preference, and matrix analysts write A \preceq B when B - A is positive semidefinite. In convex optimization the generalized inequality x \preceq_K y uses a subscript for the cone. \preccurlyeq looks similar, with a curved lower bar, and some authors prefer it to avoid confusion with \leq. The reverse is \succeq, and \npreceq negates it.

\\succeq.meaning: Succeeds-or-equal relation, most often seen in A \succeq 0 for positive semidefinite matrices.
\\succeq.usage: Semidefinite programming constraints are written X \succeq 0, meaning X is symmetric positive semidefinite, and the Loewner order compares matrices as A \succeq B. Economists use \succeq for weak preference, read at least as good as. It is a relation with standard spacing. The strict version is \succ, the curly variant \succcurlyeq, and the negation \nsucceq. For numeric comparisons stick with \geq so readers do not look for a nonstandard order. In a semidefinite program, the constraint is usually listed on its own line after s.t.

\\asymp.meaning: Asymptotic-equivalence relation: two functions grow at the same rate up to constant factors.
\\asymp.usage: In analysis and number theory f \asymp g means there are constants c, C > 0 with c g \le f \le C g for large arguments, equivalent to f = \Theta(g) in computer science. It is weaker than f \sim g, which requires the ratio to tend to 1. The glyph, a pair of opposed arcs, should not be confused with \approx or with \smile and \frown. It is a relation, so spacing is automatic. Some physics texts also use it loosely for asymptotically equal, so define it if precision matters.

:=.meaning: Colon-equals, the definition assignment: the left side is defined to equal the right side.
:=.usage: Writing f(x) := x^2 + 1 marks a definition rather than a claim of equality, and the colon sits on the side of the thing being defined (=: reverses the direction). Typed directly, the colon and equals sign are both relations, so TeX sets them without space between them, but the colon is not vertically centered on the equals sign, which bothers some typographers. The \coloneqq command from a math tools package fixes that alignment. In pseudocode it also denotes assignment, x := x + 1. Alternatives include \triangleq and \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}.

\\triangleq.meaning: Equals sign topped with a small triangle, read is defined as.
\\triangleq.usage: Signal processing, control theory and information theory papers often prefer \triangleq for definitions, as in H(X) \triangleq -\sum p(x) \log p(x). It plays the same role as := but is symmetric, so it does not indicate which side is new. Some readers find it unfamiliar, so mention the convention once in the notation section. Alternatives include \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} or \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}, and \equiv in physics. It is a relation, so spacing is automatic. Spell out the convention for any reader outside your field.

\\oplus.meaning: Circled plus, for direct sums of spaces or modules and exclusive or (XOR) in Boolean algebra.
\\oplus.usage: Linear algebra writes V = U \oplus W when every vector splits uniquely into parts from U and W, and module theory builds \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}. In computing and cryptography a \oplus b is bitwise XOR, as in one-time pads c = m \oplus k. It is a binary operator, so it gets medium spacing. For a direct sum over an index set, use the large operator \bigoplus_{i \in I} V_i, which takes limits like \sum. Do not confuse it with \pm or a plain +; in some algebras \oplus also denotes a deformed addition.
\\oplus.example: c = m \oplus k \implies m = c \oplus k

\\otimes.meaning: Circled times, the tensor product of vectors, spaces, modules or matrices (Kronecker product).
\\otimes.usage: Multilinear algebra writes V \otimes W, quantum mechanics writes composite states |\psi\rangle \otimes |\phi\rangle, and matrix algebra uses A \otimes B for the Kronecker product. In machine learning it sometimes appears for outer products. It is a binary operator with medium spacing. For iterated products use the big operator \bigotimes_{i=1}^n V_i, and for the tensor product over a ring put the ring as a subscript, M \otimes_R N. Do not use \times, which is the Cartesian or cross product.

\\odot.meaning: Circled dot, commonly used for the elementwise (Hadamard) product of vectors or matrices.
\\odot.usage: Deep learning papers write h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) for elementwise products in LSTMs and attention masks, and numerical linear algebra uses A \odot B for the Hadamard product, often alongside \circ for the same meaning. Physics diagrams use a circled dot for a vector pointing out of the page, though there it is a symbol, not an operator. It is a binary operator with medium spacing; the big form \bigodot also exists. State in your notation section whether \odot means Hadamard product, since some authors use it for XNOR or other operations.

\\ominus.meaning: Circled minus, used for orthogonal complements within a space and some difference-type operations.
\\ominus.usage: In Hilbert space theory H \ominus K denotes the orthogonal complement of a closed subspace K inside H, the counterpart of \oplus. Morphological image processing uses A \ominus B for erosion, and some set-theory texts use it for symmetric difference, though \triangle is more common there. It is a binary operator, so spacing is automatic. Because its meaning varies, define it once in your paper. There is no standard large-operator version. In symmetric-difference usage, A \ominus B equals (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A).

\\oslash.meaning: Circled slash, typically denoting elementwise (Hadamard) division of vectors or matrices.
\\oslash.usage: Matrix computation and machine learning texts write A \oslash B for entrywise division, pairing it with \odot for entrywise multiplication, as in normalized updates x \oslash \sqrt{v}. LaTeX treats it as a binary operator, so it gets the same medium spacing as \odot and \otimes. Note that it is different from \varnothing and \emptyset, which look like a slashed circle but are ordinary symbols for the empty set, and from the Scandinavian letter \o. Since it is not universally known, introduce it in the notation section.

\\star.meaning: Five-pointed star binary operator, used for convolution, Hodge duality and custom products.
\\star.usage: Signal processing sometimes writes cross-correlation as f \star g, differential geometry uses \star for the Hodge star operator, and algebraists use it for generic binary operations or the Moyal star product. Optimal values in optimization are written x^\star, as an alternative to x^*. \star is a binary operator, distinct from \ast (the asterisk) and from the text symbol produced by \bigstar. Because its spacing is that of a binary operator, using it as a prefix operator such as the Hodge star may need braces: {\star}\omega.

\\ast.meaning: Asterisk as a binary operator, typically for convolution or a generic group operation.
\\ast.usage: In math mode \ast is the same glyph as typing *, a binary operator with medium spacing, used for convolution (f \ast g)(t) = \int f(\tau) g(t - \tau)\,d\tau and for generic binary operations in algebra. As a superscript, A^* or A^\ast denotes adjoint, conjugate transpose, dual space or Kleene star depending on the field. It sits centered on the math axis, unlike the raised text asterisk. For a starred optimal value x^\star some authors prefer \star to keep the meanings apart.

\\circ.meaning: Small circle operator, standard for function composition and also used for degrees.
\\circ.usage: (f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) is the main use. As a superscript, 90^\circ gives degrees, though a dedicated degree symbol from a text-companion font may look better, and A^\circ often means interior or the polar set. Some authors use \circ for the Hadamard product, where \odot is the clearer alternative. \circ is a binary operator, so it gets medium space; \bigcirc is a larger circle and \cdot a filled dot. Avoid using the letter o for composition.

\\bullet.meaning: Filled round dot as a binary operator, used for placeholders, generic products and graded objects.
\\bullet.usage: Category theory and homological algebra use \bullet as an index placeholder, as in C_\bullet for a chain complex and H^\bullet for total cohomology. It is also a stand-in argument, f(\bullet, y), and an operation symbol in algebra. Bullet points in itemize lists are produced by \textbullet, not by math \bullet. Compared with \cdot, it is larger and heavier; \cdot is the right choice for ordinary multiplication or dot products. As a binary operator it gets medium spacing, so as a placeholder in f(\bullet) the spacing is fine since it has no left operand.

\\diamond.meaning: Small diamond binary operator, used for generic operations and some modal and algebraic notations.
\\diamond.usage: \diamond appears as an arbitrary binary operation (a \diamond b), in the diamond product of Lie theory, and in automata theory. Modal logic writes possibility as a larger diamond, usually \Diamond or \lozenge, rather than this small binary-operator version. Because \diamond is a binary operator, using it as a prefix operator in front of a formula gives odd spacing; use \Diamond or wrap it as {\diamond}p. It differs from \diamondsuit, the card suit, which is an ordinary symbol.

\\bigcirc.meaning: Large open circle binary operator, bigger than \circ, used for special products and diagrams.
\\bigcirc.usage: \bigcirc is mainly a symbol of choice for custom operations, for example a box-like product, or in temporal logic where a circle denotes the next-time operator, \bigcirc p. It is a binary operator, not a large operator with limits, so it does not grow in display mode the way \bigcup does. To circle a symbol, overlaying \bigcirc is awkward; a drawing-package circled node or \textcircled works better. For composition the smaller \circ is standard. For a circled operator such as \oplus or \otimes, the dedicated commands are a better fit than overlays.

\\triangle.meaning: Upward-pointing open triangle, used for triangles in geometry, symmetric difference and the Laplacian.
\\triangle.usage: Geometry writes \triangle ABC for a triangle, set theory writes A \triangle B for symmetric difference, and some texts use it for the Laplace operator, although \Delta or \nabla^2 is more usual. In standard LaTeX \triangle is an ordinary symbol, not a binary operator, so in A \triangle B you may want \mathbin{\triangle} for proper spacing, or use \bigtriangleup, which is already a binary operator. It is larger and differently shaped than the Greek capital \Delta.

\\triangledown.meaning: Small downward-pointing open triangle, an ordinary symbol rather than an operator.
\\triangledown.usage: \triangledown is a smaller, ordinary-spacing triangle pointing down, used as a decoration or marker in some notations. It is not the same as \nabla, the gradient operator, which has a different shape and is what you want for \nabla f; nor is it \bigtriangledown, which is a larger binary operator. If you use \triangledown as an operation, wrap it in \mathbin for operator spacing. For filled versions, \blacktriangledown is available. In finished papers it appears rarely, mostly as a plot-marker reference in captions or as a custom operation.

\\square.meaning: Open square symbol, used for the d'Alembertian, modal necessity and end-of-proof marks.
\\square.usage: Physicists write \square for the d'Alembert wave operator, \square = \partial_t^2/c^2 - \nabla^2, modal logic uses \square p for necessarily p (often as \Box), and the hollow square serves as the QED tombstone at the end of proofs. In amsthm proofs the tombstone is placed automatically via \qedsymbol, so you rarely type it yourself. \square is an ordinary symbol; \blacksquare gives the filled version. Many logic texts write \Box for necessity; the two glyphs look nearly identical. When used as an operator before a field, no extra spacing is needed.

\\wedge.meaning: Wedge binary operator, for logical AND, the exterior (wedge) product and lattice meets.
\\wedge.usage: Differential geometry builds forms like dx \wedge dy, with \omega \wedge \eta = (-1)^{kl} \eta \wedge \omega. Logic uses p \wedge q for conjunction (\land is an alias), and lattice theory writes a \wedge b for the greatest lower bound; probabilists write s \wedge t for \min(s, t). It is a binary operator with medium spacing. For conjunctions over an index set, use the large operator \bigwedge. In topology X \wedge Y is the smash product of pointed spaces. Do not confuse it with the hat accent \hat or \widehat.

\\vee.meaning: Vee binary operator, for logical OR, lattice joins and wedge sums of spaces.
\\vee.usage: Logic writes p \vee q for inclusive disjunction, and \lor is an identical alias. Lattice theory uses a \vee b for the least upper bound, probability writes s \vee t for \max(s, t), and topology uses X \vee Y for the wedge sum, gluing spaces at a basepoint. For many terms, use \bigvee_{i} p_i. It differs from the letter v and from \veebar, which some texts use for exclusive or. The symbol has binary operator spacing.

\\amalg.meaning: Amalgamation operator, used for disjoint unions and coproducts.
\\amalg.usage: Category theory and topology write X \amalg Y for the coproduct or disjoint union, and group theory uses G \ast_H K for amalgamated free products, with \amalg in some texts. \amalg is a binary operator. For the indexed version with limits, use the large operator \coprod_{i \in I} X_i, which looks the same but scales in display style. Alternatives for disjoint union include \sqcup and \bigsqcup, which have a flatter shape and are more common in set theory.

\\dagger.meaning: Dagger symbol, chiefly used in superscripts for adjoints and Hermitian conjugates.
\\dagger.usage: Quantum mechanics writes A^\dagger for the Hermitian adjoint, so a^\dagger is the creation operator, and linear algebra uses A^\dagger for the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse in some texts (A^+ is the alternative). The dagger also marks footnotes or special entries in tables. In math it is a binary operator, but as a superscript its spacing is irrelevant. In text mode use \textdagger. The double version \ddagger is used for second-level footnotes and some special notations. Quantum field theory uses it constantly for creation and annihilation operators.

\\ddagger.meaning: Double dagger symbol, used as a footnote marker and occasionally as a superscript decoration.
\\ddagger.usage: \ddagger is the second footnote symbol after \dagger in many styles, marking affiliations or table notes. In math it sometimes decorates operators, for example a transition state X^\ddagger in chemical kinetics (activation energy \Delta G^\ddagger). As a math command it is a binary operator, but as a superscript spacing does not matter. In text mode use \textdaggerdbl. Because its meaning is not standardized, explain it where first used. Placed as a superscript, it needs no braces: X^\ddagger works directly.

\\wr.meaning: Wreath operator, written between groups for the wreath product.
\\wr.usage: Group theory writes G \wr H for the wreath product, for example the hyperoctahedral group \mathbb{Z}_2 \wr S_n, and Sylow subgroups of symmetric groups are iterated wreath products. The symbol is a small vertical wavy line set as a binary operator. It looks a little like a rotated tilde, but unlike the relation \sim it carries binary-operator spacing. Some authors write the factors in the opposite order, so state which group acts. Rubik's cube groups and automorphism groups of trees are standard examples where wreath products appear.

\\setminus.meaning: Set difference operator: A \setminus B is the set of elements of A not in B.
\\setminus.usage: Use \setminus for set difference, A \setminus B, and for removal, \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}. It is a binary operator with proper spacing, while \backslash looks the same but is an ordinary symbol used for quotients like G \backslash X (left cosets). A smaller variant \smallsetminus suits some fonts better. Some authors write A - B instead, but \setminus avoids confusion with subtraction. Combined with \complement: A \setminus B = A \cap B^\complement. In fractions like G \backslash X / H for double cosets, keep \backslash for the quotient instead.

\\varnothing.meaning: Variant empty-set symbol: a round circle with a diagonal slash, the set with no elements.
\\varnothing.usage: \varnothing and \emptyset mean the same thing, the empty set, but look different: \emptyset in Computer Modern is a narrow, tall zero with a slash, while \varnothing is a round circle with a slash that many mathematicians prefer. Use one consistently, for example A \cap B = \varnothing for disjoint sets. It is not the Greek letter \phi or \varphi, and not the Scandinavian letter \O, so avoid those as substitutes. Some authors redefine \emptyset to \varnothing in the preamble so every occurrence switches at once.

\\ni.meaning: Reversed element-of relation: the set on the left contains the element on the right.
\\ni.usage:
A 
i x says the same as x \in A, with the set first, which reads naturally in phrases like a neighborhood U 
i x. Older texts and some logicians also used 
i for such that, though \mid or a colon is now standard. \owns is an alias of 
i. Negate it with 
ot
i. Do not confuse it with the letter epsilon or with \in turned around by hand; 
i is a proper relation with matching spacing.

\\not\\subset.meaning: Slashed subset sign: the left set is not a subset of the right set.
\\not\\subset.usage:
ot\subset overlays a slash on \subset using the generic 
ot prefix. The result is acceptable, though the slash is sometimes off-center; the dedicated glyphs 
subseteq (not a subset or equal) and 
subset in some symbol packages look better. Since \subset itself is ambiguous between proper and non-strict inclusion, 
subseteq is often the clearer negation. Example: \mathbb{Q} 
ot\subset \mathbb{Z}, because 1/2 is rational but not an integer. Keep 
ot directly before the relation, with no space or braces, so it combines correctly.

\\bigcup.meaning: Large union operator for the union of an indexed family of sets, with limits above and below.
\\bigcup.usage: \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i writes a countable union, and \bigcup_{\alpha \in I} U_\alpha a union over an index set, as in open covers. It behaves like \sum: limits go below and above in display style and to the side inline, and \limits forces them below inline. Do not use it between two sets; A \cup B uses the binary \cup. Related large operators include \bigcap, \bigsqcup for disjoint unions, and \biguplus for multiset union. De Morgan's laws pair it with \bigcap and complements.

\\bigcap.meaning: Large intersection operator for intersecting an indexed family of sets.
\\bigcap.usage: \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} (0, 1/n) = \varnothing is a standard example, and topology writes \bigcap_{\alpha} F_\alpha for intersections of closed sets. Like other large operators, its limits sit below and above in display mode and beside it inline, and it scales up in display style. For two sets use the binary \cap instead. Nested intervals, the Cantor set \bigcap_n C_n and the definition of the generated sigma-algebra as the intersection of all containing sigma-algebras all use it.

\\complement.meaning: Complement symbol, usually a superscript on a set to denote all elements outside it.
\\complement.usage: A^\complement denotes the complement of A relative to a universe, so A \cup A^\complement = U. It is an ordinary symbol that looks like a stylized C. Common alternatives are A^c, A', and \overline{A}, but the bar can be confused with topological closure and the prime with derivatives, so \complement is unambiguous. Write it as a superscript; on its own it rarely appears. De Morgan's law, (A \cup B)^\complement = A^\complement \cap B^\complement, is a classic use.

\\mathbb{N}.meaning: Blackboard-bold N, the standard symbol for the set of natural numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on.
\\mathbb{N}.usage: Whether \mathbb{N} includes 0 varies: logic and computer science usually start at 0, while number theory often starts at 1, so state your convention or write \mathbb{N}_0 or \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} and \mathbb{Z}_{>0}. The \mathbb font in the standard blackboard-bold font covers uppercase letters only, so \mathbb{1} or lowercase letters will not render as expected without another font package. Many authors define \newcommand{\N}{\mathbb{N}} for brevity. Sequences are often written (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}. Induction proofs typically begin with for all n \in \mathbb{N}.

\\mathbb{Z}.meaning: Blackboard-bold Z, the set of all integers, positive, negative and zero.
\\mathbb{Z}.usage: The Z comes from the German Zahlen. Common constructions include the cyclic group \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, the p-adic integers \mathbb{Z}_p (beware: some authors use \mathbb{Z}_n for the cyclic group instead), the lattice \mathbb{Z}^n, and \mathbb{Z}[i] for Gaussian integers. Subsets are written with subscripts such as \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}. \mathbb works only on capital letters in the standard fonts. Avoid simulating it with bold \mathbf{Z}, which was the older printed convention. In ring theory, \mathbb{Z} is the initial ring, and every abelian group is a \mathbb{Z}-module.

\\mathbb{Q}.meaning: Blackboard-bold Q, the field of rational numbers (fractions of integers).
\\mathbb{Q}.usage: Q stands for quotient. It appears in field extensions like \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}), in density statements such as \mathbb{Q} being dense in \mathbb{R}, and in algebraic number theory with \overline{\mathbb{Q}} for algebraic numbers. The p-adic numbers are written \mathbb{Q}_p. Positive rationals are \mathbb{Q}_{>0} or \mathbb{Q}^+. Since \mathbb only covers uppercase letters, it is fine here. Defining \newcommand{\Q}{\mathbb{Q}} saves typing in algebra-heavy documents. Its algebraic closure is countable, while its completion with respect to the usual absolute value gives \mathbb{R}. Rational points on curves are written C(\mathbb{Q}).

\\mathbb{R}.meaning: Blackboard-bold R, the set of real numbers that make up the continuous number line.
\\mathbb{R}.usage: \mathbb{R}^n is Euclidean space, f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} a real function, and \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} or \mathbb{R}_+ the nonnegative reals (conventions differ on whether \mathbb{R}^+ includes 0). Matrix spaces are written \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}. The extended reals are \overline{\mathbb{R}} or [-\infty, \infty]. Avoid \Re, which prints a fraktur R for the real part of a complex number, not the set of reals. Many authors define a short macro \R. Its completeness, every bounded set having a supremum, is what separates it from \mathbb{Q}.

\\mathbb{C}.meaning: Blackboard-bold C, the field of complex numbers of the form a + bi with a and b real.
\\mathbb{C}.usage: Complex analysis works with functions f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}, linear algebra with \mathbb{C}^n and Hermitian matrices in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}, and algebraic geometry with \mathbb{C}[x] polynomial rings. The punctured plane is \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\} or \mathbb{C}^\times, and the Riemann sphere \hat{\mathbb{C}} or \mathbb{C} \cup \{\infty\}. The fundamental theorem of algebra says \mathbb{C} is algebraically closed. Do not use \mathcal{C}, which usually denotes a category or a class of functions such as C^\infty. Complex projective space is written \mathbb{CP}^n or \mathbb{P}^n_\mathbb{C}.

\\mathcal{P}.meaning: Calligraphic P, the usual notation for the power set (the set of all subsets) of a set.
\\mathcal{P}.usage: \mathcal{P}(A) is the power set, with |\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|} for finite A, and Cantor's theorem says there is no surjection A \to \mathcal{P}(A). Some authors use \wp, the Weierstrass p, or 2^A instead. \mathcal{P} is also used for probability measures, partitions, or the class P in complexity theory, so context matters. The calligraphic alphabet covers uppercase letters only. For a more script-like P, a script font command such as \mathscr from an extra package is an alternative.

|A|.meaning: Vertical bars around a set, giving its cardinality: the number of elements it contains.
|A|.usage: For finite sets |A| counts elements, as in the inclusion-exclusion formula |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|; for infinite sets it is the cardinal number. The same notation means absolute value for numbers and determinant for matrices, so context decides. Alternatives include \#A and \operatorname{card}(A). For spacing that knows left from right, write \lvert A \rvert, and use \left| ... \right| around tall contents like \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}). In combinatorics, |A| = |B| for finite sets is often proved by exhibiting a bijection.

\\aleph.meaning: Hebrew letter aleph, used for infinite cardinal numbers, starting with countable infinity aleph-null.
\\aleph.usage: \aleph_0 is the cardinality of \mathbb{N}, \aleph_1 the next cardinal, and the continuum hypothesis states 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1. Write subscripts as \aleph_0 rather than \aleph0. Other Hebrew letters available in math include \beth, \gimel and \daleth, with \beth numbers \beth_1 = 2^{\aleph_0} measuring the continuum. \aleph is an ordinary symbol. Do not confuse it with \alpha or with N for natural numbers. Cantor's diagonal argument shows that the reals are uncountable, so their cardinality strictly exceeds \aleph_0.

\\nexists.meaning: Negated existential quantifier: there does not exist an object with the stated property.
\\nexists.usage:
exists x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 = 2 states that 2 has no rational square root. The glyph is a slashed \exists designed as a single glyph; 
ot\exists also works but the slash may be misplaced. Logically it is equivalent to  orall x\, 
eg P(x), and many logicians prefer writing 
eg \exists x for clarity. Add a small space or a colon after the bound variable, as in 
exists x \, P(x). For unique existence the symbol is \exists!.

\\neg.meaning: Logical negation sign, an L-shaped hook placed before a formula to mean not.
\\neg.usage:
Logic writes 
eg p for not p and 
eg
eg p \equiv p in classical logic; \lnot is an exact alias. Some texts use \sim p, an overline  ar{p}, or p' instead, especially in Boolean algebra and digital circuits. 
eg is an ordinary symbol, so no space appears between it and its operand, which is the desired look. De Morgan's laws, 
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q, are a typical display. In programming contexts ! or \lnot are both seen.

\\land.meaning: Logical AND (conjunction), true exactly when both operands are true.
\\land.usage: \land is an alias for \wedge, chosen for readability in logic, as in p \land q or \forall x\, (P(x) \land Q(x)). Because LaTeX classes it as a binary operator, the space around p \land q is set automatically; do not add \, by hand. For a conjunction over many formulas, use the large operator \bigwedge_{i=1}^{n} p_i. In Boolean algebra, AND is often written as multiplication, pq or p \cdot q, instead. Use \land in logic and \wedge in exterior algebra so the source reads clearly, even though they print identically.

\\lor.meaning: Logical OR (disjunction), true when at least one operand is true.
\\lor.usage: \lor is an alias of \vee, used in propositional and predicate logic: p \lor \neg p is the law of excluded middle. LaTeX spaces it as a binary operator, so p \lor q needs no manual spacing commands. For many disjuncts, \bigvee_{i} p_i is the large operator. Exclusive or is a different symbol: \oplus or \veebar. Boolean algebra and circuit design often write OR as +. Prefer \lor in logical formulas and \vee in lattice theory for readable source, though both render the same.

\\vdash.meaning: Turnstile, meaning the right-hand formula is derivable (provable) from the left-hand assumptions.
\\vdash.usage: Proof theory writes \Gamma \vdash \varphi for syntactic consequence, and type theory uses it in typing judgments \Gamma \vdash e : \tau. It differs from \models, which states semantic consequence (truth in all models); soundness and completeness say the two coincide in first-order logic. Negate it with \nvdash. \vdash is a relation, so spacing is automatic. For inference rules, \frac or a dedicated proof-tree package produces the horizontal line, with judgments containing \vdash above and below. The mirror symbol is \dashv.

\\models.meaning: Double turnstile: semantic entailment or satisfaction, meaning true in every model.
\\models.usage: \mathcal{M} \models \varphi says structure M satisfies formula \varphi, and \Gamma \models \varphi says every model of \Gamma satisfies \varphi. It contrasts with \vdash, which is syntactic provability. Its negation is \not\models or the dedicated glyph \nvDash. The similar \vDash has slightly different proportions and is used in some logics alongside \Vdash for forcing in set theory. As a relation, it gets spacing on both sides. Model checking writes s \models \phi for a state satisfying a temporal formula.

\\therefore.meaning: Three dots in a triangle, read therefore, introducing a conclusion.
\\therefore.usage: \therefore is common in school mathematics and informal derivations: x + 2 = 5, \therefore x = 3. Formal papers usually prefer words like hence or the implication arrow \implies. It is set as a relation, so spacing is automatic between expressions. The upside-down version, \because, means because. In text, it must still be in math mode, for example $\therefore$, unless you load a text symbol alternative. Because its meaning is clear to most readers, it works well in slides and worked solutions where space is tight.

\\because.meaning: Three dots forming an inverted triangle, read because or since, introducing a reason.
\\because.usage: \because introduces a justification, typically in step-by-step school solutions: \angle A = \angle B \quad \because AB = AC. It is the mirror of \therefore, with the single dot at the bottom. Formal writing usually spells out since or uses a text annotation like \text{(by Lemma 2)}. As a relation symbol it has spacing on either side, and \quad or \qquad before it separates the reason from the equation. Use it sparingly in papers. In proofs, writing the reason in words is usually kinder to readers.

\\bot.meaning: Up tack (bottom) symbol: falsum or contradiction in logic, and the least element of a lattice.
\\bot.usage: Logic uses \bot for an always-false proposition, so deriving \bot proves the negation, and \neg p can be defined as p \to \bot. Domain theory and lattices use \bot for the bottom element, and type theory for the empty type. \bot is an ordinary symbol; the same glyph with relation spacing is \perp, which you want for orthogonality between two objects. Its dual is \top. In proofs by contradiction some authors write \bot or \Rightarrow\Leftarrow at the end of the contradictory step.

\\top.meaning: Down tack (top) symbol: verum, the always-true proposition, and the greatest element of a lattice.
\\top.usage: In logic \top is a tautology, the identity for conjunction (p \land \top \equiv p). Lattices and domain theory use it for the top element, and type theory for the unit type. It is also widely used as a superscript for matrix transpose, A^\top, as an alternative to A^T or A^\intercal. \top is an ordinary symbol. Do not confuse it with the letter T, which sits on the baseline with different proportions. Its dual is \bot.

\\not\\equiv.meaning: Slashed triple bar: not congruent modulo n, or not identically equal.
\\not\\equiv.usage:
Number theory writes a 
ot\equiv b \pmod{n} when n does not divide a - b, for example in Fermat's little theorem hypothesis a 
ot\equiv 0 \pmod{p}. The 
ot prefix overlays a slash on the relation; place it immediately before \equiv. In some fonts the slash looks slightly off-center, but there is no standard dedicated glyph among the common symbol fonts, so 
ot\equiv is the usual choice. In logic it means not logically equivalent. For simple inequality, use 
eq instead.

\\int.meaning: Draws the integral sign, used for antiderivatives and definite integrals such as the area under a curve.
\\int.usage: Write limits as a subscript and superscript: \int_a^b f(x)\,dx gives a definite integral, and the bounds sit beside the sign in display style by default. Add \limits right after \int to stack the bounds above and below, a style some physics texts prefer. Put a thin space \, before the differential so dx does not collide with the integrand. For repeated integrals, \int\int leaves an awkward gap; use \iint or \iiint, which tighten the spacing automatically. In inline math the sign shrinks noticeably, so long or nested integrals usually read better in a display environment.

\\iint.meaning: Double integral sign for integrating a function of two variables over a planar region.
\\iint.usage: A double integral appears whenever you integrate over an area, as in \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA for mass, for probability over a joint density, or for flux through a surface. Typing \int\int by hand produces two signs with too much space between them; \iint kerns them into a single tight pair. Put the region as one subscript, \iint_{D}, rather than splitting bounds across both signs. If you need separate bounds for each variable, write \int_a^b\!\int_c^d instead, since the combined command only takes one set of limits. The \! negative thin space keeps such hand-built pairs from drifting apart.

\\iiint.meaning: Triple integral sign, used to integrate over a three-dimensional solid region.
\\iiint.usage: Volume integrals such as \iiint_V \rho\,dV for total mass, or the left side of the divergence theorem \iiint_V \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}\,dV, use this symbol. Like \iint, it spaces the three signs closer than \int\int\int would, so the result reads as one operator. The region goes in a single subscript; for explicit iterated bounds on each variable, chain separate \int commands instead. There is also \iiiint for four signs and \idotsint, which draws two signs separated by dots for an n-fold integral. In spherical coordinates, remember the Jacobian: dV = r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi.

\\oint.meaning: Integral sign with a small circle, marking integration around a closed curve.
\\oint.usage: Complex analysis relies on it heavily: Cauchy's integral theorem says \oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 0 for holomorphic f, and the residue theorem evaluates such integrals as 2\pi i times a sum of residues. In physics it appears in circulation and in Ampere's and Faraday's laws, for example \oint_C \mathbf{B}\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}. Name the contour in the subscript; \oint_{\partial S} signals the boundary of a surface. A closed surface integral with a circle over two signs is not part of the standard command set, so many authors simply write \iint_{\partial V} and say the surface is closed.

\\frac{d}{dx}.meaning: Leibniz notation for the derivative operator with respect to x, built from a fraction.
\\frac{d}{dx}.usage: Writing \frac{d}{dx} gives the operator form used in rules like \frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x, while \frac{dy}{dx} names the derivative of a dependent variable. Many style guides set the differential d upright, as \mathrm{d}, to separate it from a variable named d; a macro such as \newcommand{\diff}{\mathrm{d}} keeps this consistent. In running text, \frac shrinks to tiny script size, so prefer \tfrac or the slash form dy/dx there. For higher orders write \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}, with the exponent on d in the numerator but on x in the denominator.

\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial x}.meaning: Operator for the partial derivative with respect to x, holding every other variable fixed.
\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial x}.usage: Multivariable calculus and PDEs are full of it: the heat equation \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = k\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}, gradients, and Jacobian matrices all use it. The curly \partial distinguishes it from the ordinary d of \frac{d}{dx}, which is reserved for functions of one variable. Mixed partials are written \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}, with a thin space between the factors in the denominator. When fractions get crowded, the subscript shorthand \partial_x f or f_x is a compact alternative, common in physics and in long PDE systems where stacked fractions would blow up line height.

\\lim_{x \\to a}.meaning: Limit operator with the approach condition x \to a written beneath it.
\\lim_{x \\to a}.usage: Because \lim is a predefined operator, it sets in upright roman and places its subscript underneath in display math, as in \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1. Inline, the subscript moves to the side to save line height; force it below with \lim\limits_{x\to a} only if the extra height is acceptable. One-sided limits use x \to a^+ or x \to a^-, and limits at infinity x \to \infty. The related operators \limsup and \liminf behave the same way. Use \to rather than a hyphen and greater-than sign for the arrow, which would print as two separate symbols.

\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}.meaning: Summation sign with index starting at n = 1 and running to infinity, the shape of an infinite series.
\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}.usage: Infinite series such as the Basel problem \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} or the divergent harmonic series are written this way. In display math the bounds stack above and below a large sigma; inline they shift to the right of a smaller one, which keeps line spacing even. Add \limits if you need stacked bounds inline, or \displaystyle sparingly. Do not use the Greek letter \Sigma as a substitute: it is an ordinary-size letter, not an operator, and will not take limits correctly. Convergence is often stated through partial sums, S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n.

\\prod_{n=1}^{\\infty}.meaning: Product operator over n from 1 to infinity, used to write infinite products.
\\prod_{n=1}^{\\infty}.usage: Classical results such as Euler's product for the zeta function and the Wallis product for \pi are written with it. Like \sum, the bounds go under and over the operator in display style and to the side inline.
