Do not confuse it with \Pi, the capital Greek letter, which has a similar shape but stays ordinary size and takes limits as plain subscripts. An infinite product is said to converge when its partial products approach a nonzero limit, so authors often write \prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1+a_n) alongside the condition \sum |a_n| < \infty, which guarantees convergence.

dx.meaning: Differential of x, closing an integral and naming the variable of integration.
dx.usage: Typed as plain dx, the d comes out italic and sits flush against the integrand, so the usual fix is a thin space: \int f(x)\,dx. ISO style and many journals set the d upright with \mathrm{d}x; a macro like \newcommand{\dd}{\mathrm{d}} keeps this consistent throughout a paper. In multiple integrals, separate differentials with thin spaces, dx\,dy, or abbreviate them as dA or dV. The same differential appears in Leibniz derivatives \frac{dy}{dx} and in differential forms, where products are written dx \wedge dy and order matters because the wedge product is antisymmetric.

f'(x).meaning: Lagrange prime notation for the first derivative of f evaluated at x.
f'(x).usage: Typing an apostrophe in math mode produces a prime as a superscript, so f' is shorthand for f^{\prime}. Prime notation is compact for single-variable functions, as in the mean value theorem f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}. If you also need an exponent, write f'^2, which combines both into one superscript, or group as (f'(x))^2; writing f^2' triggers a double superscript error. Avoid pasting a curly quote character, which does not become a prime, and avoid a bare \prime outside a superscript, which prints full size on the baseline. In physics, a prime can also mark a transformed coordinate such as x'.

f''(x).meaning: Second derivative of f at x in prime notation, describing concavity or acceleration.
f''(x).usage: Two apostrophes in math mode combine into a single superscript with two primes, matching f^{\prime\prime}. The second derivative test uses it: if f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, then c is a local minimum. In mechanics, x''(t) gives acceleration, though the dot form \ddot{x} is preferred for time derivatives. Three primes f''' are still readable, but beyond that switch to f^{(4)}(x), with the order in parentheses so it is not mistaken for a power. Never type a double quote character in place of two apostrophes; it renders as a different glyph entirely.

\\to.meaning: Rightward arrow read as 'tends to' in limits or 'maps to' between sets.
\\to.usage: It serves double duty: in limits, x \to 0 or n \to \infty; in function signatures, f\colon X \to Y. \to is simply an alias for \rightarrow, so the output is identical; pick whichever reads better in source. Do not confuse it with \mapsto, which shows where an individual element goes (x \mapsto x^2), or \longrightarrow, a longer arrow for displays. For modes of convergence, decorate it: \xrightarrow{d} for convergence in distribution, or stack a label with \overset{p}{\to}. It has relation spacing, so no manual spaces are needed around it.

\\Big|_{a}^{b}.meaning: Vertical evaluation bar with limits, showing an antiderivative evaluated from a to b.
\\Big|_{a}^{b}.usage: After integrating, writing F(x)\Big|_{a}^{b} = F(b) - F(a) is the standard shorthand from the fundamental theorem of calculus. \Big fixes the bar at one enlarged size, which suits ordinary fractions; for taller expressions use \bigg| or pair \left. with \right|_{a}^{b} so the bar grows to match whatever precedes it. Some authors prefer square brackets, \Big[ F(x) \Big]_a^b, which leave no doubt about how much is being evaluated. A plain | without sizing is too short and makes the limits crowd the antiderivative, especially after a fraction.

\\mathbf{x}.meaning: Bold upright letter, the usual print convention for a vector such as x in R^n.
\\mathbf{x}.usage: Linear algebra texts and physics papers mark vectors in bold, as in A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}. \mathbf only affects Latin letters and digits; Greek letters such as \alpha stay unchanged, so use \boldsymbol{\alpha} for those. Note that \mathbf gives upright bold, whereas \boldsymbol{x} gives bold italic; ISO style prefers bold italic for vectors, while many textbooks use upright. Alternatives include \vec{x} with an arrow, common in introductory physics, and an underline in handwriting-style notes. Choose one convention and apply it consistently, ideally through a macro so it can be changed in one place.

A^{\\top}.meaning: Transpose of matrix A written with the \top symbol, flipping rows and columns.
A^{\\top}.usage: Using \top as the superscript gives a clean upright T-shaped mark that cannot be confused with a variable named T, which is why many machine-learning and statistics papers write \mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{y} or (AB)^{\top} = B^{\top}A^{\top}. A^T looks similar but uses an italic T, and \intercal is a third option that sits lower and is narrower. Whatever you choose, define a short macro for it so switching styles later is a one-line edit. For complex matrices, the conjugate transpose is usually A^{*} or A^{H}, with \dagger common in physics.

A^T.meaning: Transpose of A marked with a superscript italic T, the most common textbook form.
A^T.usage: Writing A^T is quick and universally understood: the least-squares normal equations A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} appear this way in most linear algebra books. The drawback is ambiguity when T is also a variable, such as a time horizon or temperature, since A^T could then be read as a power. In that situation switch to A^{\top} or the upright A^{\mathsf{T}}. Braces are needed once the superscript has more than one token, so the inverse transpose is A^{-T}, not A^-T. A symmetric matrix is one with A^T = A.

A^{-1}.meaning: Inverse of square matrix A, the matrix whose product with A is the identity.
A^{-1}.usage: It satisfies AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I and exists only when \det(A) \neq 0. The braces are required: A^-1 would superscript only the minus sign and leave the 1 on the baseline. For a 2 by 2 matrix, the explicit formula with \frac{1}{ad-bc} times the adjugate is often typeset in full using bmatrix. In numerical papers, readers understand that the inverse is rarely computed explicitly, so writing \mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b} is fine as notation. Pseudoinverses use A^{+} or A^{\dagger}, and (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} reverses the order.

\\det(A).meaning: Determinant of a square matrix A, the scalar giving its signed volume scaling factor.
\\det(A).usage: \det is a predefined operator, so it prints upright with correct spacing; typing det(A) would italicize three separate variables. Key identities include \det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B) and \det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det(A). Unlike \sin, \det can take limits placed under it in display style, like \lim. For an explicit matrix, the vmatrix environment draws vertical bars directly, so \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc reads naturally. Parentheses are optional when the argument is a single letter, \det A, as with other operators.
\\det(A).example: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc

\\text{tr}(A).meaning: Trace of A, the sum of its diagonal entries, written with an upright 'tr' label.
\\text{tr}(A).usage: The trace appears in identities like \operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA) and in the Frobenius norm \lVert A \rVert_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}A). Using \text{tr} gets upright letters, but it inherits the surrounding text font, turning italic inside a theorem, and adds no operator spacing. The sturdier choice is \operatorname{tr}, or a global \DeclareMathOperator{\tr}{tr} in the preamble, so \tr A spaces correctly without parentheses. Physicists often write Tr with a capital, especially for density matrices. The trace also equals the sum of the eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

\\text{rank}(A).meaning: Rank of A: the dimension of its column space, written with an upright label.
\\text{rank}(A).usage: The rank-nullity theorem reads \operatorname{rank}(A) + \operatorname{nullity}(A) = n, and a square matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is full. \text{rank} gives upright letters, but a theorem environment's italics can leak into it and it has no operator spacing. Prefer \operatorname{rank}(A), or declare \DeclareMathOperator{\rank}{rank} once and write \rank A. There is no built-in \rank command, so typing it without a definition causes an undefined control sequence error. Low-rank approximation via the truncated SVD is a common place you will typeset this.

\\lVert x \\rVert.meaning: Double vertical bars around x, denoting its norm, length or magnitude.
\\lVert x \\rVert.usage: Using \lVert and \rVert instead of \| on both sides tells LaTeX which bar opens and which closes, giving correct spacing in expressions like \lVert -x \rVert, where \|-x\| would treat the minus as a binary operator. Subscripts select the norm: \lVert x \rVert_2 for Euclidean, \lVert x \rVert_1, \lVert x \rVert_\infty, or \lVert A \rVert_F for Frobenius. For tall contents, use \left\lVert ... \right\rVert. The triangle inequality \lVert x+y \rVert \le \lVert x \rVert + \lVert y \rVert is a typical use, and a \norm macro saves a lot of typing in long papers.

\\langle x, y \\rangle.meaning: Angle brackets around two vectors, denoting their inner product.
\\langle x, y \\rangle.usage: Inner products generalize the dot product: \langle x, y \rangle = \sum_i x_i y_i in R^n, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |\langle x, y \rangle| \le \lVert x \rVert \lVert y \rVert is the classic example. Never type the less-than and greater-than signs instead; < and > are relations with wide spacing and the wrong angle. For large arguments, \left\langle ... \right\rangle scales the brackets. In quantum mechanics the same brackets build bra-ket notation, \langle \psi | \phi \rangle, with a bar in the middle. Some books write (x, y) or x \cdot y for the same quantity.

\\delta_{ij}.meaning: Kronecker delta: equals 1 when the indices i and j match and 0 otherwise.
\\delta_{ij}.usage: It packages the identity matrix entrywise, I_{ij} = \delta_{ij}, and expresses orthonormality of a basis, \langle e_i, e_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}. In index notation it acts as a substitution operator: \sum_j \delta_{ij} a_j = a_i, which simplifies tensor calculations. Do not confuse it with the Dirac delta \delta(x), a distribution on continuous variables, even though both use lowercase \delta. Braces around ij keep both indices in the subscript; \delta_ij would lower only the i and leave j on the baseline. In tensor work with mixed indices, write \delta^i_j instead.

I_n.meaning: The n by n identity matrix, with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
I_n.usage: The subscript records the size, so for an m by n matrix A both AI_n = A and I_m A = A hold, with different identities on each side. When the dimension is obvious, plain I is enough; some authors prefer bold \mathbf{I} or write E, especially in older European texts. For multi-character sizes, add braces: I_{n+1} or I_{10}, because I_10 would lower only the 1. The characteristic polynomial \det(A - \lambda I_n) is the standard place it appears, and \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} spells out I_2 explicitly.

\\mathbf{0}.meaning: Bold zero, denoting the zero vector or zero matrix as opposed to the scalar 0.
\\mathbf{0}.usage: Bold distinguishes the additive identity of a vector space from the number zero, as in A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} for a homogeneous system or \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v}. \mathbf works on digits, so this is the simplest form; \boldsymbol{0} gives the same result in most fonts. For a zero matrix of explicit size, write \mathbf{0}_{m \times n} or a capital O_{m \times n}. Many papers drop the bold and write 0 when context makes the type clear, which is acceptable if consistent. Match whichever bold style you use for other vectors.

\\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\\\ c & d \\end{.meaning: bmatrix environment typesetting a matrix in square brackets, with & between columns.
\\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\\\ c & d \\end{.usage: Entries in a row are separated by &, rows end with \\, and the brackets size themselves to the content, so no \left[ is required. Sibling environments change only the delimiters: pmatrix uses parentheses, vmatrix vertical bars for determinants, Vmatrix double bars, and plain matrix none at all. The array environment is the older alternative; it needs a column specification like {cc} but allows vertical rules and per-column alignment. For generic matrices, fill gaps with \cdots, \vdots and \ddots, as in a_{11} & \cdots & a_{1n}. Inline, smallmatrix inside \bigl[ \bigr] avoids stretching the line.

\\begin{pmatrix} x \\\\ y \\end{pmatrix}.meaning: pmatrix with one column, stacking x over y as a column vector in parentheses.
\\begin{pmatrix} x \\\\ y \\end{pmatrix}.usage: Each \\ starts a new row, so a single column of entries becomes a vertical vector, the usual way to write coordinates in R^2 or the right-hand side of a linear system. Parentheses (pmatrix) and square brackets (bmatrix) are equally standard; pick one style for the whole document. To save vertical space in running text, write a transposed row instead, (x, y)^{\top}. For long vectors, use \vdots in a middle row, as in x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_n. Inline column vectors look cramped and push lines apart; smallmatrix is the compact alternative when one is unavoidable.

\\mathbb{P}.meaning: Blackboard-bold P, the probability measure applied to events.
\\mathbb{P}.usage: Measure-theoretic probability writes \mathbb{P}(A) for the probability of event A, with axioms such as \mathbb{P}(\Omega) = 1. The blackboard style separates the measure from a plain P that might name a matrix, a polynomial or a partition. With the standard fonts \mathbb works only on capital letters, so lowercase input produces wrong glyphs. Pair it with \mathbb{E} and an upright Var for a consistent style. A probability space is the triple (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}), with calligraphic F for the sigma-algebra. Some authors use \Pr, a predefined upright operator, instead.

P(A).meaning: Probability of event A, written with an ordinary italic capital P.
P(A).usage: Introductory texts write P(A) for the chance that A occurs, with 0 \le P(A) \le 1 and the complement rule P(A^c) = 1 - P(A). The plain italic P is fine when nothing else in the document uses that letter; otherwise \Pr(A), a predefined upright operator, or \mathbb{P}(A) avoid the clash. For large arguments, let the parentheses grow: P\left(\bigcup_i A_i\right). Typing Pr(A) without a backslash gives italic P and r as two variables multiplied. Conditional probability puts \mid inside the parentheses, P(A \mid B), rather than a bare vertical bar.

\\mathbb{E}[X].meaning: Expected value of a random variable X, written with a blackboard-bold E.
\\mathbb{E}[X].usage: Expectation is the mean of X weighted by its distribution, \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x x\,p(x) or \int x f(x)\,dx. Machine learning papers use it everywhere, often with a subscript naming the distribution: \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}[\ell(x)]. Square brackets are conventional, and \left[ \right] or \bigl[ \bigr] help when the argument contains fractions. The blackboard E sets the operator apart from an energy E or an edge set E. Linearity, \mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y], holds even without independence, which is why it is used so freely.

E[X].meaning: Expectation of X in plain italic E, the mean of its distribution.
E[X].usage: Many statistics textbooks write E[X] or E(X) for the expected value, with the variance identity \operatorname{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 as a standard example. An italic E can collide with other meanings such as energy or an event called E, which is why \mathbb{E} or an upright \mathrm{E} are common in research papers. If you settle on upright, define \DeclareMathOperator{\E}{E} so spacing and font stay uniform everywhere. Conditional expectation follows the same style, E[X \mid Y]. Whichever form you choose, use it consistently from start to finish.

\\text{Var}(X).meaning: Variance of X, the expected squared deviation from its mean, with an upright label.
\\text{Var}(X).usage: The usual identities are \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 and \text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\text{Var}(X). \text{Var} looks right in most places, but inside italic theorem text the label turns italic too, because \text copies the surrounding font. \operatorname{Var} or a preamble \DeclareMathOperator{\Var}{Var} is more robust and spaces correctly. Some authors write \mathbb{V}, \sigma^2 or \mathrm{Var} instead. For independent variables, variances add: \text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y), while the general case adds twice the covariance.

\\text{Cov}(X,Y).meaning: Covariance of X and Y, measuring how the two random variables vary together.
\\text{Cov}(X,Y).usage: Defined by \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y], it underlies the correlation \rho = \text{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y) and covariance matrices, usually written \Sigma. Independent variables have zero covariance, though the converse fails in general. As with Var, \operatorname{Cov} or a declared operator gives sturdier output than \text{Cov}, which picks up italics in theorem statements. Add a thin space after the comma, (X,\,Y), if the arguments look cramped. For a random vector, \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) denotes the full covariance matrix. A positive value means the variables tend to move in the same direction.

\\mathcal{N}(\\mu, \\sigma^2).meaning: Normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean mu and variance sigma squared.
\\mathcal{N}(\\mu, \\sigma^2).usage: Write X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) to state that X is normally distributed; the second parameter is the variance, not the standard deviation, a frequent source of confusion when reading software documentation. The multivariate form is \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma) with a covariance matrix. \mathcal gives the script N and works only on capital letters. The density \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)} often follows in a display. The standard normal is \mathcal{N}(0, 1), and its cumulative distribution function is usually written \Phi.

\\perp\\!\\!\\!\\perp.meaning: Two \perp signs overlapped with negative spaces, the usual hand-built symbol for statistical independence.
\\perp\\!\\!\\!\\perp.usage: Probabilists write X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y for independent random variables and X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z for conditional independence, notation popularized by graphical models and causal inference. Three \! negative thin spaces pull the second \perp almost onto the first, creating a double-stemmed upside-down T. Because it is assembled by hand, its exact look varies a little between fonts; define a macro such as \newcommand{\indep}{\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}} so it also gets relation spacing. A single \perp is used for independence in some texts, but it collides with orthogonality.

\\mid.meaning: Vertical bar with relation spacing, read as 'given', 'such that' or 'divides'.
\\mid.usage: Unlike a plain |, \mid adds space on both sides, which is exactly what conditional probability P(A \mid B), set-builder notation \{x \mid x > 0\} and divisibility 3 \mid 12 need. Use | or \vert for absolute values, where no extra space is wanted, and \lvert ... \rvert when the bar brackets something. In set-builder notation with tall content, \middle| between \left\{ and \right\} grows the bar to match. Its negation is \nmid, for does not divide. Many authors use a colon in set-builder notation instead, which avoids confusion when divisibility also appears.

P(A \\mid B).meaning: Conditional probability of A given that the event B has already occurred.
P(A \\mid B).usage: Defined by P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B) for P(B) > 0, it is the building block of Bayes' theorem. Always use \mid rather than |: the bare bar gets no surrounding space and the expression looks cramped. For tall arguments, write P\left(A \,\middle|\, B\right) so the bar scales with the parentheses. Chains of conditioning, P(A \mid B, C), put a comma after the bar rather than a second bar. In likelihood notation, p(x \mid \theta) follows the same convention, and some statisticians use a semicolon, p(x; \theta), when \theta is a fixed parameter rather than a random variable.

\\chi^2.meaning: Chi-squared: the Greek letter chi squared, naming a distribution and a test statistic.
\\chi^2.usage: Pearson's statistic \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i} compares observed and expected counts, and \chi^2_k denotes the distribution with k degrees of freedom. Note that \chi is the Greek letter chi; do not type an x, which looks somewhat similar but is a different glyph and sits differently on the baseline. To attach both the degrees of freedom and the square, write \chi^2_{k} or \chi_{k}^{2}; LaTeX stacks them identically either way. In results sections, report tests as \chi^2(2) = 6.1, p = 0.047, following your field's style guide.

\\binom{n}{k}.meaning: Binomial coefficient n choose k, the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set.
\\binom{n}{k}.usage: It appears in the binomial theorem (x+y)^n = \sum_k \binom{n}{k} x^k y^{n-k}, in Pascal's rule and in the binomial distribution P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}. \binom sizes itself to the current style; force the large form with \dbinom inline or the small one with \tbinom in display. The older {n \choose k} syntax still works in plain TeX style but is discouraged in LaTeX documents. Some texts write C(n,k) or a prefixed nCk instead; the parenthesized stack is the standard in research writing.

n!.meaning: Factorial of n, the product of all positive integers up to n.
n!.usage: Typing n! needs no command: the exclamation mark prints directly in math mode, with 0! = 1 by convention. Factorials fill combinatorics and analysis, from \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} to Taylor coefficients \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}. Watch spacing in products like n!\,m!, where a thin space keeps the marks from crowding the next letter, and parenthesize compound arguments, (n+1)!. Do not confuse the character with \!, which is a negative thin space. Related notations include the double factorial n!! and Stirling's approximation n! \approx \sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n.

\\sum.meaning: Capital-sigma summation operator, adding up the terms of a sequence.
\\sum.usage: Attach bounds with _ and ^: \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}. In display math the bounds are centered under and over an enlarged sigma, while inline they sit to the side and the sign stays small; \limits and \nolimits override this. Use \sum rather than \Sigma, which is just the Greek letter and neither scales nor stacks limits. For multi-line conditions under the sign, \substack{0 \le i \le m \\ 0 < j < n} stacks them neatly. A sum with only a subscript, \sum_i, is common in physics and machine learning when the range is obvious.

\\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty}.meaning: Sum indexed from n = 0 to infinity, the form used for power series.
\\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty}.usage: Starting at zero is natural for power and Taylor series: e^x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!} and the geometric series \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n = \frac{1}{1-r} for |r| < 1. Check the starting index carefully, since shifting from n = 0 to n = 1 drops the first term and changes the closed form. In display mode the limits are stacked; inline they move beside the sigma. When the upper bound is infinity, \sum_{n \ge 0} is a compact alternative. Generating functions of a sequence a_n are written the same way, \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n.

\\prod.meaning: Capital-pi product operator, multiplying the terms of a sequence.
\\prod.usage: Bounds work as for \sum: n! = \prod_{k=1}^{n} k, and the likelihood L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i \mid \theta) in statistics. It is larger than the letter \Pi and positions limits above and below in display style, so do not substitute the Greek letter. Taking logarithms turns a product into a sum, \log\prod_i a_i = \sum_i \log a_i, a step in nearly every maximum-likelihood derivation. Cartesian products of sets, \prod_{i \in I} X_i, use the same command. Its upside-down counterpart \coprod denotes coproducts.

\\coprod.meaning: Upside-down product sign denoting the coproduct, such as a disjoint union of sets.
\\coprod.usage: Category theory and algebraic topology use \coprod_{i \in I} X_i for the coproduct of a family: disjoint union for sets and spaces, direct sum for abelian groups or modules. It is a large operator like \prod, so limits stack under and over it in display style. Do not confuse it with \amalg, its small binary counterpart for exactly two objects, X \amalg Y. Disjoint unions are also written \bigsqcup, which has a cup-like shape; pick whichever your field uses. The dual construction, the categorical product, uses \prod.

\\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}.meaning: Big union over an indexed family of sets, from A_1 through A_n.
\\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}.usage: Finite and countable unions, \bigcup_{i=1}^{n} A_i or \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n, appear in measure theory for countable additivity, in the union bound of probability, and in topology for open covers. \bigcup is the large operator; \cup is the binary version for two sets, A \cup B. Limits stack under and over in display math and move to the side inline. Index sets need not be numeric: \bigcup_{\alpha \in \Lambda} U_\alpha is common for arbitrary covers. For a union of pairwise disjoint sets, switch to \bigsqcup or state the disjointness in words.

\\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}.meaning: Big intersection over an indexed family of sets, A_1 through A_n.
\\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}.usage: Intersections of indexed families state results like the nested interval property, \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} [a_n, b_n] \neq \varnothing, or define the sigma-algebra generated by a collection as the intersection of all that contain it. Use \bigcap for families and \cap for two sets, A \cap B. De Morgan's law links the two big operators: \left(\bigcup_i A_i\right)^c = \bigcap_i A_i^c. In display style the indices sit below and above; inline, add \limits only if needed. An intersection over an empty index family only makes sense relative to an ambient set, so say what that is.

\\bigwedge.meaning: Large wedge operator for a conjunction over many statements or an exterior power.
\\bigwedge.usage: In logic, \bigwedge_{i=1}^{n} \varphi_i is the conjunction of n formulas, the n-ary form of \wedge (also \land); conjunctive normal form is a \bigwedge of clauses. In lattice theory it denotes the meet, or infimum, of a set, and in differential geometry \bigwedge^k V is the k-th exterior power of a vector space. Limits behave like those of \sum: stacked in display, beside the sign inline. Do not confuse it with \Lambda, the Greek capital, which some authors use for exterior powers at ordinary size. Its dual operator is \bigvee.

\\bigvee.meaning: Large vee operator for a disjunction over many statements or a lattice join.
\\bigvee.usage: Logic uses \bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi_i for an n-fold disjunction, generalizing \vee (also \lor); disjunctive normal form is literally a \bigvee of \bigwedge terms. In order theory and lattices, \bigvee S is the join or supremum of a set S. As a large operator, its limits stack in display math and move aside inline. Avoid using the letter V or a subscripted \vee in its place, since those stay small and do not position limits. In algebraic topology, \bigvee_{i} S^1 denotes a wedge sum of circles, gluing pointed spaces at their basepoints.

\\bigoplus.meaning: Large circled plus, the direct sum of a family of spaces or modules.
\\bigoplus.usage: A diagonalizable operator splits its space into eigenspaces, V = \bigoplus_{\lambda} E_\lambda, and graded rings appear as \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} R_n. \oplus is the binary form for two summands, U \oplus W. In computer science and cryptography, \bigoplus_{i} x_i often means the XOR of many bits, reusing the same glyph. Limits stack in display style like \sum. Note that the direct sum of infinitely many modules differs from the direct product \prod, which allows infinitely many nonzero components, so choose the operator that matches your construction.

\\bigotimes.meaning: Large circled times, the tensor product of a family of spaces or operators.
\\bigotimes.usage: Quantum computing writes the state space of n qubits as \bigotimes_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{C}^2, and multilinear algebra builds the tensor algebra T(V) = \bigoplus_k V^{\otimes k}. The binary form \otimes joins two factors, A \otimes B, which also denotes the Kronecker product of matrices. As a large operator, \bigotimes takes stacked limits in display math. Keep the superscript form V^{\otimes n} for repeated tensor powers of one space; it is more compact than a big operator with bounds. Mention the base ring or field when it is not obvious, as in \otimes_R.

\\bigodot.meaning: Large circled dot, used for an n-ary elementwise or symmetric product.
\\bigodot.usage: \bigodot is the big-operator version of \odot. In machine learning \odot is the Hadamard or elementwise product, so \bigodot_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{v}_i can denote the elementwise product of many vectors; tensor decomposition papers use \odot for the Khatri-Rao product, and some algebra texts use it for symmetric powers. Because its meaning varies by field, define it in your notation section. Limits stack like those of \sum in display style. Do not confuse it with \bigcirc, which is a large empty circle with binary-operator spacing, not a big operator.

\\bigsqcup.meaning: Large square cup, denoting the disjoint union of an indexed family of sets.
\\bigsqcup.usage: Writing X = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} X_i signals both a union and that the pieces are pairwise disjoint, a convention common in topology, measure theory and category theory. The binary form is \sqcup, as in A \sqcup B. \coprod is an alternative some authors prefer for the same categorical construction, while \bigcup alone says nothing about disjointness. In domain theory and denotational semantics, \bigsqcup instead denotes the least upper bound of a directed set. As a large operator, its limits stack in display math and sit to the side inline.

\\sum_{i=1}^{m} \\sum_{j=1}^{n}.meaning: Two nested sums, over i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n, as when adding a matrix's entries.
\\sum_{i=1}^{m} \\sum_{j=1}^{n}.usage: Double sums add up every entry of an m by n array, as in the Frobenius norm \lVert A \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}^2. LaTeX places the two operators side by side with suitable spacing, so no manual space is needed between them. When both indices share a condition, a single sign such as \sum_{i,j} or \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} is more compact, and \substack stacks several conditions under one sigma. Swapping the order of finite double sums is always valid, but infinite ones need absolute convergence or nonnegative terms.

\\sum_{k \\in K}.meaning: Sum over every element k of a set K rather than over a numeric range.
\\sum_{k \\in K}.usage: Set-indexed sums are natural when the index set is not an interval: sums over primes \sum_{p \le x}, over divisors \sum_{d \mid n}, or over vertices in the handshake lemma \sum_{v \in V} \deg v = 2|E|. They make sense for any finite set, and for infinite ones when the series converges absolutely, since no ordering is implied. For several conditions use \substack, as in \sum_{\substack{k \in K \\ k \ne 0}}. In display mode the condition sits centered under the sigma, so keep it short to avoid a wide gap around the operator.

f(x).meaning: Function f applied to an argument x, the basic notation for a function value.
f(x).usage: Single-letter names like f, g and h are set in italic, which is correct for symbols that stand for functions. Multi-letter named functions are different: write \sin x or \log x, and for your own names use \operatorname{softmax}(z) so they print upright instead of as a product of italic letters. In optimization, f(x) is often the objective, as in \min_x f(x) subject to constraints. When the argument is tall, use \left( \right) or \bigl( \bigr) to size the parentheses. For vector arguments, f(\mathbf{x}) with a bold x is common.

f: A \\to B.meaning: Declares f as a function from the domain A to the codomain B.
f: A \\to B.usage: This signature line opens most definitions in analysis and algebra, often followed by the element rule x \mapsto x^2. Typing a bare colon gives relation spacing on both sides, which looks too wide; \colon gives proper tight punctuation spacing, f\colon A \to B. \to and \rightarrow produce the same arrow; \longrightarrow adds emphasis in displays. Pair it with \mapsto for the element-level rule: f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, x \mapsto x^2. Diagrams with several maps between several objects are better drawn with a dedicated commutative-diagram environment.

f \\circ g.meaning: Composition of f with g, meaning apply g first and then f to the result.
f \\circ g.usage: Composition is read right to left: (f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)), and it is associative but usually not commutative. \circ is a binary operator, so spacing around it is automatic. Do not use a baseline \circ for degrees, which need ^{\circ}, and do not confuse it with \cdot or \bullet, which suggest multiplication. Repeated composition is often written f^{\circ n} to avoid ambiguity with powers f^n. The chain rule is the classic formula involving it: (f \circ g)'(x) = f'(g(x))\,g'(x), with the inner derivative on the right.

f^{-1}.meaning: Inverse function of f, the map that undoes f so f^{-1}(f(x)) = x.
f^{-1}.usage: Only bijections have inverses on their whole codomain, but f^{-1}(B) is also used for the preimage of a set B under any function, which is a different concept that needs no invertibility. The superscript -1 does not mean reciprocal: f^{-1}(x) differs from 1/f(x), a common student confusion that also affects \sin^{-1}. Braces are needed because -1 is two tokens. The inverse function theorem gives the derivative (f^{-1})'(y) = 1/f'(x) where y = f(x), provided f'(x) \neq 0.

\\text{Im}(f).meaning: Image of f, the set of all outputs f actually takes, written with an upright 'Im'.
\\text{Im}(f).usage: In linear algebra \text{Im}(T) is the column space of the map, and the rank-nullity theorem reads \dim\ker T + \dim \text{Im}\, T = \dim V. Be aware that \Im is a different command: it gives a fraktur I used for the imaginary part of a complex number. Many authors write \operatorname{im} in lowercase or declare \DeclareMathOperator{\im}{im}, which spaces correctly and does not inherit italic theorem text the way \text does. Set notation f(A) is an alternative when you want the image of a particular subset rather than the whole domain.

\\ker(f).meaning: Kernel of f: everything f sends to zero, a subspace or normal subgroup.
\\ker(f).usage: \ker is a predefined operator, so it prints upright with the right spacing: \ker T = \{v \in V \mid T(v) = 0\}. A homomorphism is injective exactly when its kernel is trivial, and the first isomorphism theorem states G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi. Parentheses are optional for a single symbol, \ker A. In linear algebra the kernel is also called the null space, sometimes written N(A) or \operatorname{null}(A). There is no built-in operator for image to pair with it, so declare \im or use \operatorname{im}.

\\text{dom}(f).meaning: Domain of f, the set of inputs on which the function is defined.
\\text{dom}(f).usage: Convex analysis uses it heavily: \operatorname{dom} f = \{x \mid f(x) < \infty\} is the effective domain of an extended-valued convex function. \text{dom} prints upright but can pick up italics in a theorem environment and lacks operator spacing; \operatorname{dom} avoids both problems. In a signature f\colon A \to B, A is already the domain, so \text{dom}(f) is most useful when the domain is implicit or partial, as with unbounded operators on Hilbert spaces. Some texts use D(f) or D_f instead, so match the convention of your field.

\\text{cod}(f).meaning: Codomain of f, the target set declared for the function's outputs.
\\text{cod}(f).usage: In f\colon A \to B the codomain is B, which may be larger than the image; f is surjective exactly when \text{Im}(f) = \text{cod}(f). Category theory writes \operatorname{cod} f alongside \operatorname{dom} f for the target and source of a morphism. As with other text-based labels, \operatorname{cod} gives better spacing and avoids italic leakage inside theorem statements. Some authors spell out \operatorname{codom} for clarity. Distinguishing codomain from range matters, because some books use the word range to mean the codomain and others the image.

\\text{range}(f).meaning: Range of f, usually meaning the set of values f actually attains.
\\text{range}(f).usage: The word is ambiguous: most modern texts treat range as the image, but some older ones use it for the codomain, so state your definition. In linear algebra, \text{range}(A) is the column space, and the fundamental theorem of linear algebra says it is the orthogonal complement of the null space of A^{\top}. Typesetting with \operatorname{range} gives upright letters with operator spacing; operator theorists often write \mathcal{R}(A) or \operatorname{ran} T instead. \text{range} works, but it follows the surrounding text font, including italics.

\\twoheadrightarrow.meaning: Arrow with a double head, marking a surjective (onto) map or morphism.
\\twoheadrightarrow.usage: Algebraists write f\colon A \twoheadrightarrow B to say f is onto, for example the quotient map G \twoheadrightarrow G/N. It pairs with \hookrightarrow for injections, so a short exact sequence 0 \to A \hookrightarrow B \twoheadrightarrow C \to 0 shows both at a glance. There is a leftward version, \twoheadleftarrow, for maps drawn in the other direction. The arrow is a relation, so spacing around it is automatic. Avoid using it to mean convergence or implication; \to and \implies are standard there.

f|_A.meaning: Restriction of f to a subset A, keeping the rule but shrinking the domain.
f|_A.usage: The restriction f|_A keeps the rule but shrinks the domain, so f|_A\colon A \to B. A plain bar is short and the subscript can look detached from it; many authors write f\big|_A for a taller bar, or use the \restriction arrow, which looks like a half-harpoon. Do not confuse this with an evaluation bar, F(x)\big|_a^b, which uses the same shape for a different purpose. Restrictions are common in topology, where continuity of f|_U on open sets is checked, and in sheaf theory, where s|_U restricts a section to a smaller open set.

f(x) = y.meaning: States that the function f sends the input x to the output value y.
f(x) = y.usage: The equation is the element-level reading of a function: y is the image of x, also written x \mapsto y. In algebra courses, solving f(x) = y for x is how inverse functions are found, giving x = f^{-1}(y). Spacing around = is automatic, so avoid adding manual spaces. For a list of values, align several equations with the align environment, putting & before each equals sign. When the function name has several letters, use \operatorname so it is not italic: \operatorname{relu}(x) = y rather than relu(x) = y.

f(x) = \\begin{cases} a & x > 0 \\\\ b &.meaning: Piecewise definition with the cases environment, giving different rules on different intervals.
f(x) = \\begin{cases} a & x > 0 \\\\ b &.usage: Inside cases, each row holds a value, an &, then its condition, and rows end with \\; LaTeX adds the left brace automatically and no right delimiter. Typical uses are the absolute value, the ReLU activation, the sign function and the Heaviside step. Wrap words in \text{}, as in \text{if } x > 0, so they print upright with normal spacing. Fractions in the rows are set in text style by default, so use \dfrac when they look too small. Make sure the conditions cover the domain without overlap, often ending with an \text{otherwise} row.

\\sin.meaning: Sine function, printed upright as a named operator with correct spacing.
\\sin.usage: Always type \sin rather than sin; the bare letters set as three italic variables multiplied together. The operator adds a thin space before its argument, so \sin x needs no parentheses for a single symbol, while \sin(2x) or \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) group longer ones. Powers go right after the command: \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1. Note \sin^{-1} x is the inverse function, not the reciprocal \csc x. Common formulas include the double-angle identity \sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta and the Taylor series x - x^3/3! + \cdots.

\\cos.meaning: Cosine function, typeset upright as a named math operator like \sin.
\\cos.usage: \cos appears in the law of cosines c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C, in Euler's formula e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta, and in the angle form of the dot product, where cosine similarity in machine learning comes from. Typing cos without a backslash gives italic letters and wrong spacing. Write \cos^2\theta for the square of the cosine; \cos\theta^2 means the cosine of theta squared, which is a different quantity. The command takes no argument itself, so group compound arguments with parentheses, as in \cos(\omega t + \phi).

\\tan.meaning: Tangent function, the ratio of sine to cosine, typeset upright.
\\tan.usage: Defined as \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}, it is undefined where \cos\theta = 0, at odd multiples of \pi/2. Slopes in geometry are tangents of inclination angles, and the identity 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta comes from dividing the Pythagorean identity by \cos^2\theta. Some European texts write tg instead, which has no built-in command; use \operatorname{tg} if you need it. The angle addition formula \tan(a+b) = \frac{\tan a + \tan b}{1 - \tan a\tan b} is a common display equation.

\\cot.meaning: Cotangent, the reciprocal of tangent, written as an upright operator.
\\cot.usage: \cot\theta = \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \frac{1}{\tan\theta}, with poles at integer multiples of \pi. It appears in the identity 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta and in the classic partial-fraction expansion of \pi\cot\pi z used to sum \sum 1/n^2. Russian and some European texts write ctg; use \operatorname{ctg} for that. Its inverse is commonly written arccot, which has no predefined command. Remember that \cot x is the reciprocal of the tangent, not the inverse function \tan^{-1} x. Its derivative is -\csc^2 x.

\\sec.meaning: Secant, the reciprocal of cosine, as an upright named operator.
\\sec.usage: \sec\theta = 1/\cos\theta, and its square appears as the derivative of tangent, \frac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x. The integral \int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + C is a classic of calculus courses and of Mercator projection formulas. Typing sec without a backslash leaves italic letters and loses the space before the argument. In geometry, a secant line is a different object, named in words rather than with this command. Like the other trig commands, powers attach directly, \sec^2 x, with the argument after them.

\\csc.meaning: Cosecant, the reciprocal of sine, set as an upright operator.
\\csc.usage: \csc\theta = 1/\sin\theta, undefined at integer multiples of \pi. Its derivative is \frac{d}{dx}\csc x = -\csc x\cot x, and the identity 1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x completes the Pythagorean trio. Some books, especially older British ones, abbreviate it cosec; that form needs \operatorname{cosec}. A common error is writing \sin^{-1} x when \csc x is meant: the superscript -1 denotes the inverse function arcsine, not the reciprocal. Powers attach right after the command, as in \csc^2 x, with the argument following.

\\arcsin.meaning: Arcsine, the inverse of sine restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2], as an upright operator.
\\arcsin.usage: \arcsin x returns the angle in [-\pi/2, \pi/2] whose sine is x, for x in [-1, 1]. It is the unambiguous alternative to \sin^{-1} x, which some readers misread as 1/\sin x. Its derivative \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} gives the standard integral \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \arcsin x + C, a staple of trigonometric substitution. Software libraries call it asin, but programming names should not appear in typeset math; always use the backslashed command so it prints upright and spaced. Group compound arguments with parentheses.

\\arccos.meaning: Arccosine, returning the angle in [0, pi] whose cosine is a given value.
\\arccos.usage: The angle between two vectors, \theta = \arccos\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert}, is perhaps its most common appearance. Its range is [0, \pi] and its derivative is -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}, which is why \arcsin x + \arccos x = \frac{\pi}{2} for every x in [-1, 1]. \cos^{-1} x means the same thing, but \arccos avoids confusion with the reciprocal. Wrap long arguments in \left( \right) for clarity, since the operator supplies no brackets of its own. In computational geometry it is often clamped to [-1, 1] first to avoid rounding errors.

\\arctan.meaning: Arctangent, giving the angle in (-pi/2, pi/2) whose tangent is x.
\\arctan.usage: \arctan x appears in \int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \arctan x + C and in Machin's formula \frac{\pi}{4} = 4\arctan\frac{1}{5} - \arctan\frac{1}{239}. For the polar angle of a point (x, y) in all four quadrants, programmers use atan2; in papers, write \operatorname{atan2}(y, x) or the complex argument \arg(x + iy). \tan^{-1} x is an accepted synonym, more common in engineering. The series \arctan x = x - x^3/3 + x^5/5 - \cdots converges for |x| \le 1 and gives the Leibniz series at x = 1.

\\text{arccot}.meaning: Inverse cotangent, typed via \text because LaTeX has no built-in \arccot.
\\text{arccot}.usage: Standard LaTeX defines \arcsin, \arccos and \arctan but not \arccot, so this entry builds the label from text. A cleaner approach is \operatorname{arccot} x, which adds operator spacing, or \DeclareMathOperator{\arccot}{arccot} in the preamble so \arccot x works like its built-in siblings. Conventions for its range differ: some texts use (0, \pi), others (-\pi/2, \pi/2] without 0, so state which you mean. Its derivative is -\frac{1}{1+x^2} under either choice. Some authors write \cot^{-1} instead. Pick one form and use it throughout.

\\text{arcsec}.meaning: Inverse secant, written with \text since LaTeX has no predefined \arcsec.
\\text{arcsec}.usage: Defined for |x| \ge 1, \text{arcsec}\, x = \arccos(1/x). Its derivative is \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}} under the usual range [0, \pi] excluding \pi/2, and the absolute value is a frequent omission in student work. Because \text adds no operator spacing, insert \, before the argument or switch to \operatorname{arcsec}. Declaring \DeclareMathOperator{\arcsec}{arcsec} once lets you write \arcsec x just like \arccos x. Integral tables express \int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2-1}} in terms of it. It is rarely used in modern papers, which tend to rewrite it as an arccosine of the reciprocal.

\\text{arccsc}.meaning: Inverse cosecant, assembled with \text because no built-in \arccsc exists.
\\text{arccsc}.usage: For |x| \ge 1, \text{arccsc}\, x = \arcsin(1/x), with values in [-\pi/2, \pi/2] excluding 0. Its derivative is -\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}. It is the least used of the six inverse trigonometric functions, so most writers convert it to arcsine form in final answers. For proper spacing, use \operatorname{arccsc} or declare it as a math operator in the preamble rather than relying on \text, which also turns italic inside theorem environments. Some books write \csc^{-1} x, with the usual risk of being read as a reciprocal.

\\sin^{-1}.meaning: Inverse sine written with a superscript -1, equivalent to arcsine.
\\sin^{-1}.usage: Calculators and many engineering texts label arcsine as \sin^{-1}, so \sin^{-1}(0.5) = \frac{\pi}{6}. The notation clashes with \sin^2 x = (\sin x)^2: by analogy, \sin^{-1} x could be misread as 1/\sin x, which is actually \csc x. For that reason pure mathematics writing tends to prefer \arcsin. Braces around -1 are mandatory, and LaTeX places the superscript right after the operator name, so \sin^{-1} x renders with the exponent before the argument. Whichever notation you choose, use it consistently throughout the document.

\\cos^{-1}.meaning: Inverse cosine in superscript notation, the same function as arccos.
\\cos^{-1}.usage: Physics and engineering often write \cos^{-1} for angles, for instance the angle between two vectors computed from their normalized dot product. It is not the reciprocal 1/\cos x, which is \sec x; the superscript -1 here means function inverse. The output range is [0, \pi], so \cos^{-1}(-1) = \pi. Pure mathematics papers usually choose \arccos to avoid the ambiguity. If your text mixes \cos^2 x for squares and \cos^{-1} x for inverses, mention the convention once so readers are not left guessing.

\\tan^{-1}.meaning: Inverse tangent written as tan to the power -1, equivalent to arctan.
\\tan^{-1}.usage: Engineering and physics use \tan^{-1} for phase angles, as in \phi = \tan^{-1}(\omega L / R) for an RL circuit, and for converting slopes to angles. As with the other inverse forms, it is not \cot x, the reciprocal. Its range is (-\pi/2, \pi/2), so it cannot tell opposite quadrants apart; papers needing the full angle should say they use the two-argument version. Many style guides prefer \arctan in mathematics but accept \tan^{-1} in applied work, as long as the meaning is consistent.

\\sinh.meaning: Hyperbolic sine, (e^x - e^{-x})/2, typeset as an upright operator.
\\sinh.usage: \sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2} parametrizes the unit hyperbola together with \cosh, which is why \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1. It appears in special relativity through rapidity, in catenary problems, and in solutions of y'' = y. Its derivative is \cosh x with no sign change, unlike the circular sine. The inverse is often written \operatorname{arsinh} or \sinh^{-1}; LaTeX provides no built-in command for it. Typing sinh without the backslash gives four italic letters and poor spacing.

\\cosh.meaning: Hyperbolic cosine, (e^x + e^{-x})/2, as an upright named operator.
\\cosh.usage: A hanging chain takes the shape of a catenary, y = a\cosh(x/a), the textbook application. The function is even, always at least 1, and satisfies \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1 and \cosh(ix) = \cos x. In special relativity, the Lorentz factor equals the hyperbolic cosine of the rapidity. Like other operators, \cosh adds a thin space before a single-symbol argument, so \cosh x is fine without parentheses. Its inverse has no predefined command; use \operatorname{arcosh} or \cosh^{-1}.

\\tanh.meaning: Hyperbolic tangent, sinh over cosh, with outputs between -1 and 1.
\\tanh.usage: Neural networks use \tanh as an activation function, often compared with the logistic sigmoid through \tanh x = 2\sigma(2x) - 1. Its derivative is 1 - \tanh^2 x, which keeps backpropagation formulas compact. In physics it appears in mean-field magnetization, m = \tanh(\beta J z m), and in relativistic velocity addition. The output range (-1, 1) makes it handy for squashing unbounded quantities. Its inverse \operatorname{artanh} must be written by hand or declared, as LaTeX has no built-in command for it.

\\text{arcsinh}.meaning: Inverse hyperbolic sine, labelled with \text as LaTeX has no built-in command for it.
\\text{arcsinh}.usage: It equals \ln\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}\right) and gives the antiderivative of \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}. ISO notation calls it arsinh, for area sine, because its argument is an area rather than an arc; many authors still write arcsinh or \sinh^{-1}. Whichever name you choose, \operatorname{arsinh} or a preamble \DeclareMathOperator gives better spacing than \text, which also inherits theorem italics. Data scientists use it as a variance-stabilizing transform because, unlike the logarithm, it handles zero and negative values.

^{\\circ}.meaning: Superscript circle marking degrees, for angles and for temperatures.
^{\\circ}.usage: The usual math-mode degree sign is ^{\circ}, as in 90^{\circ} or \angle ABC = 45^{\circ}; it raises \circ, the composition ring, to superscript size. For temperatures, write 25^{\circ}\mathrm{C} with an upright C. Do not use a superscript letter o or digit 0, which have the wrong shape, or \circ on the baseline, which means function composition. In text mode, \textdegree gives a matching sign without entering math. Documents with many measurements benefit from a units-aware macro that handles spacing and fonts consistently.

\\text{rad}.meaning: Upright 'rad' unit label marking an angle measured in radians.
\\text{rad}.usage: Radians are dimensionless, so most mathematics leaves the unit off and writes \theta = \pi/2; physics and engineering often add it explicitly, as in \omega = 2\pi\,\text{rad/s}. Put a thin space \, between the number and the unit and keep the unit upright; \text does this, though \mathrm{rad} is safer because \text copies the surrounding font in italic contexts. The conversion is \theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\text{deg}} \cdot \pi/180. Note that rad also abbreviates the radical of an ideal in algebra, usually written \operatorname{rad}(I).

\\angle.meaning: Angle sign placed before vertex labels, as in angle ABC at vertex B.
\\angle.usage: Geometry proofs write \angle ABC for the angle at vertex B, and \angle ABC \cong \angle DEF for congruent angles. The symbol is an ordinary math symbol, so no extra space is added after it, which suits names like \angle A. American textbooks often give measures as m\angle A = 60^{\circ}, separating the angle from its size. Related symbols include \measuredangle, which adds an arc to signal a measured or directed angle, and \sphericalangle for angles on a sphere. Avoid it as a prose abbreviation for the word angle.

\\measuredangle.meaning: Angle sign with an arc, often used for a measured or oriented angle.
\\measuredangle.usage: Some geometry texts reserve \angle for the angle as a figure and \measuredangle for its numerical measure, writing \measuredangle ABC = 30^{\circ}. In olympiad geometry, \measuredangle frequently denotes directed angles modulo 180^{\circ}, which makes cyclic quadrilateral arguments independent of the diagram's configuration: A, B, C, D are concyclic exactly when \measuredangle ABC = \measuredangle ADC. Because conventions differ, define what you mean in a notation remark. It behaves like an ordinary symbol, so spacing next to letters is tight.

\\sphericalangle.meaning: Spherical angle sign, used for angles between great-circle arcs on a sphere.
\\sphericalangle.usage: Spherical geometry, navigation and astronomy use it for angles formed by arcs on a sphere, where the angles of a triangle sum to more than 180^{\circ}. Girard's theorem gives the area of a spherical triangle as R^2(A + B + C - \pi), the spherical excess. Its shape differs from both \measuredangle and the plain \angle, so do not swap them freely. Some authors repurpose it for solid or oriented angles, so a one-line definition helps readers. It is an ordinary symbol, so add \, if it sits too close to a following label.

\\ncong.meaning: Slashed congruence sign: two figures or objects are not congruent or not isomorphic.
\\ncong.usage:
In geometry, 	riangle ABC 
cong 	riangle DEF says the triangles fail to be congruent; in algebra, \cong often means isomorphic, so G 
cong H says two groups are not isomorphic. It is a relation, so spacing is automatic. Prefer this precomposed glyph over 
ot\cong, which overlays a generic slash that can sit off-center on the symbol. Related negated relations include 
eq and 
sim. When using \cong for isomorphism, mention the category or structure if it is not obvious, since spaces can be homeomorphic without being isomorphic as groups.

\\simeq.meaning: Tilde over a single line, read as homotopy equivalent, asymptotically equal or isomorphic.
\\simeq.usage: Its meaning depends on the field: topologists write X \simeq Y for homotopy equivalence, category theorists for equivalence of categories, and physicists for approximate equality. Compare it with \cong (tilde over two lines), usually reserved for isomorphism or congruence, \approx (two tildes) for numerical approximation, and \sim for asymptotic equivalence or equivalence relations. Because the conventions overlap, state which one you use. As a relation symbol, it gets wide spacing on both sides automatically, so no manual spaces are needed.

\\frown.meaning: Frown-shaped arc, sometimes placed over letters to mark an arc of a circle.
\\frown.usage: On its own, \frown is a relation-class arc, and set theorists use it for concatenation of sequences, s^\frown t. For the geometric arc between points A and B, the symbol must sit over the letters; \overset{\frown}{AB} does this, though the arc does not stretch, and dedicated wide-arc accents from additional fonts look better on long labels. Its mirror image is \smile, and the two combine in some notations for compatibility relations. Because the plain symbol has relation spacing, check the result when it appears between letters.

'.meaning: A single prime, marking feet, arcminutes or minutes of time after a number.
'.usage: In math mode an apostrophe turns into a superscript prime, so 5'\,9'' reads five feet nine inches, and 12^{\circ}\,30' gives twelve degrees thirty arcminutes. Outside math mode, the apostrophe is a plain closing quotation mark and does not look like a prime, so put measurements in math mode. The same character produces derivative primes, f'(x), and marks transformed points or variables, A' and x'. For geographic coordinates like 40^{\circ}\,26'\,46'', insert thin spaces between the components so they do not run together.

''.meaning: Two primes, marking inches, arcseconds or seconds after a number.
''.usage: In math mode, '' becomes a single superscript of two primes, so 6'' denotes six inches or six arcseconds, and 2^{\circ}\,15'\,30'' writes an angle in degrees, minutes and seconds. Typing a double quote character instead produces a different glyph and should be avoided. In text mode two apostrophes make a closing quotation mark, not a prime, so measurements belong in math mode. The same construct writes second derivatives, f''(x), and doubly transformed points such as A''. Astronomers use it for arcseconds, as in a resolution of 0.1''.

\\overline{AB}.meaning: Bar over AB, the standard notation for the line segment between points A and B.
\\overline{AB}.usage: Geometry texts write \overline{AB} for the segment and plain AB for its length, so \overline{AB} \cong \overline{CD} pairs with AB = CD. The bar stretches over the whole argument, unlike \bar{x}, which is a fixed-width accent for a single letter. Other meanings of \overline include the complex conjugate \overline{z}, the closure of a set \overline{A}, and negation in Boolean algebra, \overline{A \cdot B}. Rays and lines use \overrightarrow{AB} and \overleftrightarrow{AB}, which mark direction or infinite extent.

\\nmid.meaning: Slashed vertical bar stating that one integer does not divide another.
\\nmid.usage:
Number theorists write 3 
mid 10 and use it in hypotheses such as Fermat's little theorem: if p 
mid a, then a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p. It is the negation of \mid and has the same relation spacing; 
ot\mid produces a slash that is often poorly placed, so prefer 
mid. Avoid a plain | with a slash typed by hand. In computer science it appears in conditions on strides, periods and hash table sizes, such as k 
mid n. Related precomposed negations include 
parallel and 
leq.

\\gcd(a, b).meaning: Greatest common divisor of a and b, the largest integer dividing both.
\\gcd(a, b).usage: \gcd is a predefined operator, so it prints upright, and like \lim it accepts limits under it in display style. Bezout's identity says \gcd(a, b) = ax + by for some integers x and y, and a and b are coprime when \gcd(a, b) = 1. Many number theory papers drop the name and write (a, b), which is compact but clashes with ordered pairs and open intervals. The Euclidean algorithm rests on \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b), where \bmod gives binary-operator spacing. There is no matching built-in command for the least common multiple.

\\text{lcm}(a, b).meaning: Least common multiple of a and b, the smallest positive integer both divide.
\\text{lcm}(a, b).usage: Unlike \gcd, there is no built-in \lcm command, which is why this entry uses \text. A preamble line \DeclareMathOperator{\lcm}{lcm} gives a proper operator with matching spacing, or use \operatorname{lcm} inline. The identity \gcd(a, b)\cdot\text{lcm}(a, b) = |ab| links the two. Least common multiples appear when adding fractions with different denominators, in the period of combined cycles, and in the order of an element of a product group. Some texts write [a, b] for the LCM, mirroring (a, b) for the GCD.

\\pmod{n}.meaning: Parenthesized 'mod n' after a congruence, giving the modulus.
\\pmod{n}.usage: Write a \equiv b \pmod{n} to state that n divides a - b. \pmod adds the parentheses and generous spacing before them, which suits displayed congruences. Its siblings serve other cases: \bmod is the binary operator for a remainder, as in a \bmod n = r; \mod gives the word mod without parentheses; and \pod gives only the parentheses. In inline text, the large space \pmod inserts can look excessive, so some authors switch to \bmod or a custom macro. Statements of the Chinese remainder theorem chain several congruences with different moduli.

\\varphi(n).meaning: Euler's totient: how many integers from 1 to n are coprime to n, using the curly phi.
\\varphi(n).usage: Euler's theorem a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n for \gcd(a, n) = 1 and the product formula \varphi(n) = n\prod_{p \mid n}(1 - 1/p) are the standard appearances. \varphi gives the open, looped form, while \phi gives the form with a straight stroke through a circle; both name the same function, and the choice is house style. Many number theory texts pick \varphi so that \phi stays free for other uses, such as the golden ratio or an angle. RSA key generation uses \varphi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1).

\\phi(n).meaning: Euler's totient written with the straight-stroke phi rather than the curly variant.
\\phi(n).usage: Many textbooks write the totient as \phi(n), for instance \phi(p) = p - 1 for a prime p and \phi(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1}. In the default Computer Modern font, \phi is a circle crossed by a vertical stroke, whereas \varphi is the looped form. Both denote the same function, so choose one and stay consistent. If the golden ratio, an angle or a potential also appears, reserve \phi for one meaning and \varphi for the other. Multiplicativity, \phi(mn) = \phi(m)\phi(n) for coprime m and n, is a common display.

p.meaning: Lowercase italic p, the conventional letter for a prime number in number theory.
p.usage: By convention p, and q for a second prime, denote primes, so statements like 'for every prime p' or sums and products indexed by p need little further explanation. Euler's product \zeta(s) = \prod_p (1 - p^{-s})^{-1} is the classic case where the index runs over primes implicitly. Typing p in math mode gives the italic letter; keep it in math mode in prose too, so it matches the displays. To avoid ambiguity with probabilities or p-values, state the convention early. Prime powers are written p^k, and the p-adic numbers \mathbb{Q}_p.

p_n.meaning: Subscripted p_n naming the n-th prime, so p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, p_3 = 5.
p_n.usage: Sequences of primes are indexed this way in results like Euclid's proof, where p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1 has a prime factor outside the list, and in the asymptotic p_n \sim n\ln n from the prime number theorem. Multi-character subscripts need braces, p_{n+1}, otherwise only the n is lowered. Bertrand's postulate becomes p_{n+1} < 2p_n. The primorial, the product of the first n primes, is often written p_n\#. The prime-counting function \pi(x) is essentially the inverse of n \mapsto p_n.

\\left(\\frac{a}{p}\\right).meaning: Legendre symbol (a/p): 1, -1 or 0 depending on whether a is a quadratic residue mod p.
\\left(\\frac{a}{p}\\right).usage: For an odd prime p, \left(\frac{a}{p}\right) equals 1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, -1 if it is not, and 0 if p \mid a. Quadratic reciprocity is the famous identity relating \left(\frac{p}{q}\right) and \left(\frac{q}{p}\right) through the sign (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}\frac{q-1}{2}}. \left( \right) sizes the parentheses to the fraction automatically. Do not use \binom, which omits the fraction bar the symbol requires; \genfrac{(}{)}{}{}{a}{p} is an equivalent alternative. Euler's criterion computes it as a^{(p-1)/2} modulo p.

[x].meaning: Square brackets around x, an older notation for the integer part or floor of x.
[x].usage: Classical number theory and many olympiad texts write [x] for the greatest integer not exceeding x, as in Legendre's formula for the exponent of p in n!, which sums [n/p^k] over k \ge 1. Modern writing prefers \lfloor x \rfloor, which is unambiguous, because square brackets also group expressions, denote closed intervals and serve as Iverson brackets. If you keep [x], define it explicitly. For negative numbers, floor and truncation differ: \lfloor -2.5 \rfloor = -3, while truncation toward zero gives -2.

\\{x\\}.meaning: Fractional part of x, defined as x minus its floor, written with escaped braces.
\\{x\\}.usage: Since bare braces only group in LaTeX, the visible ones must be escaped as \{ and \}. The fractional part satisfies x = \lfloor x \rfloor + \{x\} with 0 \le \{x\} < 1, and it appears in equidistribution results such as Weyl's theorem that \{n\alpha\} is uniformly distributed for irrational \alpha. The same braces also denote sets, so \{x\} could be read as the singleton containing x; define the notation or write \operatorname{frac}(x). For taller contents, use \left\{ ... \right\}.

\\sigma(n).meaning: Sum-of-divisors function: the total of all positive divisors of n.
\\sigma(n).usage: \sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d, so \sigma(6) = 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 12. A number is perfect exactly when \sigma(n) = 2n, and the general form \sigma_k(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d^k includes the divisor count as \sigma_0. The function is multiplicative, with \sigma(p^k) = \frac{p^{k+1}-1}{p-1} for prime powers, so it can be computed from a factorization. Lowercase \sigma also means standard deviation, so a short remark helps in interdisciplinary work. Capital \Sigma is unrelated here.

\\mu(n).meaning: Möbius function: 0 if a squared prime divides n, otherwise (-1)^k for k prime factors.
\\mu(n).usage: Its main role is Möbius inversion: if g(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d), then f(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d)\, g(n/d). It also satisfies \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(d) = 0 for n > 1, and its Dirichlet series is the reciprocal of the zeta function, \frac{1}{\zeta(s)} = \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\mu(n)}{n^s}. The letter \mu is heavily overloaded, meaning a mean in statistics and a measure in analysis, so introduce it explicitly. In math mode, use the Greek \mu, never a Latin u as a lookalike.

d(n).meaning: Divisor-counting function: how many positive divisors n has.
d(n).usage: d(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} 1, so d(12) = 6. For n = p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}, the formula d(n) = (a_1+1)\cdots(a_k+1) shows it is multiplicative. Other common names are \tau(n) and \sigma_0(n), so check which one your reference uses. Dirichlet's divisor problem studies the average order, \sum_{n \le x} d(n) = x\ln x + (2\gamma - 1)x + O(\sqrt{x}). Watch out: the letter d is also the usual divisor variable inside such sums, so prefer \tau(n) when both would appear in one formula.

\\preccurlyeq.meaning: Curly 'precedes or equal' relation, used for non-strict orders and preference relations that are not the usual numeric ≤.
\\preccurlyeq.usage: Order theorists and economists reach for \preccurlyeq when an abstract preorder needs a symbol visibly different from \leq, for example a consumer's weak preference x \preccurlyeq y or the dominance order on partitions. Its strict partner is \prec, and its mirror is \succcurlyeq. Do not confuse it with \preceq, which has a straight bar underneath instead of the curved one; some authors use both in one paper to mark two distinct orders. Because it is a relation, TeX surrounds it with thick spaces automatically, so never pad it with manual \, or \; commands.
\\preccurlyeq.example: x \preccurlyeq y \text{ and } y \preccurlyeq z \implies x \preccurlyeq z

\\succcurlyeq.meaning: Curly 'succeeds or equal' relation, the reverse of \preccurlyeq for weak orders, preferences, and majorization.
\\succcurlyeq.usage:
In microeconomics x \succcurlyeq y reads 'x is weakly preferred to y', and in linear algebra it sometimes marks majorization or a generalized inequality. The straight-barred \succeq looks similar and is the more common choice for positive semidefinite matrices (A \succeq 0), so pick one convention and keep it consistent through a paper. The strict version is \succ. Since a relation symbol can be negated awkwardly with 
ot, check the output: dedicated negations such as 
succeq exist for the straight-bar form and usually look better than 
ot\succcurlyeq.

\\nless.meaning: Negated less-than sign: states that one quantity is not strictly smaller than another.
\\nless.usage:
Writing a 
less b is logically the same as a \geq b in a total order, but in a partial order the two say different things, which is exactly when 
less earns its place: two incomparable elements satisfy both a 
less b and b 
less a. The glyph is a single precomposed symbol with a slash, so it is cleaner than 
ot< whose slash can sit off-centre. Its companion for the other direction is 
gtr. For negated non-strict versions use 
leq or 
leqslant rather than stacking 
ot.

\\ngtr.meaning: Negated greater-than sign, asserting that the left side is not strictly larger than the right.
\\ngtr.usage:
The command name drops the vowels of 'greater' (
gtr, not 
gt or 
greater), which trips people up when typing from memory. In a linear order x 
gtr y simply means x \leq y, so most writers prefer the positive form; 
gtr is more natural in partial orders, lattices, or when quoting the failure of a hypothesis, such as a sequence that is not eventually greater than a bound. Pair it with 
less for the opposite direction and 
geq for the negated non-strict version. It has relation spacing like > itself.

\\nleq.meaning: Not less than or equal to: negation of ≤ with a slash through the horizontal-bar form.
\\nleq.usage:
Use 
leq when stating that an inequality fails, for example in counterexamples or in posets where x 
leq y does not imply y \leq x. There are three related glyphs: 
leq negates the single-bar \leq, 
leqslant negates the slanted \leqslant, and 
leqq negates the double-bar \leqq. Match the negation to whatever un-negated style the rest of your document uses so the symbols look like a family. A precomposed 
leq is preferable to 
ot\leq, which places a generic slash that may not align with the bar.
\\nleq.example: \exists\, x, y \in P : x \nleq y \text{ and } y \nleq x

\\ngeq.meaning: Not greater than or equal to: the slashed form of ≥, signalling that the inequality fails.
\\ngeq.usage:
In real analysis x 
geq 0 is just x < 0, but in vector or matrix orderings it is weaker: a vector can fail to be componentwise nonnegative without being negative, so 
geq is the honest symbol there. It belongs to the same set as 
leq, 
geqslant and 
geqq, and you should choose the version whose un-negated twin appears in your text. Avoid 
ot\geq if you care about appearance, since the generic slash is positioned for = and can look misplaced. Like all relations it takes thick spacing automatically.

\\min.meaning: Minimum operator, giving the smallest value of a finite set or the least value a function attains.
\\min.usage: \min is a predefined operator name: it prints upright 'min' with correct spacing, and in display math a subscript goes underneath, as in \min_{x \in S} f(x). Inline, the subscript moves to the side to save line height; force it below with \min\limits_{x} if you really need to. Typing plain min in math mode gives three italic variables multiplied together, a frequent mistake. For the minimizing argument there is no built-in command, so define \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} in the preamble. Distinguish \min from \inf, which need not be attained.

\\max.meaning: Maximum operator: the largest element of a set or the greatest value a function reaches on its domain.
\\max.usage: Optimization problems, the max norm \|x\|_\infty = \max_i |x_i|, and ReLU activations \max(0, x) all rely on \max. It behaves like \sum with respect to limits: below the operator in display style, beside it in inline text. Brackets after it are not auto-sized, so write \max\left( a, b \right) or \max\bigl( \dots \bigr) when the argument contains fractions. When the maximum might not exist, use \sup instead. For an argmax operator, declare one with the starred \DeclareMathOperator* so its subscript also goes underneath in displays.

\\inf.meaning: Infimum, the greatest lower bound of a set of reals, which exists even when no minimum does.
\\inf.usage: The set \{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} has \inf equal to 0 but no minimum, the classic example of why analysis needs \inf instead of \min. The command typesets upright 'inf' with operator spacing and display-style limits underneath, so \inf_{n \ge 1} a_n looks right in an equation environment. A common slip is confusing \inf with \infty, which is the infinity symbol. Related operators include \liminf, which already exists as a command, and essential infimum, which you would define yourself, for instance with \operatorname*{ess\,inf}.

\\sup.meaning: Supremum: the least upper bound of a set, central to completeness of the reals and to norm definitions.
\\sup.usage: Operator norms are written \|A\| = \sup_{\|x\| = 1} \|Ax\|, and the uniform norm of a function is \sup_x |f(x)|. The command places its subscript below in display mode and to the right inline, just like \lim. Use \limsup for the limit superior rather than combining \lim and \sup by hand, and remember that \sup exists for every bounded nonempty subset of the reals whereas \max may not. When the subscript condition is long, stack lines with \substack{...} under the operator instead of cramming one wide subscript.

\\text{lub}.meaning: Abbreviation 'lub' for least upper bound, an older synonym of supremum common in order theory and lattices.
\\text{lub}.usage: Textbooks on posets and lattices sometimes write \text{lub}\, S instead of \sup S, and the join a \vee b is the lub of a pair. Typesetting it with \text works, but it has two drawbacks: \text copies the surrounding font, so inside an italic theorem it turns italic, and it gives no operator spacing before the argument. The cleaner approach is \operatorname{lub} or a preamble line \DeclareMathOperator{\lub}{lub}, which keeps it upright and spaced like \sup. Use the starred declaration if you want subscripts placed underneath in displays.

\\text{glb}.meaning: Abbreviation 'glb' for greatest lower bound, the order-theoretic name for the infimum of a set.
\\text{glb}.usage: In lattice theory the meet a \wedge b is defined as the glb of a and b, and complete lattices are those where every subset has a glb and lub. Because LaTeX has no built-in \glb, people write \text{glb}, which renders upright in normal text but inherits italics inside theorem environments and lacks the thin space an operator should have. Prefer \operatorname{glb} or \DeclareMathOperator{\glb}{glb} for consistent results. If your readers come from analysis rather than order theory, \inf may be the more familiar notation for the same concept.

\\barwedge.meaning: Wedge with a bar above it, used as the NAND (Sheffer stroke) connective: true unless both inputs are true.
\\barwedge.usage: NAND is functionally complete, so every Boolean function can be built from p \barwedge q alone, and digital designers use it for exactly that reason. Logicians also write the Sheffer stroke as a vertical bar, p \mid q or p \uparrow q, so state your notation once. \barwedge is a binary operator, giving medium spacing on each side. Do not mix it up with \veebar, which has the bar beneath a vee and usually denotes exclusive or, or with \doublebarwedge, which carries two bars. Its truth table is the complement of \wedge.

\\bar{\\vee}.meaning: A vee with a bar accent on top, built by hand to represent NOR (Peirce's arrow): true only when both inputs are false.
\\bar{\\vee}.usage: There is no standard single command for the NOR glyph in the common math fonts, so \bar{\vee} fakes it by putting an accent over the or symbol. One side effect: an accented symbol becomes an ordinary atom and loses the binary-operator spacing that \vee had, so write \mathbin{\bar{\vee}} to restore it, ideally inside a \newcommand. The alternative notation p \downarrow q (Peirce's arrow) is widely understood and avoids the issue. Do not confuse this with \veebar, whose bar sits below the vee and normally means XOR.

A \\cdot B.meaning: Centred dot between two variables, the engineering notation for Boolean AND (logical conjunction).
A \\cdot B.usage: Switching algebra and digital electronics write conjunction multiplicatively: A \cdot B, or simply AB, mirroring how AND behaves like multiplication on 0 and 1. In formal logic the same operation is written A \wedge B or A \land B. \cdot is a binary operator, so it already gets medium spacing; do not use a period, which in math mode is punctuation-like and sits on the baseline. Many textbooks drop the dot entirely in sum-of-products expressions such as AB + \overline{A}C, keeping \cdot only where juxtaposition would be ambiguous, for example between multi-letter signal names.

A + B.meaning: Plus sign used as Boolean OR in switching algebra: the output is 1 when at least one input is 1.
A + B.usage: Circuit designers write disjunction as A + B, so sum-of-products forms like AB + \overline{A}C read naturally. Be careful about the arithmetic meaning: in Boolean algebra 1 + 1 = 1, while in the field with two elements the plus sign means XOR and 1 + 1 = 0, which is why XOR often gets its own symbol \oplus. Logicians write the same OR as A \vee B or A \lor B. No special command is needed; the + already carries binary-operator spacing, and in long expressions you can break lines before a + inside a multline environment.

\\overline{A}.meaning: Bar drawn across the full width of its argument; marks Boolean NOT in logic circuits and set closure in topology.
\\overline{A}.usage: In digital logic \overline{A} is the inverted signal, and \overline{A \cdot B} draws one continuous bar over a whole expression, which is the visual reason engineers favour it over a prefix \neg. Topologists use the same construct for the closure of a set. Compared with \bar{A}, which is a fixed-width accent meant for a single letter, \overline stretches to cover everything inside the braces. Nested negations like \overline{\overline{A}} stack cleanly. For a slightly shorter bar on single letters some authors prefer \bar; either is fine as long as you are consistent.

A'.meaning: A prime after a variable or set, a compact notation for the complement or Boolean negation of A.
A'.usage: Set theory courses often write A' for the complement U \setminus A, and some logic design books write A' instead of \overline{A} because it fits on one line and is easy to type. In math mode the apostrophe becomes a superscript \prime automatically, so A'' gives a double prime with correct spacing. The danger is ambiguity: A' also denotes derivatives, derived sets in topology, and dual spaces. Alternatives include A^c and A^{\complement}. Whichever you pick, define it once near the start of the document.
