\\overline{A \\cdot B} = \\overline{A} +.meaning: De Morgan's law in Boolean notation: the complement of an AND equals the OR of the complements.
\\overline{A \\cdot B} = \\overline{A} +.usage:
This identity lets designers convert AND-based circuits to OR-based ones and is the reason a NAND gate equals an OR gate with inverted inputs. Its dual reads \overline{A + B} = \overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}. The example shows why \overline matters: one long bar over A \cdot B visibly differs from separate bars over each letter, and that distinction is the whole content of the law. In set notation the same law is (A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c, and in logic 
eg(p \wedge q) \equiv 
eg p \vee 
eg q.

\\exists!.meaning: There exists exactly one: the existential quantifier followed by an exclamation mark to demand uniqueness.
\\exists!.usage: Uniqueness statements such as the existence of a unique solution to an initial value problem, or a unique identity element in a group, are written \exists! x. The exclamation mark is a closing symbol in TeX math, so \exists! x spaces sensibly, though some authors add \, before the variable for clarity. Formally \exists! x\, P(x) abbreviates \exists x\,(P(x) \wedge \forall y\,(P(y) \to y = x)). Avoid \exists_1, which some readers parse as a subscripted variable. In prose, 'there is a unique' often reads better than the symbol.
\\exists!.example: \forall a \in G\; \exists!\, b \in G : ab = e

\\forall x.meaning: Universal quantifier applied to x, asserting that the following statement holds for every value of x.
\\forall x.usage: Definitions of continuity, group axioms, and induction principles all open with \forall x. The \forall symbol is an ordinary math atom, so TeX inserts no space after the variable; adding \, or a colon, as in \forall x\, P(x) or \forall x : P(x), makes long formulas much easier to read. Some authors put the quantifier after the statement in words ('for all x'), which is gentler in prose. Keep \forall out of running sentences as an abbreviation for 'for all' unless your audience expects that shorthand.

\\exists x.meaning: Existential quantifier binding x, claiming at least one value of x makes the statement true.
\\exists x.usage: Typical uses include the definition of a limit (\exists \delta > 0), surjectivity (\forall y\, \exists x : f(x) = y), and witnesses in logic. Order matters: \forall y \exists x differs from \exists x \forall y, so write quantifier strings carefully. Its negated form \nexists exists as its own symbol for 'there is no'. Like \forall, \exists gets no automatic space after the bound variable, so add a thin space or colon before the predicate. For uniqueness, append an exclamation mark to get \exists!.

\\forall x \\in A.meaning: Bounded universal quantifier: the statement must hold for every element x of the set A.
\\forall x \\in A.usage: Restricting the quantifier to a set, as in \forall x \in A, is shorthand for \forall x\,(x \in A \to P(x)) and is how most mathematicians actually write. \in has relation spacing, so the phrase spaces itself; just separate it from the predicate with a comma, colon, or \; for readability. With several variables you can write \forall x, y \in A rather than repeating the quantifier. Do not confuse \in with \epsilon or \varepsilon, which look similar in some fonts but are letters, not the membership relation.

\\exists x \\in A.meaning: Bounded existential quantifier: some element x belonging to A satisfies the condition that follows.
\\exists x \\in A.usage: This compact form replaces \exists x\,(x \in A \wedge P(x)), and it appears constantly in analysis, for example the density of the rationals: between any two reals \exists q \in \mathbb{Q}. The negation of \exists x \in A\, P(x) is \forall x \in A\, \neg P(x), a rule worth keeping in mind when negating definitions. Use \nexists x \in A for 'no element of A'. Put a colon, 'such that', or \; before the predicate so the reader can see where the quantifier ends.

:.meaning: Colon read as 'such that' in quantified statements and set-builder notation, separating a variable from its condition.
:.usage: In math mode a plain colon is treated as a relation, getting equal thick space on both sides, which suits \{x : x > 0\} and \forall x : P(x). For a function signature use \colon instead, since it has punctuation spacing: f\colon A \to B looks right, whereas f : A \to B leaves a gap before the colon. For definitions, := built from two characters can look misaligned vertically; a dedicated definition symbol from an extension package fixes that. Some authors prefer \mid or a vertical bar in set-builder notation; choose one and stay consistent.

\\{ x \\mid P(x) \\}.meaning: Set-builder notation: the set of all x for which the property P(x) holds, written with braces and a divider.
\\{ x \\mid P(x) \\}.usage: Braces must be escaped as \{ and \} in math mode, otherwise they only group and vanish from the output. \mid is a relation, so it gets proper space on both sides, unlike a bare | which is an ordinary symbol and crowds the letters. When the condition contains fractions or tall material, size everything together: \left\{ x \;\middle|\; \frac{x}{2} \in \mathbb{Z} \right\}. A colon works equally well as the separator and avoids confusion when the condition itself contains absolute values.

\\forall x \\exists y : P(x, y).meaning: A nested quantifier sentence: for every x some y exists making P(x, y) true, with y allowed to depend on x.
\\forall x \\exists y : P(x, y).usage: This pattern underlies epsilon-delta definitions and statements like 'every integer has a successor'. Swapping the order to \exists y \forall x produces a much stronger claim, a single y working for all x, and confusing the two is a classic error in proofs. The colon separates the quantifier prefix from the matrix formula; if your colon convention clashes with function notation elsewhere, use a period or brackets instead. For readability in longer prefixes, add \, between quantifier blocks, or set each in its own phrase: for all x there exists y.

i.meaning: The imaginary unit, a number whose square is −1; the basis of complex arithmetic.
i.usage: Mathematicians and physicists write i for the square root of -1, giving z = a + bi and the Schrodinger equation's i\hbar. In math mode plain i is italic, the same as an index variable, so in papers that also sum over i it is safer to use upright \mathrm{i}, which is what the ISO typesetting standard recommends; a macro such as \newcommand{\iu}{\mathrm{i}} keeps this consistent. Do not use \imath for the imaginary unit: it is a dotless i meant for placing accents like \hat{\imath} for unit vectors. Game theorists also use i for a player index.

j.meaning: Engineering symbol for the imaginary unit, chosen because i is reserved for electric current.
j.usage: Electrical engineers write impedances as Z = R + jX and phasors as V e^{j\omega t}, and Python uses j for complex literals for the same historical reason. Signal-processing texts follow this too, writing the Fourier transform with e^{-j\omega t}. As with i, an upright \mathrm{j} distinguishes the constant from an index variable j. \jmath, the dotless j, is for accents such as \hat{\jmath}, not for the imaginary unit. Note that many textbooks place j before the number, writing j5 rather than 5j.

z = a + bi.meaning: Rectangular (Cartesian) form of a complex number, with real part a and imaginary part b.
z = a + bi.usage: Every complex number can be written as a + bi with a and b real; this form is best for addition and for reading off \Re z = a and \Im z = b. Multiplication and powers are usually easier in polar form r e^{i\theta}. Writing bi, with the unit last, is the common convention, though engineers often write a + jb. If your document typesets i upright, keep it upright here too: a + b\mathrm{i}. When b is negative, write a - bi rather than a + (-b)i, and for specific numbers put i after numerals, as 3 + 4i.

\\Re(z).meaning: Real part of the complex number z: for z = a + bi it returns the real number a.
\\Re(z).usage: The built-in \Re prints a Fraktur capital R, the traditional real-part symbol, but many modern authors find it hard to read and write \operatorname{Re}(z) instead, which renders upright 'Re' with operator spacing. Either way, \Re is just a symbol, not an operator, so TeX adds no space before the argument; use parentheses or a thin space. A useful identity is \Re z = (z + \bar{z})/2. In signal processing, \Re\{\cdot\} with braces is common for extracting the physical signal from a phasor.

\\Im(z).meaning: Imaginary part of z, the real coefficient b in z = a + bi (not the term bi itself).
\\Im(z).usage: A frequent student error is thinking \Im(3 + 4i) = 4i; it is 4, a real number. The symbol is a Fraktur I, and like \Re it can look obscure, so \operatorname{Im}(z) is a popular, more legible alternative. Beware that Im also abbreviates the image of a map in algebra; if both meanings appear, write \operatorname{im} f for the image to avoid clashes. Useful facts include \Im z = (z - \bar{z})/(2i) and that the upper half-plane is the set where \Im z > 0.

\\bar{z}.meaning: Complex conjugate of z, reflecting it across the real axis: the conjugate of a + bi is a − bi.
\\bar{z}.usage: Mathematicians write \bar{z}, and identities like z\bar{z} = |z|^2 make it central to dividing complex numbers. \bar is a fixed-width accent meant for one character; for a conjugated expression use \overline{z + w}, which stretches across the whole argument and makes \overline{z + w} = \bar{z} + \bar{w} legible. Physicists more often write z^* and reserve the bar for other purposes, such as Dirac adjoints \bar{\psi}. In Wirtinger calculus \partial / \partial \bar{z} treats \bar{z} as an independent variable.

z^*.meaning: Asterisk notation for the complex conjugate, standard in physics and electrical engineering.
z^*.usage: Quantum mechanics writes probabilities as \psi^* \psi and inner products with conjugated components, so z^* is the norm there. In a superscript the asterisk is fine as typed; z^{\ast} gives the same glyph. For matrices, A^* often means the conjugate transpose in mathematics, while physicists write A^\dagger for that and keep A^* for plain entrywise conjugation, so state your convention. A star can also mark an optimum (x^*) or a dual space (V^*), so avoid the notation if those meanings appear nearby.

|z|.meaning: Modulus (absolute value) of z, its distance from the origin: √(a² + b²) for z = a + bi.
|z|.usage: Bare vertical bars work for simple cases but are ambiguous to TeX, which cannot tell opening from closing; that causes bad spacing in expressions like |-z|. Use \lvert z \rvert, or define a macro, to get correct spacing, and \left| \frac{z}{w} \right| when the content is tall. Never use \mid here: it is a relation with wide spacing. Key properties are |zw| = |z||w| and the triangle inequality |z + w| \leq |z| + |w|. In vector contexts the double bars \| \| denote a norm instead.

\\arg(z).meaning: Argument of z: the angle from the positive real axis to z, defined up to multiples of 2π.
\\arg(z).usage: \arg is a built-in operator name, so it prints upright and sets correct spacing; typing arg without the backslash gives italic letters. Because the angle is multivalued, \arg z is often treated as a set \{\theta + 2\pi k\}, and \arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w holds only modulo 2\pi. For the single-valued principal value people write \operatorname{Arg} z with a capital letter. Do not confuse \arg with argmax-style operators, which return a minimizing input and need their own declaration.

\\text{Arg}(z).meaning: Principal value of the argument, the unique angle in (−π, π] that z makes with the positive real axis.
\\text{Arg}(z).usage: The capital letter separates this single-valued Arg from the multivalued \arg. The branch cut lies along the negative real axis, which is why \text{Arg}(-1) = \pi but values just below the cut approach -\pi. Some books use [0, 2\pi) instead, so say which interval you mean. LaTeX has no \Arg command; \text{Arg} works but turns italic inside theorem environments. \operatorname{Arg} or \DeclareMathOperator{\Arg}{Arg} is more robust and gives proper spacing before the argument. For example, \text{Arg}(i) = \pi/2 while \arg i is the whole set \pi/2 + 2\pi k.

r e^{i\\theta}.meaning: Polar (exponential) form of a complex number: modulus r times a unit complex number at angle θ.
r e^{i\\theta}.usage: Multiplying in polar form simply multiplies moduli and adds angles, so (r e^{i\theta})^n = r^n e^{in\theta}, which is De Moivre's theorem in compact dress. Roots of unity e^{2\pi i k/n} and phasors A e^{i\omega t} come straight from this notation. Put the whole exponent in braces; e^i\theta would raise e to i only. When exponents become crowded, \exp(i\theta) is easier to read than a tiny superscript. Some style guides set the constant as upright \mathrm{e} to distinguish it from a variable.

e^{i\\theta} = \\cos\\theta + i\\sin\\th.meaning: Euler's formula, linking the complex exponential to cosine and sine; it puts e^{iθ} on the unit circle.
e^{i\\theta} = \\cos\\theta + i\\sin\\th.usage: Setting \theta = \pi gives Euler's identity e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0, and solving the formula for cosine yields \cos\theta = (e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta})/2. Note how \cos and \sin are operator commands: they print upright and add a thin space before \theta, while writing cos would give three italic letters. No parentheses are needed for a single symbol argument like \theta, but use them for compound arguments, \sin(2\theta). In engineering contexts the same identity is written with j in place of i.

e^{z}.meaning: Exponential function evaluated at a complex number z = x + iy, equal to eˣ(cos y + i sin y).
e^{z}.usage: The complex exponential is entire, never zero, and periodic with period 2\pi i, which is why its inverse, the logarithm, is multivalued. With short exponents e^{z} is fine; for something like e^{-(x - \mu)^2/2\sigma^2} the superscript becomes tiny, and \exp\left( -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right) reads better. \exp is a predefined operator. Always brace multi-token exponents. Some publishers ask for upright \mathrm{e} as the constant, which keeps it distinct from a variable e. Its derivative is itself, which makes it the building block of linear ODE solutions.

\\log z.meaning: Complex logarithm of z, a multivalued inverse of the exponential: ln|z| + i arg z.
\\log z.usage: Because the exponential repeats every 2\pi i, \log z has infinitely many values differing by 2\pi i k. The principal branch is often written with a capital, \operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i \operatorname{Arg} z, and is analytic away from the branch cut on the negative reals. \log and \ln are both built-in operators; analysts commonly write \log for the natural logarithm, while \ln makes the base explicit. A thin space appears automatically after \log, so \log z needs no parentheses for a single variable.

z^w.meaning: Complex power z raised to w, defined as exp(w log z) and generally multivalued.
z^w.usage: The surprising fact i^i = e^{-\pi/2} (on the principal branch) comes from this definition. Since \log z is multivalued, z^w has many values unless w is an integer, and rules like (z^a)^b = z^{ab} can fail. Brace exponents with more than one token: z^{w+1}, not z^w+1. For towers like z^{w^v}, TeX shrinks each level, so consider \exp notation for readability. State the branch explicitly when you rely on a particular value, for example by writing \exp(w \operatorname{Log} z).

|z| = 1.meaning: Equation of the unit circle in the complex plane: all complex numbers at distance 1 from the origin.
|z| = 1.usage: Points on the unit circle are exactly e^{i\theta}, and the n-th roots of unity lie on it. It is often named \mathbb{T} or S^1, and as a group under multiplication it is the circle group used in Fourier analysis. Contour integrals over it are written \oint_{|z|=1} with the condition as a subscript. For conjugation on the circle \bar{z} = 1/z, a handy simplification. If spacing around the bars looks off in context, use \lvert z \rvert; the open disc |z| < 1 and the closed disc |z| \le 1 follow the same pattern.

\\mathbb{H}.meaning: Blackboard-bold H, most often the upper half-plane {z : Im z > 0}; also the quaternions.
\\mathbb{H}.usage: In complex analysis and number theory \mathbb{H} is the domain of modular forms, acted on by SL_2(\mathbb{Z}) through Mobius transformations, and it carries the hyperbolic metric. In algebra the same letter denotes Hamilton's quaternions, named for him, so if both appear, write \mathcal{H} or spell out which one you mean. \mathbb only provides capital letters with the standard fonts; lowercase arguments produce garbage or errors. Related sets typeset the same way: \mathbb{C}, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Z}. Its boundary is the real line together with a point at infinity.

\\aleph_0.meaning: Aleph-null, the cardinality of the natural numbers and the smallest infinite cardinal.
\\aleph_0.usage: Any set that can be listed as a sequence, such as \mathbb{Z} or \mathbb{Q}, has cardinality \aleph_0, and arithmetic like \aleph_0 + \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 shows how infinite cardinals absorb. Cantor's diagonal argument proves 2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_0, so the reals are strictly bigger. \aleph is available without extra packages and behaves as an ordinary symbol, so the subscript attaches directly. Some older texts write \omega for the corresponding ordinal; keep cardinals and ordinals distinct in your notation.

\\aleph_1.meaning: Aleph-one, the first uncountable cardinal: the next infinite size after the countable.
\\aleph_1.usage: The continuum hypothesis asserts 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1, meaning no set has size strictly between the integers and the reals; Godel and Cohen showed it is independent of ZFC. Do not write |\mathbb{R}| = \aleph_1 as a fact, since that is exactly the open assumption; use \mathfrak{c} or 2^{\aleph_0} for the continuum. \aleph_1 is also the cardinality of \omega_1, the set of countable ordinals. Larger alephs follow the pattern \aleph_\alpha with ordinal subscripts, and the subscript needs braces if longer than one token.

\\beth.meaning: Hebrew letter beth, used for beth numbers: iterated power sets starting from the countable cardinal.
\\beth.usage: The beth sequence is defined by \beth_0 = \aleph_0 and \beth_{\alpha+1} = 2^{\beth_\alpha}, so \beth_1 is the cardinality of the reals and \beth_2 that of all real functions. The generalized continuum hypothesis is the statement \aleph_\alpha = \beth_\alpha for every ordinal. Alongside \aleph, LaTeX's extended symbol set offers \beth, \gimel and \daleth, the second through fourth Hebrew letters. Like \aleph it is an ordinary symbol, so subscripts attach directly; it is rarely seen outside set theory.

\\wp.meaning: Calligraphic-style p for the Weierstrass elliptic function, a doubly periodic meromorphic function.
\\wp.usage: The Weierstrass function \wp(z) satisfies (\wp')^2 = 4\wp^3 - g_2 \wp - g_3, which is why it parametrizes elliptic curves. The glyph is a special script p unrelated to any font family, so \mathcal{P} or \mathscr{P} are different symbols. Some authors use \wp for the power set, but \mathcal{P}(X) is the more common choice and avoids clashing with the elliptic function. Note that prime notation works as usual, \wp'(z), and that the symbol sits slightly below the baseline like a descender.

\\Re.meaning: Fraktur capital R, the classical symbol for taking the real part of a complex quantity.
\\Re.usage: On its own \Re is simply a glyph, not an operator, so there is no automatic spacing before an argument; follow it with parentheses or braces, as in \Re(s) > 1 for the half-plane where the Riemann zeta series converges. Analytic number theorists use exactly this style. If you want a different look, redefine it with \renewcommand{\Re}{\operatorname{Re}} in the preamble so every occurrence changes at once. Note that \Re differs from \mathfrak{R}, which gives a Fraktur R from a different font and looks slightly different.

\\Im.meaning: Fraktur capital I, the traditional glyph for the imaginary part of a complex number.
\\Im.usage: Contour integration and spectral theory use \Im to split quantities: a Green's function's imaginary part gives the density of states, and \Im \tau > 0 defines the modular upper half-plane. As with \Re, the command prints a symbol only, so you should supply parentheses. Many readers find the Fraktur letters easy to misread, and redefining with \renewcommand{\Im}{\operatorname{Im}} switches to upright 'Im'. If your text also uses the image of a homomorphism, give that \operatorname{im} in lowercase to keep the two apart.

\\mathcal{O}.meaning: Calligraphic O, used for a family of open sets in topology and for several other structures.
\\mathcal{O}.usage: A topological space is often written (X, \mathcal{O}), with \mathcal{O} the collection of open sets, although \tau is equally common. The same letter has many other jobs: big-O asymptotics \mathcal{O}(n \log n), the structure sheaf \mathcal{O}_X in algebraic geometry, and the ring of integers \mathcal{O}_K of a number field. \mathcal only supports capital letters in standard fonts. For asymptotic notation many style guides prefer a plain italic O, so decide on one and apply it everywhere.

A^{\\circ}.meaning: Interior of A, the union of all open sets contained in A; written with a small circle superscript.
A^{\\circ}.usage: The interior is the largest open subset of A, and it pairs with closure through \partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^{\circ}. The superscript \circ is the composition ring placed high; it should not be confused with a degree sign in units. Other common notations are \operatorname{int} A and \mathring{A}, the latter putting the ring directly above the letter; \mathring is a better fit for single letters with subscripts like U_1. For a closed interval, [a, b]^{\circ} = (a, b).

\\text{ext}(A).meaning: Exterior of a set A: the interior of its complement, consisting of points with a neighbourhood missing A.
\\text{ext}(A).usage: Any space splits into three disjoint parts, the interior, boundary and exterior of A, and \text{ext}(A) = (X \setminus A)^{\circ}. Typing ext in math mode without a wrapper yields italic letters e, x, t multiplied together, so some wrapper is necessary. \text inherits the surrounding font, which turns it italic inside a theorem; \operatorname{ext} stays upright and gives operator spacing, and \DeclareMathOperator{\ext}{ext} makes it reusable. Be aware that ext also abbreviates exterior algebra and Ext groups in homological algebra.

\\partial A.meaning: Boundary of A: points every neighbourhood of which meets both A and its complement.
\\partial A.usage: The boundary of a disk is its circle, and the boundary of the rationals in the reals is everything, \partial \mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{R}. The same \partial symbol is the boundary operator in algebraic topology, \partial_n : C_n \to C_{n-1} with \partial \circ \partial = 0, and appears in Stokes' theorem \int_{\partial M} \omega = \int_M d\omega. Some texts write \operatorname{Fr} A or \operatorname{bd} A instead. Since \partial is an ordinary symbol, nothing separates it from the set name; that tight look is the intended convention.

\\varinjlim.meaning: Direct limit (colimit) of a directed system, typeset as 'lim' with a right-pointing arrow beneath it.
\\varinjlim.usage: Direct limits build objects like \mathbb{Q} as \varinjlim \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{Z} or the stalk of a sheaf, \mathcal{F}_x = \varinjlim_{U \ni x} \mathcal{F}(U). In display math, the index set goes underneath the arrow; inline it goes beside. The amsmath bundle also offers \injlim, which prints 'inj lim' in words, so choose the form your field uses. Category theorists often write \operatorname*{colim} instead, since direct limits are a special case of colimits. Its counterpart for inverse systems is \varprojlim.

\\varprojlim.meaning: Inverse (projective) limit of a system, shown as 'lim' with a left-pointing arrow underneath.
\\varprojlim.usage: The p-adic integers are the classic example, \mathbb{Z}_p = \varprojlim \mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}, and profinite groups such as Galois groups are inverse limits of finite ones. Like \lim, the subscript sits below in display style. The alternative \projlim prints the words 'proj lim' with no arrow. Category theory generalizes this to an arbitrary limit, usually written \lim. Make sure arrows point the right way: \varprojlim has the leftward arrow and corresponds to maps going down the system, \varinjlim the rightward one.

A / B.meaning: Quotient of A by B: a group, ring, module or space with B collapsed or factored out.
A / B.usage: Quotients appear as \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, G/H for cosets, and X/A for collapsing a subspace to a point. In math mode / is an ordinary symbol with no surrounding space, which is the standard look. For a quotient by an equivalence relation, brace the tilde, X/{\sim}, otherwise \sim gets relation spacing and leaves a gap. With tall operands, \big/ or \left. \middle/ \right. constructions keep the slash in proportion. Do not use \setminus here; that is set difference, a different operation. State which structure the quotient carries, since G/H is only a group when H is normal.

\\pi_1.meaning: Fundamental group of a space: homotopy classes of loops at a base point, with concatenation as product.
\\pi_1.usage: The standard computation \pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z} counts how often a loop winds around the circle, and a space with trivial \pi_1 is called simply connected. Write the base point explicitly, \pi_1(X, x_0), when it matters; for path-connected spaces it is often dropped. Higher homotopy groups follow the same pattern, \pi_n(X). Use \cong for isomorphism rather than =. If \pi also denotes the number or a projection in the same document, consider whether readers might confuse them.

H_n.meaning: n-th homology group of a space or chain complex, measuring n-dimensional holes.
H_n.usage: For spheres H_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z} while H_k(S^n) = 0 for 0 < k < n, and the Euler characteristic is the alternating sum of ranks of H_n. Coefficients are written after a semicolon, H_n(X; \mathbb{Z}/2), and relative homology as H_n(X, A). Subscripts mark homology, superscripts cohomology, so keep them straight. Variants are marked with decorations: reduced homology \tilde{H}_n, singular homology H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}. In homological algebra it is defined as \ker \partial_n / \operatorname{im} \partial_{n+1}. Long exact sequences of these groups are usually drawn as commutative diagrams.

H^n.meaning: n-th cohomology group, the dual theory to homology, carrying a ring structure via the cup product.
H^n.usage: De Rham cohomology H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}(M) classifies closed differential forms modulo exact ones, and the cup product \smile makes H^\ast(X) a graded ring. Combining a superscript and a subscript, as in H^n_{\mathrm{dR}}, stacks them neatly; use \mathrm for labels that are words, not variables. The superscript index distinguishes it from homology H_n, a convention worth respecting. Group cohomology H^n(G, M) and sheaf cohomology H^n(X, \mathcal{F}) use the same symbol with different arguments. Poincare duality relates H^k and H_{n-k} on closed oriented n-manifolds, which explains why both notations often appear together.

\\mathcal{C}.meaning: Calligraphic C, the default name for an arbitrary category; also used for constraint or feasible sets.
\\mathcal{C}.usage: Category theory writes objects as X \in \mathcal{C} and morphism sets as \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y), with a second category usually called \mathcal{D}. Concrete categories are often set in bold or sans serif, such as \mathbf{Set} or \mathsf{Grp}, to separate names from variables. Optimization uses \mathcal{C} for a convex feasible set, as in \min_{x \in \mathcal{C}} f(x). \mathcal provides only uppercase letters in the default fonts; \mathscr gives a curlier script style if you need a second family.

\\mathcal{F}.meaning: Calligraphic F, frequently naming a functor between categories, a sheaf, a sigma-algebra, or a transform.
\\mathcal{F}.usage: A functor \mathcal{F} \colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D} sends objects and morphisms while preserving composition. Outside category theory the same letter is a sheaf \mathcal{F}(U), a sigma-algebra or filtration (\mathcal{F}_t in probability), or the Fourier transform \mathcal{F}\{f\}. Because of this overloading, introduce the letter explicitly. Use \colon rather than : when writing the functor's signature, to get punctuation spacing. Many authors reserve plain italic F, G for functors and keep calligraphic letters for sheaves. A natural transformation between two functors is often written \eta \colon \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow \mathcal{G}.

\\hbar.meaning: Reduced Planck constant ħ = h/2π, the quantum of angular momentum appearing throughout quantum mechanics.
\\hbar.usage: It appears in the canonical commutator [x, p] = i\hbar, the photon energy E = \hbar\omega, and the uncertainty relation \Delta x\, \Delta p \geq \hbar/2. Its value is about 1.055 \times 10^{-34} J s. \hslash is a variant with a slanted slash instead of a horizontal bar; pick one and keep it. Plain h, without the bar, is the unreduced constant from E = h\nu. In theoretical work, units with \hbar = 1 are standard, so mention that choice when you drop it from equations.

\\langle \\psi |.meaning: A bra in Dirac notation: the dual (row) vector, a linear functional acting on kets.
\\langle \\psi |.usage: The bra \langle \psi | is the conjugate transpose of the ket |\psi\rangle, so it is what you place on the left of an inner product or expectation value. Use \langle, never the less-than sign <, which is a relation with wide spacing and the wrong shape. A bare | is acceptable here, but \rvert gives the correct closing-delimiter spacing. For repeated use, define \newcommand{\bra}[1]{\langle #1 \rvert}. When the state label is tall, \left\langle \frac{\psi}{2} \right| scales both delimiters together.

| \\psi \\rangle.meaning: A ket in Dirac notation, representing a quantum state as a column vector in Hilbert space.
| \\psi \\rangle.usage: States are kets: |0\rangle and |1\rangle for a qubit, |n\rangle for harmonic oscillator levels, and superpositions like \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle. The angle bracket is \rangle, not >. Writing \lvert \psi \rangle gives TeX an explicit opening delimiter so spacing is right even after a minus sign. A macro such as \newcommand{\ket}[1]{\lvert #1 \rangle} keeps hundreds of kets consistent. Tensor products are written |\psi\rangle \otimes |\phi\rangle or compressed as |\psi\phi\rangle. A ket times a bra, |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|, is a projector or density matrix.

\\langle \\phi | \\psi \\rangle.meaning: Inner product of two states, a bra meeting a ket; its squared modulus gives a transition probability.
\\langle \\phi | \\psi \\rangle.usage: The amplitude \langle \phi | \psi \rangle is conjugate-symmetric, \langle \phi | \psi \rangle = \langle \psi | \phi \rangle^*, and normalization reads \langle \psi | \psi \rangle = 1. Matrix elements sandwich an operator: \langle \phi | \hat{A} | \psi \rangle. Use a plain | in the middle rather than \mid, whose relation spacing pushes the halves apart. For tall contents, \left\langle \phi \middle| \psi \right\rangle makes the middle bar grow too. Mathematicians write the same thing as (\phi, \psi) or \langle \phi, \psi \rangle with a comma.

\\nabla^2.meaning: Laplace operator, the sum of second partial derivatives; it measures how a function differs from its local average.
\\nabla^2.usage:
Laplace's equation 
abla^2 \phi = 0, Poisson's equation 
abla^2 \phi = -ho/\varepsilon_0, the heat equation and the wave equation all use it. Physicists prefer 
abla^2, a reminder that it is the divergence of the gradient; mathematicians often write \Delta, which can clash with \Delta as a finite difference or change. In Cartesian coordinates 
abla^2 f = f_{xx} + f_{yy} + f_{zz}, but in curvilinear coordinates extra terms appear. For the vector Laplacian of a field, bold the operand to signal the different meaning.

\\Box.meaning: Square box symbol, the d'Alembert wave operator in relativity and the necessity operator in modal logic.
\\Box.usage: In special relativity \Box = \partial^\mu \partial_\mu combines time and space derivatives, so the wave equation is \Box \phi = 0 and the Klein-Gordon equation (\Box + m^2)\phi = 0. Sign conventions differ with the metric signature, so state yours. Modal logicians read \Box p as 'necessarily p', with \Diamond p for 'possibly p'. Some texts write \Box^2 for the operator by analogy with \nabla^2. The visually similar \square is commonly used as an end-of-proof mark; check which glyph your document class uses for QED.

\\mathcal{L}.meaning: Calligraphic L, the standard symbol for a Lagrangian density and, in machine learning, a loss function.
\\mathcal{L}.usage: Field theory writes the action as S = \int \mathcal{L}\, d^4x, with the Euler-Lagrange equation \partial_\mu \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial(\partial_\mu \phi)} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \phi}. Classical mechanics often uses plain L for the Lagrangian itself and reserves \mathcal{L} for densities. Machine-learning papers use \mathcal{L}(\theta) for a loss, and engineers use it for the Laplace transform \mathcal{L}\{f\}(s). In optimization, the Lagrangian function with multipliers is also \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda). Introduce whichever meaning you need explicitly. Its counterpart via the Legendre transform is the Hamiltonian \mathcal{H}.

\\mathcal{H}.meaning: Calligraphic H, used for the Hamiltonian (energy function) and frequently for a Hilbert space.
\\mathcal{H}.usage: In classical mechanics Hamilton's equations read \dot{q} = \partial \mathcal{H}/\partial p and \dot{p} = -\partial \mathcal{H}/\partial q. Quantum mechanics usually writes the Hamiltonian operator as \hat{H} and uses \mathcal{H} for the Hilbert space of states, so the two calligraphic meanings can collide in one paper. Statistical physics uses \mathcal{H} for a Hamiltonian functional in the Boltzmann weight e^{-\beta \mathcal{H}}. Learning theory uses it for a hypothesis class. Pick distinct letters if more than one appears. Note that \mathcal only covers capital letters in the default fonts.

T^{\\mu\\nu}.meaning: A rank-2 contravariant tensor such as the stress-energy tensor, written with two upper Greek indices.
T^{\\mu\\nu}.usage:
General relativity couples geometry to matter through G_{\mu
u} = 8\pi G\, T_{\mu
u}, and conservation reads 
abla_\mu T^{\mu
u} = 0. Braces group both indices into one superscript; T^\mu
u would put 
u on the baseline. For mixed tensors, keep horizontal order visible with an empty group: T^{\mu}{}_{
u} places the lower index after the upper one rather than beneath it. Repeated upper and lower indices follow the Einstein summation convention. Greek indices conventionally run over spacetime, Latin indices over space only.

\\Gamma^{\\lambda}_{\\mu\\nu}.meaning: Christoffel symbol of the second kind, encoding how coordinate basis vectors change for the Levi-Civita connection.
\\Gamma^{\\lambda}_{\\mu\\nu}.usage:
It is computed from the metric as \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu
u} =  rac{1}{2} g^{\lambda\sigma}(\partial_\mu g_{\sigma
u} + \partial_
u g_{\sigma\mu} - \partial_\sigma g_{\mu
u}) and appears in the geodesic equation and covariant derivatives. Despite the index notation it is not a tensor. Writing the superscript and subscript on the same base stacks them vertically, which is the usual style here because the symbol is symmetric in its lower pair. Capital Gamma is upright by default; \varGamma gives an italic version if your style requires it.

\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial t}.meaning: Partial derivative operator with respect to time t, holding all spatial variables fixed.
\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial t}.usage: It drives evolution equations: the heat equation \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = k \nabla^2 u, the continuity equation, and Schrodinger's equation. Inline, a full \frac is cramped, so write \partial u/\partial t or the compact \partial_t u; the subscripted form is standard in PDE papers. In display math use \frac, and \dfrac if it appears inside a fraction or matrix and must stay full size. Distinguish it from the total derivative d/dt and from the material derivative D/Dt used in fluid mechanics.

\\vec{E}.meaning: Arrow accent over a letter marking it as a vector, here the electric field E.
\\vec{E}.usage: Introductory physics writes vectors with arrows, \vec{E}, \vec{F} = q\vec{E}, while most journals and advanced texts prefer bold, \mathbf{E}, or for Greek letters \boldsymbol{\omega}. \vec is a short fixed-width accent sized for a single character; for multi-letter vectors such as a segment AB, \overrightarrow{AB} stretches across the whole label. Pick one vector style for the entire document. Unit vectors are typically hatted, \hat{x}, and for dotless i and j inside accents use \imath and \jmath.

\\nabla \\cdot.meaning: Divergence operator, nabla dotted with a vector field, giving the net outward flux per unit volume.
\\nabla \\cdot.usage:
Gauss's law 
abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = ho/\varepsilon_0 and the no-monopole law 
abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0 are its best-known uses, and incompressible flow requires 
abla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0. \cdot carries binary-operator spacing, which is the expected look. Use \cdot, not a period or  ullet. Some mathematical texts prefer \operatorname{div} \mathbf{F}, which avoids treating nabla as a vector. The divergence theorem links it to boundary flux: \int_V 
abla \cdot \mathbf{F}\, dV = \oint_{\partial V} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}.

\\nabla \\times.meaning: Curl operator, nabla crossed with a vector field, measuring its local rotation or circulation density.
\\nabla \\times.usage: Faraday's law \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\partial \mathbf{B}/\partial t and Ampere's law with Maxwell's correction are written with it, and in fluids \nabla \times \mathbf{u} is the vorticity. Two identities are worth remembering: the curl of a gradient is zero and the divergence of a curl is zero. \times is a binary operator, so spacing is automatic. European texts sometimes write \operatorname{rot} \mathbf{F} instead, and others use \operatorname{curl}. Curl is only defined this way in three dimensions.

\\rightleftharpoons.meaning: Pair of opposing half-arrows (harpoons) showing a chemical reaction at dynamic equilibrium.
\\rightleftharpoons.usage: IUPAC recommends harpoons for equilibrium, as in N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3, while two full arrows indicate a reversible process in general. The top harpoon points right, matching the forward reaction. Its mirror is \leftrightharpoons, with the leftward harpoon on top. It is a relation, so TeX spaces it like =. To print conditions above the arrow, such as a catalyst, you can use \overset{\text{Fe}}{\rightleftharpoons}, though dedicated chemistry tools give longer arrows. In physics the same symbol sometimes denotes a two-way correspondence.

\\leftrightarrows.meaning: Two stacked full arrows, leftward on top and rightward below, used for reversible reactions or two-way maps.
\\leftrightarrows.usage: Some chemistry texts use full double arrows for a reaction that can run in both directions, keeping harpoons (\rightleftharpoons) for true equilibrium; most modern writing uses harpoons for both. Note the stacking order: \leftrightarrows puts the left arrow on top, while \rightleftarrows puts the right arrow on top, which is usually what you want when the forward reaction runs left to right. Do not confuse these with \leftrightarrow, a single double-headed arrow. In category theory the pair often denotes an adjunction or a pair of parallel maps.

{}^{14}_{6}\\text{C}.meaning: Nuclide notation with mass number as a left superscript and atomic number as a left subscript, here carbon-14.
{}^{14}_{6}\\text{C}.usage: The empty group {} gives the scripts something to attach to, placing them to the left of the element symbol. One flaw: TeX left-aligns the subscript under the superscript, so the single-digit 6 ends up far from the C. Pad it with \phantom{1}6 to right-align the numbers against the symbol. Nuclear equations combine these, as in beta decay of carbon-14 to nitrogen-14. Use \text or \mathrm for the element so it stays upright; atomic numbers are often omitted when the element already implies them, giving {}^{14}\text{C}.

\\text{Na}^{+}.meaning: Ion notation with the charge as a superscript, here the sodium cation carrying a single positive charge.
\\text{Na}^{+}.usage: Write multi-charge ions with the number before the sign, \text{Ca}^{2+} and \text{SO}_4^{2-}, following IUPAC order. Braces matter: ^{2+} keeps both characters in the superscript. A trailing minus in a superscript is treated as unary, so ^{-} renders cleanly. Use \mathrm{Na} instead of \text{Na} if the formula might appear inside an italic theorem or caption, since \text copies the surrounding font while \mathrm is always upright. When subscripts and charges coincide, the charge sits above the count, as in sulfate.

\\text{H}_2\\text{O}.meaning: Molecular formula for water, with the subscript 2 counting hydrogen atoms in each molecule.
\\text{H}_2\\text{O}.usage: Element symbols must be upright, which is why each letter group is wrapped in \text; italic H_2O would look like variables. A shorter equivalent is \mathrm{H_2O}, which keeps everything upright including the subscript and is immune to surrounding italics. Subscripts count atoms only and should never be confused with superscript charges. Formulas with parentheses follow the same pattern, \mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}. For extensive chemistry, a dedicated chemistry package saves effort, but for a few formulas this manual approach is perfectly adequate.

^{\\circ}\\text{C}.meaning: Degree Celsius unit, formed from a raised circle and an upright C; water freezes at 0 °C.
^{\\circ}\\text{C}.usage: The degree mark is \circ in a superscript; an o or 0 is wrong. SI style puts a space between number and unit, so write 25\,^{\circ}\text{C} with a thin space, and never place a space between the degree sign and the C. Temperature differences in Celsius equal differences in kelvin, a fact that matters in heat-capacity work. \text turns italic inside theorems; \mathrm{C} avoids that. Unit packages provide semantic commands, but this construction is the common manual approach and works everywhere, including KaTeX.

\\text{C}-\\text{C}.meaning: Single covalent bond between two carbon atoms, drawn as a short line between the element symbols.
\\text{C}-\\text{C}.usage: In math mode the hyphen becomes a minus sign with binary-operator spacing, so the bond appears with gaps around it, which looks more like subtraction. Wrapping it as \text{C}{-}\text{C} removes the spacing and gives a tight bond. Bond lengths and energies are often quoted alongside, for example a C-C bond of about 154 pm. For condensed structural formulas like \mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_3}, the same braced trick applies. For anything beyond a few bonds, drawing tools or a structure package produce real skeletal formulas.

\\text{C}=\\text{C}.meaning: Carbon-carbon double bond, one sigma and one pi bond, characteristic of alkenes such as ethene.
\\text{C}=\\text{C}.usage: Because = is a relation in math mode, TeX inserts thick spaces on both sides, which looks like an equation rather than a bond. Bracing it, \text{C}{=}\text{C}, turns it into an ordinary symbol and pulls the atoms together. Alkenes are written like \mathrm{H_2C{=}CH_2}. The double bond is shorter and stronger than a single bond and restricts rotation, giving cis-trans isomers. Make sure readers cannot mistake the bond for an equals sign in a reaction line by keeping it tight against the atoms.

\\text{C}\\equiv\\text{C}.meaning: Carbon-carbon triple bond, typical of alkynes like ethyne (acetylene), drawn with three horizontal lines.
\\text{C}\\equiv\\text{C}.usage: \equiv is a relation, the same symbol used for congruence (a \equiv b \pmod n) and identity, so by default it is spaced widely; {\equiv} produces a tighter bond between atoms. A triple bond has one sigma and two pi components and is the shortest of the carbon-carbon bonds. Nitrogen gas is written \mathrm{N{\equiv}N}. Some fonts draw \equiv slightly wide, which suits chemistry well. Avoid \cong or \approx, which look somewhat similar but mean isomorphism and approximation.

\\delta^{+}.meaning: Partial positive charge on an atom in a polar bond, written as a lowercase delta with a plus.
\\delta^{+}.usage: In water the hydrogens carry \delta^{+} and the oxygen \delta^{-}, the charge separation that drives hydrogen bonding. Delta here means 'a fraction of', not a change, so do not confuse it with \Delta. To place the label above an atom, use \overset{\delta^{+}}{\text{H}}, which keeps the formula readable. Some texts write \delta+ inline without superscripting; the superscript form is more common in typeset work. Pair it with \delta^{-} on the electronegative partner, and \delta\delta^{+} denotes an even smaller partial charge.

e^{-}.meaning: Symbol for the electron, a lowercase e with a negative charge superscript, used in redox half-reactions.
e^{-}.usage: Half-equations balance charge with electrons, as in \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \to \text{Cu}. The positron is e^{+}. Physics style guides often set particle symbols upright, \mathrm{e}^{-}, which also avoids confusion with Euler's number when exponentials appear nearby. Because e^- with a single-token superscript works, braces are optional, but they keep things consistent with multi-character charges. In nuclear notation an electron may also be written {}^{\phantom{-}0}_{-1}e or as \beta^{-} when emitted in decay. The antineutrino in beta decay is written \bar{\nu}_e alongside it.

\\text{(aq)}.meaning: State symbol for aqueous: the species is dissolved in water, as for ions in solution.
\\text{(aq)}.usage: State symbols follow the formula, either inline as \text{NaCl(aq)} or as a subscript, \text{NaCl}_{\text{(aq)}}; both are accepted, so choose one. Typing (aq) in math mode without \text would give italic a and q with math spacing, so the wrapper matters. Net ionic equations rely on this label to show which species dissociate. When writing many equations, define a macro such as \newcommand{\aq}{\text{(aq)}}. \mathrm{(aq)} is an alternative that stays upright in italic contexts. It also marks hydrated protons, written \text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}.

\\text{(s)}.meaning: State symbol marking a species as solid, often a precipitate or a metal electrode.
\\text{(s)}.usage: Precipitation reactions end with a solid, like \text{AgCl(s)}, and thermochemistry depends on it: the enthalpy of formation of carbon refers to graphite in the solid state. Some older texts use a downward arrow for a precipitate instead; the parenthesized symbol is the IUPAC-preferred form. Write it immediately after the formula with no space. Wrapping it in \text keeps the s upright; in math mode an unwrapped s would be italic and might be mistaken for the unit second or a variable.

\\text{(l)}.meaning: State symbol for a pure liquid, such as water or mercury, written after the chemical formula.
\\text{(l)}.usage: Combustion equations distinguish \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} from \text{H}_2\text{O(g)} because the enthalpy change differs by the heat of vaporization. Note the difference between (l), a pure liquid, and (aq), a solution in water. Upright text is especially important here: in some fonts an italic l looks like the digit 1 or a vertical bar, which can confuse readers. Using \text or \mathrm ensures a clear upright letter. Keep the symbol directly attached to the formula without extra spacing.

\\text{(g)}.meaning: State symbol for the gaseous phase, attached to formulas of gases and vapours in equations.
\\text{(g)}.usage: Gas-phase species matter for equilibrium constants in pressure, K_p, and for ideal-gas calculations; marking them with (g) makes those dependencies explicit. Older texts sometimes use an upward arrow to show a gas escaping, but the state symbol is preferred today. A useful habit is labelling every species in a thermochemical equation so enthalpy values are unambiguous. If your document has many formulas, a macro like \newcommand{\gas}{\text{(g)}} prevents typos. \mathrm{(g)} gives the same upright result inside italic text.

\\text{\\AA}.meaning: Angstrom unit, 10⁻¹⁰ metres (0.1 nm), used for atomic radii, bond lengths and X-ray wavelengths.
\\text{\\AA}.usage: \AA is a text-mode command, so in math it must be wrapped in \text, as shown; using it bare in math mode produces a warning and incorrect output. Crystallographers and structural biologists still quote distances like 1.54\,\text{\AA} for the copper K-alpha wavelength, though SI prefers nanometres or picometres. A lookalike \mathring{A} works in math mode but is an accented variable, not the unit symbol. Put a thin space between number and unit. The lowercase \aa gives the Scandinavian letter, not the unit.

^{\\circ}\\text{F}.meaning: Degree Fahrenheit temperature unit; water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F at standard pressure.
^{\\circ}\\text{F}.usage: Conversion is T_F = \frac{9}{5} T_C + 32, and a temperature difference of one Fahrenheit degree equals 5/9 of a kelvin. The construction mirrors the Celsius one: a superscripted \circ followed by an upright F, with a thin space between number and degree sign. US weather data, HVAC and some engineering standards still use it, but scientific journals almost always expect SI. Avoid writing the degree with a lowercase o or with \degree unless that command is defined in your setup.

\\text{K}.meaning: Kelvin, the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, with zero at absolute zero.
\\text{K}.usage: Since 1967 the unit is written K with no degree sign: 300 K, not 300 °K. Absolute zero is 0 K, water's triple point 273.16 K, and T(\text{K}) = T(^{\circ}\text{C}) + 273.15. Unit symbols must be upright, which \text provides; an italic K is a variable, such as an equilibrium constant or a stiffness. Leave a thin space between number and unit, 4.2\,\text{K}. In italic theorem text \mathrm{K} is safer since \text would follow the italic font.

\\text{m}.meaning: Metre, the SI base unit of length, defined via the speed of light in vacuum.
\\text{m}.usage: An upright m is the unit, while italic m usually means mass, so \text{m} or \mathrm{m} is essential: compare m = 2\,\text{kg} with h = 2\,\text{m}. SI style puts a space between value and unit and never pluralizes the symbol. Derived units combine with powers, \text{m}^2 and \text{m}^3, and prefixes attach directly, \text{km}, \text{mm}. Velocity is written \text{m/s} or \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}; journals vary, so check the house style. Do not confuse the symbol with the prefix milli, which also uses m.

\\text{kg}.meaning: Kilogram, the SI base unit of mass, now fixed through the Planck constant rather than a physical prototype.
\\text{kg}.usage: It is the only SI base unit with a prefix built in, so multiples are formed from the gram: write \text{mg}, not \mu\text{kg}. Densities are given in \text{kg}/\text{m}^3 or \text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}; water is about 1000\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}. Keep the symbol lowercase, since Kg or KG are incorrect. Units go upright, so wrap in \text or \mathrm; and add \, between the number and kg. In derived units like the newton, kg sits first by convention, \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}. Its symbol and its name stay lowercase even at the start of a sentence.

\\text{s}.meaning: Second, the SI base unit of time, defined by the caesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency.
\\text{s}.usage: An upright s is the unit; italic s often stands for displacement or arc length, so the formatting carries meaning in s = 5\,\text{m} versus t = 5\,\text{s}. Avoid abbreviations like sec in technical writing. Inverse seconds, \text{s}^{-1}, measure rates and are the same as hertz when describing frequency. Prefixed forms include \text{ms}, \mu\text{s} and \text{ns}; for the micro prefix, an upright mu is preferred by SI style, which plain \mu does not provide in the default fonts.

\\text{A}.meaning: Ampere, the SI base unit of electric current, defined through the elementary charge.
\\text{A}.usage: Circuits are full of A: I = 2\,\text{A}, current density in \text{A}/\text{m}^2, and charge as one coulomb equals one ampere-second. An italic A usually means area or a vector potential, so upright formatting distinguishes the unit. Prefixed forms like \text{mA} and \mu\text{A} are common in electronics. Write the number, a thin space, then the symbol. In prose the unit name is lowercase, ampere, even though the symbol is capitalized because it honours Andre-Marie Ampere. A milliampere is one thousandth, written 5\,\text{mA}.

\\text{V}.meaning: Volt, the SI unit of electric potential difference: one joule of energy per coulomb of charge.
\\text{V}.usage: Ohm's law V = IR uses italic V for the voltage quantity, while the unit itself is upright, as in 230\,\text{V}; mixing them up is a common typesetting slip. Italic V also denotes volume in thermodynamics, another reason to keep units upright. Equivalent expressions include \text{J}/\text{C} and \text{W}/\text{A}. Electric field strength is measured in \text{V}/\text{m}. Prefixed versions \text{mV} and \text{kV} attach directly without a space, while the number and unit are separated by \,. Batteries, for instance, are rated at 1.5\,\text{V} or 9\,\text{V}.

\\text{W}.meaning: Watt, the SI unit of power: one joule transferred per second.
\\text{W}.usage: Power appears in P = VI, P = I^2 R, and radiative flux in \text{W}/\text{m}^2, as in the solar constant of about 1361\,\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}. The italic letter W usually means work, so the upright unit and the italic quantity can sit side by side: W = 10\,\text{J} over 2\,\text{s} gives 5\,\text{W}. Energy bills use kilowatt-hours, written \text{kW}\,\text{h} or \text{kWh}. Do not write W/s for energy; a watt is already a rate. Large plants are rated in megawatts, \text{MW}, and transmission losses are computed as I^2 R.

\\text{J}.meaning: Joule, the SI unit of energy, work and heat, equal to one newton-metre or kg·m²/s².
\\text{J}.usage: Kinetic energy \frac{1}{2}mv^2 comes out in joules when SI units are used, and molar quantities use \text{kJ}/\text{mol}. Torque is also N m dimensionally, but by convention it is written \text{N}\,\text{m} rather than J to signal it is not energy. Upright formatting keeps the unit distinct from italic J, which might be current density, a moment of inertia, or a Jacobian. Write the multiplication of units with a thin space or \cdot, such as \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2}. Food energy in kilocalories converts at 1\,\text{kcal} = 4184\,\text{J}.

\\text{N}.meaning: Newton, the SI unit of force: the force that accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared.
\\text{N}.usage: Weights and forces are quoted in newtons, so a 1 kg mass weighs about 9.81\,\text{N} at Earth's surface. Stress and pressure divide by area, \text{N}/\text{m}^2, which is the pascal. An upright N is the unit; italic N is often a normal force, a count, or Avogadro-related numbers, and blackboard \mathbb{N} is the natural numbers. Keep a thin space between number and unit. Spring constants are measured in \text{N}/\text{m}. The unit honours Isaac Newton, so the symbol is capitalized but the unit name is not.

\\text{Pa}.meaning: Pascal, the SI unit of pressure and stress, one newton per square metre.
\\text{Pa}.usage: Because a pascal is tiny, practical values use prefixes: atmospheric pressure is about 101.325\,\text{kPa}, weather maps use hectopascals (hPa), and material strengths are given in MPa or GPa. Young's modulus for steel is around 200\,\text{GPa}. The symbol has a capital P and lowercase a, which must stay upright; \text{Pa} achieves that. Pressure itself is an italic p or P. Writing the unit as \text{N}/\text{m}^2 is equivalent but less common in modern texts. Gauge and absolute pressures differ by about one atmosphere, so state which one you mean.

\\text{Hz}.meaning: Hertz, the SI unit of frequency: one cycle per second, dimensionally equal to inverse seconds.
\\text{Hz}.usage: Signal processing and acoustics quote frequencies like 440\,\text{Hz} for concert A and sampling rates like 44.1\,\text{kHz}; processors run in GHz. Angular frequency \omega = 2\pi f is customarily given in \text{rad}/\text{s}, not hertz, to avoid a factor-of-2\pi confusion. Keep the capital H and lowercase z. Prefixes attach directly, \text{MHz}, and the number takes a thin space before the unit. For radioactive activity the same dimension is named the becquerel instead. The period is the reciprocal, T = 1/f.

/.meaning: Solidus used to mean 'per' in compound units like m/s, dividing one unit by another.
/.usage: In math mode / is an ordinary symbol with no extra spacing, which gives the tight \text{m}/\text{s} look units need. SI rules allow only one solidus in a unit, so acceleration is \text{m}/\text{s}^2 and never m/s/s; for complicated units, negative exponents such as \text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1} are clearer. Use parentheses when the denominator has several factors: \text{W}/(\text{m}^2\,\text{K}). For general fractions in displayed equations, \frac is usually better than a slash, but inline the slash avoids cramped stacked numbers.

^2.meaning: Superscript 2, raising a quantity or unit to the second power, as in x² or square metres.
^2.usage: Typing ^2 attaches the next single token as a superscript; for longer exponents you need braces, x^{12}, since x^12 would give x^1 followed by a 2. Units squared, like \text{m}^2, describe areas, and \text{s}^2 appears in acceleration. Applied to functions, \sin^2 x means (\sin x)^2, a convention that does not extend to \sin^{-1}, which denotes the inverse. Double superscripts like x^2^3 produce an error; write x^{2^3} or (x^2)^3 depending on what you mean. Use \text{m}^2 rather than sq m in scientific text.

^3.meaning: Superscript 3 for cubing: third powers of numbers or variables, and cubic units of volume.
^3.usage: Volumes are expressed in \text{m}^3, \text{cm}^3 or litres (1\,\text{L} = 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3), and densities use per-cubic units, \text{kg}/\text{m}^3. In algebra, cubes appear in identities like a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2). The superscript applies to the preceding token only, so a prefixed unit is cubed as a whole, \text{cm}^3, which means (cm) cubed rather than c times m cubed. Brace multi-token exponents: x^{3n}. The cube root is written \sqrt[3]{x}. Write \text{m}^3, not cu m, in scientific text.

O(n).meaning: Asymptotic upper bound: f(n) = O(n) means f grows no faster than a constant multiple of n for large n.
O(n).usage: Big O is the workhorse of algorithm analysis: linear search runs in O(n), merge sort in O(n \log n), naive matrix multiplication in O(n^3). Strictly, O(g) is a set of functions, so f \in O(g) is the precise form, though f(n) = O(g(n)) is the near-universal convention. Some authors prefer a calligraphic \mathcal{O}(n) to separate the operator from a variable named O; pick one and stay consistent across the paper. Write the argument with the real cost inside, such as O(n^2 \log n), rather than O(n^2) \cdot \log n, and remember that O only bounds from above, so it does not claim the bound is tight.

\\Omega(n).meaning: Asymptotic lower bound: f(n) = Omega(n) means f grows at least as fast as a constant times n for large n.
\\Omega(n).usage: Capital omega states lower bounds, most famously that any comparison-based sort needs \Omega(n \log n) comparisons in the worst case. It is typed with the upright Greek capital \Omega; amsmath also offers \varOmega for a slanted form, which some typographers prefer for variables but which looks odd as an operator. Note that analytic number theory uses Hardy and Littlewood's older meaning, where \Omega means the bound fails to be o(g), so check which definition a source follows. Pair it with O to bracket a running time, and switch to \Theta once both sides match.

\\Theta(n).meaning: Tight asymptotic bound: f(n) = Theta(n) means f is bounded above and below by constant multiples of n.
\\Theta(n).usage: Theta is the right claim when you have proved matching upper and lower bounds: binary search is \Theta(\log n), and the Master Theorem's middle case yields \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log n). Formally, f \in \Theta(g) exactly when f \in O(g) and f \in \Omega(g). Many papers write O where \Theta is meant; reviewers in theory venues notice, so use \Theta when tightness is the point. The capital \Theta is upright by default; do not confuse it with lowercase \theta, which usually names an angle or a parameter vector, and avoid \vartheta, a variant of the lowercase letter.

o(n).meaning: Strict asymptotic upper bound: f(n) = o(n) means f(n)/n tends to 0 as n grows.
o(n).usage: Little o expresses that one function is negligible against another, as in \log n = o(n) or n = o(n^2). It is strictly stronger than big O: every o(g) function is O(g), but n is O(n) without being o(n). Analysts use it constantly in Taylor expansions, such as \sin x = x + o(x) as x \to 0, so always state the limit point when it is not infinity. Since it is just an italic letter o, there is no special command; make sure readers do not mistake it for a zero, and keep it lowercase to avoid colliding with big O.

\\omega(n).meaning: Strict asymptotic lower bound: f(n) = omega(n) means f(n)/n grows without bound.
\\omega(n).usage: Little omega is the mirror image of little o: f = \omega(g) exactly when g = o(f), so n^2 = \omega(n) and n \log n = \omega(n). It appears less often than \Omega, mainly in lower-bound proofs and randomized algorithms where a quantity must grow strictly faster than linear. Use the lowercase Greek \omega, not the Latin w, which looks similar in some fonts. Be aware the same symbol is overloaded: in graph theory \omega(G) is the clique number and in number theory \omega(n) counts distinct prime factors, so define your usage when context is mixed.

\\bmod.meaning: Binary modulo operator: typesets 'mod' between two operands, as in a mod n, with operator spacing.
\\bmod.usage: Use \bmod for the remainder operation inside an expression, such as 17 \bmod 5 = 2 or the hash function h(k) = k \bmod m. It produces upright mod with medium spacing on both sides, just like a binary operator. For congruences, use \pmod instead: a \equiv b \pmod{n} prints the parenthesized form with extra space before it. amsmath also defines \mod{n}, which gives a wider unparenthesized gap, and \pod{n}, which keeps the parentheses but drops the word. Typing the bare letters mod would italicize them as a product of variables, so always use one of these commands.

\\log.meaning: Typesets the logarithm function name in upright roman type with correct spacing before its argument.
\\log.usage: \log is one of LaTeX's predefined function names, so it prints upright log and inserts a thin space before the argument, unlike typing log, which italicizes three variables. Add a base with a subscript, as in \log_2 n for binary logarithms; in algorithm analysis an unsubscripted \log usually means base 2, while in mathematics it often means the natural log, so state the convention. LaTeX also predefines \lg for base-2 logs and \ln for natural logs. When the argument is more than one symbol, add parentheses, for example \log(n+1), and use \left( \right) for tall arguments.

\\ln.meaning: Prints the natural logarithm name, ln, in upright type with operator spacing.
\\ln.usage: \ln is the predefined command for the base-e logarithm, giving upright ln followed by proper spacing, the same way \sin or \exp behave. It shows up in calculus identities like \frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}, in information theory when entropy is measured in nats, and in log-likelihoods. Many mathematicians write \log to mean the natural log, while engineers and computer scientists reserve \ln for base e and \log for base 10 or 2, so pick consistently. For an argument like a fraction, wrap it with \left( and \right) so the parentheses scale.

\\mathbb{E}.meaning: Blackboard bold E, the standard notation for expected value of a random variable.
\\mathbb{E}.usage: Expectation appears everywhere in probability and machine learning: \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x x\,p(x), the risk \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}[\ell(f(x),y)], or variance as \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mathbb{E}[X]^2. Put the distribution in a subscript to make the source of randomness explicit. Older texts use a plain roman E or \operatorname{E}; both are fine if used consistently. Note that \mathbb only provides uppercase letters, so \mathbb{e} gives garbage. Use square brackets for the argument and \left[ \right] when it contains tall fractions. Defining a macro such as \newcommand{\E}{\mathbb{E}} keeps notation uniform.

D_{\\text{KL}}(P \\| Q).meaning: Kullback-Leibler divergence of Q from P: the expected extra log-loss from using Q in place of the true distribution P.
D_{\\text{KL}}(P \\| Q).usage: KL divergence is D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q) = \sum_x P(x) \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}, central to variational inference, the ELBO, and policy regularization in reinforcement learning. It is not symmetric, so the order of P and Q matters, and the double bar separates them. \| is an ordinary symbol with no surrounding space, which can look cramped; many authors write \parallel, which gets relation spacing, or add \, on both sides. \text{KL} in the subscript inherits the surrounding font, so \mathrm{KL} is safer inside italic theorem text. For large fractions inside, use \left( \right).

\\text{KL}(P \\| Q).meaning: Shorthand notation for the Kullback-Leibler divergence between distributions P and Q, without the D prefix.
\\text{KL}(P \\| Q).usage: Many machine learning papers drop the D and write \text{KL}(P \| Q), especially in loss functions like the VAE objective with a term \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z)). It means exactly the same as D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q), including the asymmetry: forward KL tends to be mass-covering, reverse KL mode-seeking. Because \text{} copies the font of surrounding text, KL can come out italic inside a theorem; \operatorname{KL} or \mathrm{KL} fixes that and \operatorname also adds the right space before the parenthesis. Consider \,\|\, or \parallel for more air around the bars.

\\arg\\max.meaning: The argument of the maximum: the input value at which a function attains its largest value.
\\arg\\max.usage: Written as \arg\max, it combines two predefined operators: \arg, which never takes limits, and \max, which does. The result is that a subscript in display style lands under max only, so the constraint sits off-center. A cleaner approach is \operatorname*{arg\,max}, or defining \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} in the preamble, which centers the subscript beneath the whole word. It appears in classification rules like \hat{y} = \arg\max_k p(k|x), in maximum likelihood estimation, and in greedy policies in reinforcement learning. Note that it returns a set when the maximizer is not unique.

\\arg\\min.meaning: The argument of the minimum: the input at which a function reaches its smallest value.
\\arg\\min.usage: \arg\min is how most optimization and learning problems define a solution, for instance least squares \hat{\beta} = \arg\min_\beta \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 or k-means cluster assignment. Typed this way, it is \arg followed by \min, so in display math the subscript centers under min rather than under the whole phrase. For a centered subscript, use \operatorname*{arg\,min} or declare a starred operator in the preamble. Some authors write argmin as one word without a space; the thin space in arg\,min follows the most common style. Remember the result may be a set if minimizers are not unique.

\\arg\\max_{\\theta}.meaning: Argmax with the optimization variable theta in the subscript: the parameter value maximizing an objective.
\\arg\\max_{\\theta}.usage: This form names the variable being optimized, the standard way to write maximum likelihood, \hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log p(x_i|\theta), and MAP estimation. Because the subscript attaches only to \max, in display mode theta sits below max, not centered under the full arg max. Replacing it with \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} or a declared \argmax gives a centered placement and is what most journals expect. In inline math the subscript appears to the right either way. You can also list constraints in the subscript, such as \theta \in \Theta, using \substack for multiple lines.

\\arg\\min_{\\theta}.meaning: Argmin over theta: the parameter value that minimizes a loss or objective function.
\\arg\\min_{\\theta}.usage: This is how empirical risk minimization is usually written: \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i). In display style the subscript goes under min only, which looks slightly off-center; \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta} fixes that and keeps spacing consistent. If you write it often, a preamble macro saves typing and guarantees identical output. Regularized objectives commonly add a penalty term, as in ridge or lasso. When the minimizer is unique, the equals sign is fine; otherwise, \in is the more precise relation because argmin returns a set.

\\text{softmax}.meaning: Softmax function name: maps a vector of logits to a probability distribution by exponentiating and normalizing.
\\text{softmax}.usage: Softmax is defined componentwise as \text{softmax}(z)_i = e^{z_i} / \sum_j e^{z_j}, and it closes nearly every classifier and the attention mechanism, where \text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V. Because \text{} uses the surrounding text font, it turns italic inside theorem or emphasis environments. \operatorname{softmax} is usually the better choice: it is always upright and adds operator spacing before the parenthesis, just like \sin. A temperature parameter is written as \text{softmax}(z/T). Use \left( \right) when the argument contains a fraction. In code-heavy papers, say which axis softmax normalizes over, such as the class dimension.

\\text{ReLU}.meaning: Name of the rectified linear unit activation, which outputs max(0, x) and zeroes negative inputs.
\\text{ReLU}.usage: ReLU is defined as \text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x), with derivative 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative ones. It is the default hidden-layer activation in modern networks; variants include Leaky ReLU, \max(\alpha x, x), and GELU. Writing \text{ReLU} works, but it follows the surrounding text style, so in an italic environment it slants; \operatorname{ReLU} or \mathrm{ReLU} stays upright and \operatorname also handles spacing before the argument. When applied to a vector, state that it acts elementwise, as in \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}).

\\nabla_{\\theta} \\mathcal{L}.meaning: Gradient of the loss L with respect to the parameters theta: the vector of partial derivatives used in training.
\\nabla_{\\theta} \\mathcal{L}.usage:
This is the quantity backpropagation computes, and it drives the gradient descent update 	heta \leftarrow 	heta - \eta 
abla_	heta \mathcal{L}. The subscript on 
abla names which variables you differentiate with respect to, which matters when the loss depends on both parameters and inputs, for example 
abla_x \mathcal{L} in adversarial attacks. \mathcal gives the script L and supports uppercase letters only. In inline text, the subscript sits to the lower right of the nabla, which is standard. For stochastic estimates, a hat helps: \hat{
abla}_	heta \mathcal{L} or 	ilde{g}.

\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial.meaning: Partial derivative of the loss L with respect to a parameter theta, the per-parameter sensitivity of the loss.
\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial.usage: This fraction is the scalar building block of backpropagation; the chain rule becomes \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a} \frac{\partial a}{\partial w}. Use \partial, the curly d, for partial derivatives and a plain d for total derivatives. In running text, \frac shrinks to fit, which is often hard to read; \tfrac, the slash form \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta, or a \dfrac in display can work better. For repeated use, a macro or the physics-style \pdv command keeps typing short. When theta is a vector, many authors switch to \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} instead.

\\theta^*.meaning: Theta with a star superscript: the optimal parameter value, typically the minimizer of a loss.
\\theta^*.usage: A starred symbol marks the optimum, as in \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta), and convergence results bound \|\theta_t - \theta^*\|. Typing ^* raises an asterisk in superscript size. Alternatives are ^\ast, which is identical, and ^\star, which gives a five-pointed star some authors prefer because the asterisk can be confused with a conjugate or adjoint. Distinguish it from \hat{\theta}, which conventionally denotes an estimate from data rather than the true optimum. If theta also carries a subscript, either order works, but \theta^*_t and \theta_t^* render the same.

\\mathbf{W}.meaning: Bold upright W, the conventional notation for a weight matrix in a neural network layer.
\\mathbf{W}.usage: Bold capitals denote matrices and bold lowercase letters denote vectors, so a dense layer is \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}, with layer-specific weights written \mathbf{W}^{(l)} or \mathbf{W}_l. \mathbf produces upright bold Latin letters; it does not bold Greek letters or most symbols, so use \boldsymbol or \bm for \boldsymbol{\Sigma} or a bold \theta. Many deep learning papers drop the bold entirely and write W; choose one convention and keep it throughout. The transpose is usually \mathbf{W}^\top, which reads more cleanly than ^T.

\\mathbf{b}.meaning: Bold lowercase b, the usual notation for a bias vector added after a linear transformation.
\\mathbf{b}.usage: The bias shifts each neuron's pre-activation, as in \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}, and per-layer versions are written \mathbf{b}^{(l)}. Bold lowercase signals a column vector by convention. \mathbf gives upright bold; if you want bold italic vectors, as some physics journals do, use \boldsymbol{b} or \bm{b} instead. Be consistent about indexing: the i-th bias entry is b_i in plain italic, not bold, since it is a scalar. In linear models, the intercept is often written as b or w_0 rather than a bold vector.

H(p, q).meaning: Cross-entropy between a true distribution p and a model q: the expected code length when coding p with q.
H(p, q).usage: Cross-entropy is H(p, q) = -\sum_x p(x) \log q(x), and it is the classification loss: with one-hot labels it reduces to -\log q(y). It decomposes as H(p, q) = H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p \| q), which explains why minimizing it over q also minimizes KL divergence. Watch the notation clash: H(X, Y) with random variables usually means joint entropy, so some authors write H_\times(p, q) or \mathrm{CE}(p, q) for clarity. The comma has normal punctuation spacing, so no manual adjustment is needed.
H(p, q).example: H(p, q) = -\sum_{x} p(x) \log q(x) = H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p \| q)

H(X).meaning: Shannon entropy of a random variable X: the average uncertainty, or information content, of its outcomes.
H(X).usage: Entropy is H(X) = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x), measured in bits with \log_2 and in nats with \ln. It is maximized by the uniform distribution, where H(X) = \log |\mathcal{X}|, and it appears in decision tree splitting via information gain and in maximum-entropy RL. Related quantities share the letter: conditional entropy H(Y|X), joint entropy H(X, Y), and differential entropy h(X) for continuous variables, usually in lowercase. Some papers write \mathbb{H}[X] to avoid confusion with a Hessian H or a hypothesis class.

I(X; Y).meaning: Mutual information between X and Y: how much knowing one random variable reduces uncertainty about the other.
I(X; Y).usage: Mutual information is I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D_{\text{KL}}(p(x,y) \| p(x)p(y)), and it is zero exactly when X and Y are independent. The semicolon is conventional and separates the two arguments, which may themselves be lists, as in I(X_1, X_2; Y); a comma would be ambiguous. TeX treats ; as punctuation and adds a thin space after it automatically. Conditional mutual information is written I(X; Y \mid Z). It underlies the information bottleneck, InfoNCE contrastive losses, and feature selection.

\\log p(x | \\theta).meaning: Log-likelihood of data x under parameters theta, the quantity maximized in maximum likelihood estimation.
\\log p(x | \\theta).usage: Taking logs turns products of independent likelihoods into sums, \log \prod_i p(x_i|\theta) = \sum_i \log p(x_i|\theta), which is easier to differentiate and numerically stable. Its negative is the familiar NLL loss. A typographic tip: a bare | is an ordinary symbol, so it gets no space on either side; \mid is a relation and adds balanced spacing, giving p(x \mid \theta). Some authors use a semicolon, p(x; \theta), to signal that theta is a fixed parameter rather than a random variable being conditioned on, which is the frequentist reading.

p(x).meaning: Probability (density or mass) of x under a distribution p, the basic notation for a distribution in ML.
p(x).usage: Lowercase p(x) denotes a density or mass function, while uppercase P(X = x) or \Pr is often reserved for probabilities of events. Machine learning overloads p freely, letting the argument decide which distribution is meant, as in p(x) versus p(z); when this gets confusing, add subscripts like p_\theta(x) or p_{\text{data}}(x). Normalization requires \sum_x p(x) = 1 or \int p(x)\,dx = 1, with a thin space \, before dx. Sampling is written x \sim p(x), using \sim.

p(y | x).meaning: Conditional probability of y given x, such as a classifier's predicted label distribution for an input.
p(y | x).usage: Discriminative models learn p(y | x) directly, while generative models learn p(x | y) and p(y) and apply Bayes' rule, p(y|x) = p(x|y)p(y)/p(x). The bare vertical bar typed as | is an ordinary character and gets no space around it; \mid is a relation and yields p(y \mid x), which reads better and is what most style guides recommend. For a tall conditioning expression, \middle| between \left( and \right) scales the bar with the parentheses. Subscripts like p_\theta(y \mid x) indicate the model's parameters.

\\sum_{c=1}^{C}.meaning: Summation over classes c from 1 to C, as used in multi-class losses and probability normalization.
\\sum_{c=1}^{C}.usage: Sums over classes appear in the categorical cross-entropy, -\sum_{c=1}^{C} y_c \log \hat{y}_c, and in the softmax denominator. In display math the limits go above and below the large sigma; inline they sit to the right in smaller type, which saves line height. Force the display placement inline with \sum\limits, or the reverse with \nolimits. Using C for the number of classes and c for the index is a common convention; just do not reuse C for a cost or constant in the same equation. The symbol \Sigma is a Greek letter and should not replace \sum.

\\prod_{i=1}^{N}.meaning: Product over samples i from 1 to N, typically the likelihood of an i.i.d. dataset.
\\prod_{i=1}^{N}.usage: For independent samples, the likelihood factorizes as \prod_{i=1}^{N} p(x_i \mid \theta), and taking the log converts it into a sum. \prod is the big-operator capital pi, sized for display; do not substitute \Pi, the Greek letter, which stays small and has no limits.
