Each summed index must appear exactly once up and once down; an index appearing three times signals an error. Free indices must match on both sides of an equation, as in v^i = T^i_j u^j. When the convention might be unfamiliar to readers, state it once and give the explicit \sum form in the first equation.

A \\otimes B.meaning: Tensor product of A and B, combining two tensors or vector spaces into one of higher rank or dimension.
A \\otimes B.usage: For vector spaces, \dim(V \otimes W) = \dim V \cdot \dim W, and for tensors the components multiply, (A \otimes B)^{ij} = A^i B^j. For matrices the same symbol denotes the Kronecker product, a block matrix with entries a_{ij}B. Quantum mechanics uses it for composite systems, |\psi\rangle \otimes |\phi\rangle. \otimes is a binary operator with automatic spacing; for a product over an index set use the large operator \bigotimes_{i=1}^n V_i, and for repeated factors V^{\otimes k}.

T^i_i.meaning: Contraction of a mixed tensor: summing over a repeated upper and lower index, which gives its trace.
T^i_i.usage: Setting an upper index equal to a lower one and summing removes both, lowering the rank by two; for a (1,1) tensor the result T^i_i = \operatorname{tr} T is a scalar. The Ricci tensor is a contraction of the Riemann tensor, and scalar curvature contracts again with the metric, R = g^{ij}R_{ij}. Only an upper index may be contracted with a lower one; contracting two lower indices requires the metric. Write \operatorname{tr} rather than plain tr so the trace is upright with operator spacing.

v_i = g_{ij} v^j.meaning: Index lowering: the metric converts a vector's contravariant components v^j into covariant components v_i.
v_i = g_{ij} v^j.usage: This is the flat musical isomorphism, often written v^\flat, identifying vectors with covectors. In Euclidean space with Cartesian coordinates g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}, so lowering changes nothing numerically; in Minkowski space with signature (-,+,+,+) it flips the sign of the time component. The free index i must match on both sides while j is summed. For a full tensor, lower each index separately, T_{ij} = g_{ik} T^k{}_j, keeping track of slot order. The \flat command used for v^\flat is the music flat sign, available in standard math mode.
v_i = g_{ij} v^j.example: v_i = g_{ij} v^j,\quad v^\flat = v_i\, dx^i

v^i = g^{ij} v_j.meaning: Index raising: the inverse metric turns covariant components v_j back into contravariant components v^i.
v^i = g^{ij} v_j.usage: Raising is the sharp musical isomorphism, \alpha^\sharp, and it is how the gradient vector is built from the differential: (\operatorname{grad} f)^i = g^{ij}\partial_j f. Raising then lowering returns the original components because g^{ij} g_{jk} = \delta^i_k. In relativity, p^\mu = g^{\mu\nu} p_\nu converts a four-momentum covector to a vector. Write the inverse metric with upper indices, never as g^{-1}_{ij}, which suggests the wrong index placement. The \sharp command gives the matching sharp sign, and for a diagonal metric only the j = i term survives.

\\partial_i.meaning: Shorthand for the partial derivative with respect to the coordinate x^i, also used for the coordinate basis vectors.
\\partial_i.usage: Writing \partial_i f instead of \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i} keeps index-heavy formulas compact, and in geometry \partial_i also denotes the basis vector field \partial/\partial x^i. Relativity uses \partial_\mu over spacetime, with the d'Alembertian \partial_\mu\partial^\mu. Partial derivatives of tensor components are not tensors in curved coordinates; replace \partial_i with \nabla_i to fix that. A comma subscript, f_{,i}, is the traditional equivalent. Use \partial, not d or \delta, for partial derivatives. Partial derivatives commute, \partial_i\partial_j = \partial_j\partial_i, which is why coordinate fields have zero Lie bracket.

\\nabla_i.meaning: Covariant derivative along the i-th coordinate direction, the tensorial replacement for the partial derivative \partial_i.
\\nabla_i.usage:
On a vector it adds a Christoffel correction, 
abla_i v^j = \partial_i v^j + \Gamma^j_{ik} v^k, and on a covector the sign flips, 
abla_i w_j = \partial_i w_j - \Gamma^k_{ij} w_k. The traditional semicolon notation writes v^j{}_{;i} for the same thing. Metric compatibility means 
abla_k g_{ij} = 0, so indices can be raised and lowered through 
abla. Covariant derivatives generally do not commute; their commutator on a vector gives the Riemann tensor. Relativity texts write the same operator as 
abla_\mu.

T_{(ij)}.meaning: Symmetric part of a tensor over the indices i and j, written with round brackets around the index pair.
T_{(ij)}.usage: For two indices T_{(ij)} = \tfrac12(T_{ij} + T_{ji}), and over n indices the sum runs over all permutations divided by n!. Bracket notation is standard in general relativity, for example the Killing equation \nabla_{(i}\xi_{j)} = 0. To exclude an index from the symmetrization, set it off with vertical bars, as in T_{(i|j|k)}. Parentheses inside a subscript are ordinary characters, so no special command is needed; just mind that brackets can open and close in different subscripts.

T_{[ij]}.meaning: Antisymmetric part of a tensor over i and j, written with square brackets around the indices.
T_{[ij]}.usage: For two indices T_{[ij]} = \tfrac12(T_{ij} - T_{ji}), and in general it is the signed sum over permutations divided by n!. Any two-index tensor splits as T_{ij} = T_{(ij)} + T_{[ij]}. The first Bianchi identity reads R_{i[jkl]} = 0, and the electromagnetic field tensor satisfies \partial_{[\mu}F_{\nu\lambda]} = 0. Some authors drop the 1/n! factor, so state your normalization. Square brackets in a subscript are plain characters, with no need for \lbrack. Totally antisymmetric covariant tensors correspond to differential forms.

(p, q).meaning: Type of a tensor: p contravariant (upper) and q covariant (lower) indices, sometimes loosely called its rank.
(p, q).usage: A (p, q) tensor is an element of V^{\otimes p} \otimes (V^*)^{\otimes q}, so a vector is (1, 0), a covector (0, 1), a linear map (1, 1) and a metric (0, 2). Terminology varies: some books call p + q the rank or order and reserve type for the pair. Contraction maps type (p, q) to (p-1, q-1). In LaTeX the pair is just parentheses with a comma; a thin space after the comma is automatic in math mode, so do not add extra spacing.

e_i.meaning: Basis vectors of a vector space or tangent space, indexed with a lower index so components carry upper ones.
e_i.usage: A vector is expanded as v = v^i e_i, pairing the lower index on the basis with the upper index on the components. In geometry the coordinate basis is e_i = \partial_i, and in an orthonormal frame g(e_i, e_j) = \delta_{ij}. Physics and engineering often write bold \mathbf{e}_i or hats \hat{e}_i, and use \mathbf{e}_x, \mathbf{e}_y for Cartesian directions. Keep the index low; writing e^i for basis vectors conflicts with the dual basis convention. Under a change of basis e'_i = A^j{}_i e_j, the components transform with the inverse matrix.

e^i.meaning: Dual basis covectors, defined by e^i(e_j) = \delta^i_j, used to extract components of a vector.
e^i.usage: Applying e^i to a vector picks out its i-th component, e^i(v) = v^i, and covectors expand as \alpha = \alpha_i e^i. For coordinates the dual basis is e^i = dx^i, and in Cartan's method the orthonormal coframe e^a gives the metric as g = \delta_{ab}\, e^a \otimes e^b. Because the index is a superscript, e^i can be misread as a power of e; if there is any risk, say so or use \theta^i, a common alternative for coframes.

T'^{ij} = \\Lambda^i_k \\Lambda^j_l T^{k.meaning: Transformation law for a rank-2 contravariant tensor: each upper index picks up one factor of the transformation matrix.
T'^{ij} = \\Lambda^i_k \\Lambda^j_l T^{k.usage: Here \Lambda^i_k is the transformation matrix, a Lorentz transformation in special relativity or the Jacobian \partial x'^i/\partial x^k in general, and the primed components live in the new frame. A tensor is defined by obeying this law, and lower indices transform with the inverse matrix instead. LaTeX merges the prime and superscript in T'^{ij}, so no braces are needed around the prime. Stagger indices as \Lambda^i{}_k when the matrix is not symmetric, so readers know which slot is the row.

\\Diamond.meaning: Possibility operator: \Diamond p reads "possibly p", true at a world if p holds in some accessible world.
\\Diamond.usage: It is the dual of necessity, \Diamond p \leftrightarrow \neg\Box\neg p, and in the system T we have p \to \Diamond p. Temporal logic reads it as "eventually" and dynamic logic writes \langle a \rangle p for the same idea. \Diamond is a large ordinary symbol; \diamond is a small binary operator and \lozenge a narrow lozenge, so do not swap them. TeX treats \Diamond as an ordinary symbol, so \Diamond p sets with no gap; add \, only if your house style wants space.

\\neg\\Box.meaning: Negated necessity: \neg\Box p says p is not necessary, which is equivalent to \Diamond\neg p.
\\neg\\Box.usage:
The duality 
eg\Box p \leftrightarrow \Diamond
eg p lets you push negations inward, the modal counterpart of De Morgan's laws for quantifiers. Semantically it holds at a world when some accessible world falsifies p. 
eg is an ordinary symbol, so 
eg\Box p sets tightly; write \lnot if you prefer, it is an alias. For a struck-through box there is no standard single command, and a combined glyph would confuse readers, so keep the two-symbol form. In epistemic readings, 
eg K_a p says the agent does not know p, which is weaker than knowing 
eg p.

\\neg\\Diamond.meaning: Negated possibility: \neg\Diamond p says p is impossible, equivalent to \Box\neg p.
\\neg\\Diamond.usage:
Impossibility is necessity of the negation, 
eg\Diamond p \leftrightarrow \Box
eg p, and it holds at a world when no accessible world satisfies p. A contradiction is impossible in every normal modal logic, 
eg\Diamond ot. Epistemic readings say an agent considers p ruled out. The command 
eg can be replaced by \lnot with identical output. Avoid improvising a slashed diamond with 
ot\Diamond, which is designed for relations and places the slash poorly. Moving the negation inside, \Diamond
eg p, means something different: p could fail.

\\Box(p \\to q).meaning: Necessitated implication: \Box(p \to q) says that in every accessible world, p implies q (strict implication).
\\Box(p \\to q).usage: This is the antecedent of the distribution axiom K, \Box(p \to q) \to (\Box p \to \Box q), which every normal modal logic includes. C. I. Lewis introduced strict implication as exactly this formula, so \Box(p \to q) is often read as p strictly implies q. \to and \rightarrow give the same arrow; \implies is a long arrow with extra space, better for meta-level reasoning than object-language connectives. The parentheses are required, since \Box binds tighter than \to. Necessitation lets you derive \Box(p \to q) from any theorem p \to q.

\\Diamond(p \\land q).meaning: Possible conjunction: \Diamond(p \land q) says there is an accessible world where p and q both hold.
\\Diamond(p \\land q).usage: It implies \Diamond p \land \Diamond q, but not conversely, since p and q may be possible in different worlds; this asymmetry is a standard exam point. Its dual is \Box(\neg p \lor \neg q). \land and \wedge render the same symbol; \land reads better in logic papers. Keep the parentheses, because \Diamond p \land q parses as (\Diamond p) \land q. In Kripke terms a single witness world must satisfy both conjuncts at once. For example, rain is possible and no rain is possible, yet rain and no rain together is not.

K_a p.meaning: Epistemic knowledge operator: K_a p reads "agent a knows that p".
K_a p.usage: Epistemic logic usually models knowledge with S5: the truth axiom K_a p \to p, positive introspection K_a p \to K_a K_a p, and negative introspection. Semantically K_a p holds when p is true in every world agent a cannot distinguish from the actual one. The dual \hat{K}_a p or M_a p means a considers p possible. Use an upright K, \mathsf{K}_a or \mathrm{K}_a, if italic K clashes with the logic named K, and write multi-letter agent names as \text{Alice} in the subscript.
K_a p.example: K_a p \to p,\quad K_a p \to K_a K_a p

B_a p.meaning: Belief operator: B_a p reads "agent a believes that p", which, unlike knowledge, may be false.
B_a p.usage: Doxastic logic typically uses KD45: consistency B_a p \to \neg B_a\neg p and both introspection axioms, but no truth axiom, so B_a p \to p fails. The knowledge-belief link K_a p \to B_a p is a common bridge principle. Belief revision papers write B_a(p \mid q) for conditional belief. As with K_a, consider an upright \mathsf{B} if italic B is used for something else, and do not confuse it with the box \Box, which is the generic necessity operator.

C_G p.meaning: Common knowledge in group G: everyone knows p, everyone knows that everyone knows p, and so on without end.
C_G p.usage: With E_G p meaning everyone in G knows p, common knowledge is the infinite conjunction E_G p \land E_G E_G p \land \cdots, and it satisfies the fixed-point axiom C_G p \leftrightarrow E_G(p \land C_G p). The muddy children and coordinated attack puzzles turn on the gap between E_G and C_G. Distributed knowledge is written D_G p. G is a set of agents, so write it as a capital italic letter and define it explicitly.

\\Box p.meaning: Temporal "always": \Box p says p holds now and at every future moment of the run.
\\Box p.usage:
In linear temporal logic, \Box is often written G (globally), and safety properties take the form \Box
eg\mathit{bad}. It is dual to eventually, \Box p \leftrightarrow 
eg\Diamond
eg p, and \Box\Diamond p expresses that p happens infinitely often. The same box is necessity in alethic modal logic, so state which reading applies. \Box and \square give near-identical squares; \Box is the conventional modal operator and spacing before p is not added automatically. CTL prefixes it with a path quantifier, as in AG p.

\\Diamond p.meaning: Temporal "eventually": \Diamond p says p holds at some present or future moment.
\\Diamond p.usage: Linear temporal logic also writes it F p (future), and it can be defined from until as \Diamond p \equiv \top\,\mathcal{U}\,p. Liveness properties are typically of this shape, such as \Box(\mathit{req} \to \Diamond\mathit{grant}). \Diamond\Box p means p eventually holds forever. In alethic modal logic the same diamond means "possibly", so state the temporal reading. Use \Diamond, not \diamond, which is a smaller binary operator. In computation tree logic it is prefixed by a path quantifier, as in AF p or EF p.

p \\mathcal{U} q.meaning: Until operator of temporal logic: p \mathcal{U} q holds if q eventually holds and p holds at every moment before that.
p \\mathcal{U} q.usage: Strong until requires q to occur; weak until p \mathcal{W} q also allows p forever. Eventually is derived as \Diamond q \equiv \top \mathcal{U} q. Written plainly, \mathcal{U} is an ordinary symbol, so p\mathcal{U}q sets with no space around the U; wrap it as p \mathbin{\mathcal{U}} q to get binary-operator spacing, or define \newcommand{\until}{\mathbin{\mathcal{U}}}. Many LTL papers use a roman U, \mathbin{\mathsf{U}}, instead of the calligraphic letter. Past-time logics add since, its mirror image looking backwards.

\\bigcirc p.meaning: Next-time operator of temporal logic: \bigcirc p says p holds in the immediately following state.
\\bigcirc p.usage: It is the only LTL operator tied to discrete time steps, and is also written X p. The expansion law p \mathcal{U} q \leftrightarrow q \lor (p \land \bigcirc(p \mathcal{U} q)) uses it to unfold until one step at a time. \bigcirc is a large circle sized like \Box and \Diamond, so it matches them visually; \circ is a small composition operator and is wrong here. Some papers prefer \mathsf{X} for clarity in plain-text-heavy specifications.

w R v.meaning: Accessibility relation in Kripke semantics: w R v means world v is accessible (considered possible) from world w.
w R v.usage: Properties of R match modal axioms: reflexive gives T (\Box p \to p), transitive gives 4 (\Box p \to \Box\Box p), and an equivalence relation gives S5. Truth of \Box p at w requires p at every v with wRv. Typed as w R v, TeX treats R as an ordinary letter and the spaces vanish, producing wRv; use w \mathrel{R} v for relation spacing, or define a macro. Some authors write R(w, v) or w \to v instead.
w R v.example: w \mathrel{R} v \land v \models p \implies w \models \Diamond p

\\mathcal{M}, w \\models p.meaning: Satisfaction in a Kripke model: formula p is true at world w of model \mathcal{M}.
\\mathcal{M}, w \\models p.usage: A Kripke model \mathcal{M} = (W, R, V) has worlds, an accessibility relation and a valuation, and truth is defined world by world, for instance \mathcal{M}, w \models \Box p iff p holds at all R-successors. \models is a relation with proper spacing; \vDash gives a similar double-turnstile glyph, and its negations are \not\models or \nvDash. Do not use \vdash, which means provability rather than truth. When the model is fixed, authors abbreviate to w \models p or w \Vdash p.

w.meaning: A possible world: a point in a Kripke frame at which formulas are evaluated as true or false.
w.usage: Worlds are drawn from a set W, and a frame is the pair (W, R) with an accessibility relation. Depending on the logic, a world can stand for a state of a program, a moment in time, or an epistemic alternative. Convention uses lowercase w, v, u for worlds and w_0 for the actual one. Because a bare italic w is so common, introduce it explicitly, and prefer w \in W in the first formula to anchor the reading.

O p.meaning: Deontic obligation: O p reads "it ought to be that p" or "p is obligatory".
O p.usage: Standard deontic logic is the normal modal logic KD, with axiom D, O p \to P p, saying obligations are consistent, while the truth axiom O p \to p deliberately fails. Contrary-to-duty puzzles such as Chisholm's paradox show its limits and motivate dyadic obligation O(p \mid q). In math mode O p sets as Op with no space, so write O\,p or use an upright \mathbf{O} or \mathsf{O} to keep it from reading as big-O notation.

P p.meaning: Deontic permission: P p reads "p is permitted", the dual of obligation.
P p.usage:
Permission is defined as P p \leftrightarrow 
eg O
eg p, and forbidden as F p \leftrightarrow O
eg p. In standard deontic logic every obligation is permitted, O p 	o P p. Free choice permission, where P(p \lor q) should imply P p, is a known puzzle that the standard system does not validate. An italic P collides with probability notation, so many authors use \mathsf{P} or \mathbf{P}; add \, after it to separate the operator from the formula.

s_i.meaning: Strategy of player i: a complete plan of action chosen from that player's strategy set S_i.
s_i.usage: In a normal-form game each player picks s_i \in S_i, and the combined choice is a profile s = (s_i, s_{-i}), where s_{-i} collects everyone else's strategies. In extensive-form games a pure strategy specifies an action at every information set, even ones never reached. The subscript names the player, so use superscripts or primes, s_i', s_i^*, for alternative strategies of the same player. Write s_{-i} with braces, since s_-i puts only the minus sign in the subscript.

S_i.meaning: Strategy set of player i: all pure strategies available to that player.
S_i.usage: The space of all profiles is the Cartesian product S = S_1 \times \cdots \times S_n = \prod_i S_i, and S_{-i} = \prod_{j \ne i} S_j. Finite S_i give matrix games; compact convex subsets of \mathbb{R}^k appear in Cournot competition and other continuous games. Mixed strategies live in \Delta(S_i). Keep strategy sets in capitals and strategies in lowercase. In cooperative games S often means a coalition instead, so avoid mixing both uses in one paper.
S_i.example: S = \prod_{i \in N} S_i,\quad S_{-i} = \prod_{j \neq i} S_j

s = (s_1, \\ldots, s_n).meaning: Strategy profile: a list containing one strategy for each of the n players in the game.
s = (s_1, \\ldots, s_n).usage: Payoffs are evaluated at full profiles, u_i(s), and deviation analysis splits a profile as (s_i, s_{-i}). \ldots places the dots on the baseline, correct between commas; \cdots centers them, suited to sums like s_1 + \cdots + s_n. With amsmath, plain \dots chooses automatically from context. Some texts write profiles in bold, \mathbf{s}, to distinguish them from a single player's strategy s_i. The profile in which i switches to s_i' while everyone else keeps their strategy is written (s_i', s_{-i}). The order of players fixes the tuple, so state it once.

u_i(s).meaning: Payoff (utility) function of player i, assigning a real number to every strategy profile s.
u_i(s).usage: Formally u_i: S \to \mathbb{R}, and a normal-form game is the triple (N, (S_i), (u_i)). Mixed strategies extend it by expectation, u_i(\sigma) = \sum_s \sigma(s)\, u_i(s). Unilateral deviations are written u_i(s_i', s_{-i}). Some fields use \pi_i or v_i for payoffs instead; in cooperative games v already denotes the characteristic function, so u_i is the safer choice there. Payoffs only need to be von Neumann-Morgenstern utilities, so positive affine transformations leave equilibria unchanged. For two players, payoffs are often shown as a bimatrix.

\\mathbb{E}[u_i].meaning: Expected payoff of player i, the probability-weighted average of u_i under mixed strategies or chance moves.
\\mathbb{E}[u_i].usage: With independent mixed strategies, \mathbb{E}_\sigma[u_i] = \sum_{s} \prod_j \sigma_j(s_j)\, u_i(s), the quantity players maximize at a mixed Nash equilibrium. Subscript the distribution, \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \sigma}[u_i(s)], when it is not obvious. Blackboard \mathbb{E} is one style; \operatorname{E} and \mathrm{E} give an upright E and are common in econometrics. For tall arguments, size the brackets with \left[ \right] or \bigl[ \bigr]. When nature moves, as in Bayesian games, the expectation also runs over types, \mathbb{E}_\theta[u_i(s(\theta), \theta)]. Keep square brackets for expectation and round ones for function arguments.

BR_i(s_{-i}).meaning: Best-response correspondence: the set of strategies that maximize player i's payoff against the others' strategies s_{-i}.
BR_i(s_{-i}).usage: It is defined as BR_i(s_{-i}) = \arg\max_{s_i \in S_i} u_i(s_i, s_{-i}), and a profile is a Nash equilibrium exactly when s_i^* \in BR_i(s^*_{-i}) for all i. It is set-valued in general, which is why Kakutani's fixed-point theorem, not Brouwer's, proves existence of mixed equilibria. Typed as BR_i, TeX sets B and R as two italic variables multiplied together; write \mathrm{BR}_i or \operatorname{BR}_i for upright letters. Use \operatorname*{arg\,max} for the maximizer. Pure best responses always exist in finite games.

s^* = (s_1^*, \\ldots, s_n^*).meaning: Nash equilibrium profile: no player can gain by unilaterally switching away from its strategy s_i^*.
s^* = (s_1^*, \\ldots, s_n^*).usage: The defining condition is u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \ge u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*) for every player i and every alternative s_i. Nash proved that every finite game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies, written \sigma^*. Equilibria need not be unique or efficient, as the prisoner's dilemma shows. The star is a superscript, so s_1^* and s^*_1 render identically; use ^* rather than ^\star, the latter being a five-pointed star. In a bimatrix game, a pure equilibrium is a cell where each player's payoff is maximal given the other's choice.
s^* = (s_1^*, \\ldots, s_n^*).example: u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \geq u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*) \quad \forall s_i \in S_i

\\sigma_i.meaning: Mixed strategy of player i: a probability distribution over that player's pure strategies.
\\sigma_i.usage: A mixed strategy is \sigma_i \in \Delta(S_i), with \sigma_i(s_i) the probability of playing s_i, and the support of an equilibrium strategy contains only best responses. In matching pennies the unique equilibrium has each player mix 1/2-1/2. Extensive-form games distinguish mixed strategies from behavior strategies, often written b_i or \beta_i. Do not confuse \sigma_i with a standard deviation in papers that also do statistics; \varsigma is a different, final-form sigma and not a substitute. Under perfect recall, Kuhn's theorem makes mixed and behavior strategies equivalent.

\\Delta(S_i).meaning: Set of probability distributions over S_i, which for a finite set is a probability simplex.
\\Delta(S_i).usage: If S_i has k elements, \Delta(S_i) is the (k-1)-dimensional simplex \{x \in \mathbb{R}^k : x_j \ge 0, \sum_j x_j = 1\}. Mixed strategies, beliefs and correlated equilibria all live in sets of this form. Uppercase \Delta is upright by default; \varDelta gives an italic version if your style requires it. Do not confuse it with \triangle, a geometric triangle, or with \nabla, the inverted symbol used for gradients. For two pure strategies it is just the interval [0, 1] of probabilities on the first one.

s_i^d.meaning: Dominant strategy of player i: one that is a best response no matter what the other players do.
s_i^d.usage: Strict dominance means u_i(s_i^d, s_{-i}) > u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) for every other s_i and every s_{-i}; in the prisoner's dilemma, defecting is strictly dominant. Truthful bidding in a second-price auction is weakly dominant. The superscript d is a label, not an index, so many authors set it upright, s_i^{\mathrm{d}}, to avoid reading it as a variable. Placing ^d before or after _i gives the same stacked output. When every player has a dominant strategy, the resulting profile is a dominant-strategy equilibrium and hence a Nash equilibrium.
s_i^d.example: u_i(s_i^d, s_{-i}) > u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) \quad \forall s_i \neq s_i^d

s_i \\prec s'_i.meaning: Dominance relation: s_i \prec s'_i says strategy s_i is dominated by s'_i, which does at least as well always.
s_i \\prec s'_i.usage: Strictly dominated strategies are never played by rational players, and iterated elimination of them is a standard solution procedure. \prec is a relation with proper spacing; for weak dominance use \preceq, and for the reverse direction \succ or \succeq. Some texts write the relation with player-indexed symbols such as \prec_i. s'_i and s_i' render the same because the prime merges with the subscript stack. Direction conventions vary, and some authors write s'_i \succ s_i for the same statement, so define it. A strategy dominated by a mixed strategy can also be eliminated.
s_i \\prec s'_i.example: s_i \prec s'_i \iff u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) < u_i(s'_i, s_{-i})\ \forall s_{-i}

s^{PO}.meaning: Pareto-optimal outcome: no other profile makes some player better off without making another worse off.
s^{PO}.usage: A profile s^{PO} is Pareto optimal if there is no s with u_i(s) \ge u_i(s^{PO}) for all i and strict inequality for some i. The prisoner's dilemma shows a Nash equilibrium that is not Pareto optimal. Written s^{PO}, TeX sets P and O as two italic variables; a label belongs in upright type, s^{\mathrm{PO}}, which also stops PO from reading as a product. The same tip applies to labels like s^{\mathrm{NE}}. Pareto optimality says nothing about fairness; it only rules out unambiguous improvements.

\\min_j \\max_i.meaning: Minimax operator: minimize over j the maximum over i, the worst-case value a minimizing player can guarantee.
\\min_j \\max_i.usage: In a zero-sum matrix game with payoff a_{ij} to the row player, \min_j \max_i a_{ij} is the column player's guarantee and \max_i \min_j a_{ij} the row player's; the latter never exceeds the former. Von Neumann's minimax theorem says the two coincide in mixed strategies. In display style the indices go underneath; inline they appear as subscripts, so add \limits if you want them below in text too. For more space between the operators insert \, or use \min_{j}\,\max_{i}.

u_1 + u_2 = 0.meaning: Zero-sum condition: the two players' payoffs always cancel, so one player's gain is exactly the other's loss.
u_1 + u_2 = 0.usage: Such a game is fully described by one matrix A, with u_1 = x^\top A y and u_2 = -x^\top A y for mixed strategies x and y. Constant-sum games, u_1 + u_2 = c, are strategically equivalent. The value v = \max_x \min_y x^\top A y can be computed by linear programming. For n players write \sum_{i} u_i(s) = 0 for all profiles s. Use x^\top or x^T for the transpose, consistently. Chess and heads-up poker are classic examples.

v(S).meaning: Characteristic function of a cooperative game: the total value a coalition S can secure by itself.
v(S).usage: A transferable-utility game is a pair (N, v) with v: 2^N \to \mathbb{R} and v(\emptyset) = 0. Superadditivity, v(S \cup T) \ge v(S) + v(T) for disjoint coalitions, makes forming the grand coalition worthwhile. The core is the set of allocations x with \sum_{i \in S} x_i \ge v(S) for every S. \emptyset gives a circle with a slash; \varnothing gives the rounder, more modern form. Here S is a coalition, not a strategy set, so state that explicitly.
v(S).example: v(S \cup T) \geq v(S) + v(T),\quad S \cap T = \emptyset

\\phi_i(v).meaning: Shapley value: player i's fair share of v(N), its average marginal contribution over all orderings.
\\phi_i(v).usage: The formula is \phi_i(v) = \sum_{S \subseteq N \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|S|!\,(n-|S|-1)!}{n!}\,(v(S \cup \{i\}) - v(S)). It is the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, the null player property and additivity. Machine learning uses it for feature attribution, as in SHAP. Choose between \phi and \varphi deliberately; they look quite different. Inside the set difference, escape braces as \{i\} so they print. Exact computation sums over all 2^{n-1} coalitions per player, so sampling approximations are common in practice. In a symmetric game every player receives v(N)/n.

SPE.meaning: Subgame perfect equilibrium: a Nash equilibrium whose restriction to every subgame is also a Nash equilibrium.
SPE.usage: Selten introduced the concept to rule out non-credible threats, and in finite games of perfect information backward induction finds the SPE. Typed as SPE in math mode, the three letters are italic variables multiplied together, with poor kerning; write \mathrm{SPE} or \text{SPE} in formulas, and plain text in prose. The related solution concepts are written the same way, \mathrm{NE}, \mathrm{PBE} for perfect Bayesian equilibrium. Every SPE is a Nash equilibrium, but not conversely. Sequential bargaining and repeated games rely heavily on it.

h.meaning: Information set in an extensive-form game: decision nodes a player cannot tell apart when it is their turn.
h.usage: Each information set h belongs to one player, offers the same actions A(h) at every node in it, and captures imperfect information such as hidden moves. Behavior strategies assign a distribution \sigma_i(h) \in \Delta(A(h)) to each of the player's information sets. Conventions differ: many texts use I or I_i for information sets and reserve h for histories, so define your notation. Perfect information means every h is a single node. Perfect recall requires that a player never forgets earlier moves or information.

a_i.meaning: Action of player i, a choice made at a single decision point, as opposed to a full strategy.
a_i.usage: In one-shot games actions and pure strategies coincide, so many texts write profiles as a = (a_i, a_{-i}) with a_i \in A_i. In extensive and repeated games, actions are local moves, while strategies map histories or information sets to actions. Learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning papers use a_i^t for the action at round t. Add primes for alternatives, a_i', and braces for the complement index, a_{-i}. In repeated games a history is a sequence of action profiles, h^t = (a^0, \ldots, a^{t-1}).
